ResponsesInList.Title: Grading a quiz
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello everyone, I've been using Moodle for several years and am also the administrator for my school. I wanted to know if there was a way to provide general feedback on a quiz and/or include the "real grade." Let me explain: a quiz might get, for example, 68.5% correct answers. If I set "Maximum grade 10," it translates to 6.85, but the grade I give the student could be 6.5 or 7- or 7, depending on the grading system. How can I display the real grade in the quiz, perhaps followed by a personal evaluation? Is there a trick or plugin? Thank you!

ResponsesInList.Title: Grading a quiz
ResponsesInList.Text: In the Aggregation for the gradebook, is it set to "natural"? That should allow you to get the result you are looking for I think. When you create the quiz, there is a section for general feedback. If you set Grade boundaries you can give general feedback based on the grade a student gets there.

ResponsesInList.Title: Discussion on International Virtual Exchange Project (IVEProject)
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello there Visvanath and thank you for your interest in the IVEProject. You have helped me so often over the years so of course I would be happy to give you any information you would like regarding this project which I am the lead coordinator of. Please let me know if you have any further questions! Yes, there are thousands (in the iteration happening now we have about 4,500 students from 11+ countries participating) of students in each 8-week project. Students continue after the official exchange finishes though. As John notes, teachers are in charge of their students and we ask them to keep tabs on what is happening. We have a number of tools that help students keep track of their own work and teachers to keep in touch with their own class's work too. So far it has been very rare that either students or teachers complain about not being able to keep track - indeed we get a lot of feedback on how easy it is. Teachers have total autonomy on how they incorporate the project into their courses, though we offer suggestions to them. The present Moodle forum interface is actually the result of a Moodle Association of Japan grant - made by the IVEProject team - that pushed for changes to the original Moodle forum such that, among other changes, a means of "starring" your own forum posts, and a slide button to follow ones you are interested in, have been added. We feel this has made following your own discussions, and ones you are interested in, much easier. We also have other custom modules/addons/reports in the IVEProject that assist students and teachers. These are mentioned and, to a certain degree, showcased in the Moodle academy webinar. If you were the kind soul that introduced teachers from the open university of Sri Lanka, thank you. Some signed up to participate but have yet to follow through with actual participation. Some teachers have "lurked" and had a look at what transpires but I get the feeling they are "feeling out" the project but are yet to commit their students - hopefully next year! Anyways, if you have any further questions, I am happy to answer them. Thank you Visvanath for all you do for the Moodle community - I for one think you and the others who put so much in are absolute legends. Thank you again.

ResponsesInList.Title: Discussion on International Virtual Exchange Project (IVEProject)
ResponsesInList.Text: We use a combination of these 3 blocks/reports Visvanath, https://github.com/ponlawat-w/moodle-block_forum_report https://github.com/ponlawat-w/moodle-block_forumdashboard https://github.com/ponlawat-w/moodle-availability_forummetric The forum report allows us to see a number of data points such as number of days the students are active in the forum, how often they view the forum, and many other metrics that can be exported into various spreadsheet format. An example is: The engagement level is particularly useful to see how "deep" students are engaging with their peers. If you look at the "threaded" form of a discussion, you can better understand engagement level. For example if you look at this discussion https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=94854&mode=2 you can see the likes of Lesli S and Martin D, for example, keeping replies going "deeper"- the deeper the discussion, the higher the max engagement level and the better the average Engagement. The forum dashboard shows students most of these metrics cleanly in their dashboard and we use the availability forum metric to limit access to new forums until students have participated actively in the initial forums. For example, they have to interact with at least 2 people from 2 different countries in the first forum before they can move on to the next activities / forums. We also use the "react forum" counts in that forum report which counts how many reactions were given and received. https://github.com/ponlawat-w/moodle-mod_reactforum Our forums are particularly engaging because of these features. Our programmer, Ponlawat, is phenomenal! Hope I have answered your questions here.

ResponsesInList.Title: Gapfill more than one answers
ResponsesInList.Text: Can we use gap fill for questions that have more than one answer, or do we have to use embedded answers? because many students answered with the exact same words and the same punctuation, but their answers were detected as wrong. chatgpt reccomendation : (is it true?) Conclusion and Definitive Solution You are currently using the "Gapfill" plugin. This plugin is simpler but does not have the advanced features to accept multiple alternative answers in one fill-in-the-blank. Changing the "Delimit characters" to {} will not solve the problem . The system will not suddenly understand the Cloze format like %100% or ~. The only solution is as explained before: You must create a completely new question from the Question Bank and when selecting the question type, choose the "Embedded Answers (Cloze)" type. This question type has the "engine" that you need to handle many alternative answers. example : Some scientists do not consider Proxima Centauri b to be similar to the Earth. [Proxima Centauri b is not considered to be similar to the Earth by some scientists.|Proxima Centauri b is not considered by some scientists to be similar to the Earth.]

ResponsesInList.Text: Question to ChatGPT If I ask you a question about a given Moodle topic, why would you not consult the official Moodle documentation even if it is the vey obvious place to look for an answer. Answer from ChatGPT Great question — and you're absolutely right that the official Moodle documentation is often the best place to look for accurate, up-to-date information about how Moodle works. Here's why I might not automatically consult it: ✅ 1. I Don’t Access the Web by Default Unless you explicitly ask for current or official documentation, I work primarily from my built-in training data, which includes a lot of general Moodle knowledge up to June 2024. I don’t automatically consult external sources (like Moodle Docs ) unless: You request fresh or version-specific info The answer could be outdated or unclear You specifically say something like “check the official docs” ✅ 2. Speed and Simplicity If I already have a well-supported, accurate answer in my training data (especially for common Moodle questions), I’ll usually give it straight away — no web lookup needed. This keeps things fast and avoids overcomplicating simple issues. ✅ 3. Some Documentation Pages Can Be Vague or Version-Dependent Sometimes Moodle Docs are: Too generic (e.g., features vary by plugin or hosting setup) Written in non-technical or overly technical terms Not updated for the latest Moodle versions (especially right after releases) So I sometimes paraphrase or clarify based on broader context and experience. 🔄 If You Want Me to Use the Official Docs: Just say something like: “Check the official Moodle documentation for this” “Give me the link to the Moodle Docs page for X” “Search the latest Moodle 4.4+ docs for…” And I’ll use the web tool to fetch the most accurate source right away.

Maybe it's the combination of things: I can be a sounding board when you need to articulate something that's still forming in your mind. I can help organize complexity when a problem feels overwhelming. I can offer perspective or information you might not have considered. ResponsesInList.Title: [4.5]Suspended student on course level can't see own work
ResponsesInList.Text: I believe you may be conflating suspension at the site level with suspension at the course level. At the site level, we suspend users for reasons such as non-payment of fees. This is not the same as course-level suspension. Course-level suspension occurs automatically when a student has defined start and end dates for a course. Once the end date has passed, the student is automatically marked as “suspended.” This makes sense, as it usually means the student has completed the course. If not, they can simply renew their enrolment to remain active. What I am firmly opposed to, however, is the practice of copying courses. This approach suggests that students must be divided into groups—by year, semester, or cohort—and must all progress at the same pace. Yet if each student is meant to learn at their own rhythm, the very notion of duplicating courses becomes questionable. Why and when would such duplication even be necessary? Moreover, copying courses creates unnecessary duplication of data, which in turn doubles the size of backups and inflates storage requirements. Ultimately, this also consumes more energy. While the sustainability of digital data is not yet high on most agendas, we know that more data inevitably means higher costs and greater environmental impact. Our priority is always the students. They are the ones studying, and they deserve to do so at their own pace. For this reason, we design our system around students, not around rigid course structures. For example, if we offer a course titled How to Plan a Journey to the Moon, students should be free to begin and complete it whenever they choose. Perhaps I am overstating the case, but creating multiple versions of the same course—How to Go to the Moon (2025–2026), Semester 1 2024, Week 38, and so on—strikes me as misguided. Instead, one single course should exist, containing all the material. Students may enter and leave as needed. Only when the curriculum itself undergoes a significant change should the old course be concluded and a new one created.

ResponsesInList.Title: Need Moodle advice: How to export grades that clearly distinguish 'Absent' (never accessed course) from 'Free' (completed course but no final exam) without manual Excel filtering"
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi everyone, I manage a training platform where participants receive one of four possible statuses: Approved – Passed the course and final exam. Failed – Completed the course but didn’t meet the passing requirements. Absent – Enrolled but never accessed the course. Free – Completed the course content but never took the final exam. The challenge comes when I download the grades and try to upload them to Moodle. Currently, I can’t find any way for Moodle (or my platform) to clearly separate Absent from Free in the exported grade file. Both categories end up mixed, and I have to run a time-consuming manual process: Filter the list of participants who never accessed the course. Compare them one by one in Excel with the “Duplicate Values” function to identify the correct category. This manual comparison works, but it’s inefficient, especially with large groups. My question: Is there any way in Moodle to export or process grades so that these four statuses appear clearly (Approved, Failed, Absent, Free) without having to manually filter and compare in Excel? Thanks in advance for any tips, plugins, or workflow suggestions!

ResponsesInList.Title: Need Moodle advice: How to export grades that clearly distinguish 'Absent' (never accessed course) from 'Free' (completed course but no final exam) without manual Excel filtering"
ResponsesInList.Text: As you imply, you don't have any problem between "Approved" and "Failed." Students get the grade that they get. Of course, you still need to set the "failed" grade. In my case, I use letter grades. Any "F" means that the student has failed. This is usually a final grade below 60%. For absent, you would still need to define it. What if a student does the first week assignments, then nothing else? You might want to define this as a grade below 5% or 10%. If the registrar need more information, you might have to look at the student's last access date, which you would see in the participants listing. That "free" category is the tricky one. What do you do with these "free" students? I don't use a free category like this. If a student doesn't take the final exam, they get a "0" for it, and it is weighted into their final grade. I don't try to get into the students' heads to figure out why they choose not to take the final. But I teach adults, and I expect adults to be responsible. I normally need to export grades into Excel to prepare them for uploading grades into the university's system. So if I had to do this, I would incorporate some Excel logic that says, "If final exam grade is null, then final grade = N/A (or something like that, whatever your system uses). I don't use Moodle's "course completion" features. I just use the grade book. My school wants me to document why a student "failed." For these students, I just send the Registrar a copy of the student's grade book and let the grade book speak for itself. Again, I don't try to get into the student's head.

ResponsesInList.Title: Number of Moodle sites vs Purchasing Power Parity per capita
ResponsesInList.Text: The chart above presents data from 181 countries. Most countries, regardless of their Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) per capita, have at least one Moodle site per 25,000 inhabitants. All countries with a PPP per cap. of $25,000 or more, except South Korea and Qatar, have at least one Moodle site per 100,000 inhabitants. Most countries with a PPP per cap. below $25,000 also have at least one Moodle site per 25,000 inhabitants, but there are several countries with fewer sites — in some cases, as low as one Moodle site per 2,000,000 inhabitants (20 times fewer than one per 100,000). Very few countries deviate from these trends. Notably, China has only one Moodle site per 3,300,000 inhabitants. In summary, the situation appears excellent for most countries, but special attention should be given to some countries with a PPP per cap. below $25,000 including China. References: Moodle.org - Registered Moodle sites Worldometer - Countries in the world by population (2025) Worldometer - GDP (PPP) per Capita (2023)

ResponsesInList.Title: Research paper: Effects of Feedback Providers’ Positive Emotional Tone and Gender on Learning From a Multimedia Lesson
ResponsesInList.Text: For anyone who might find this interesting or useful: Zhang, Y., Zhao, F., & Mayer, R. E. (2025). Effects of Feedback Providers’ Positive Emotional Tone and Gender on Learning From a Multimedia Lesson . Journal of Computer Assisted Learning , 41 (3), e70052. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcal.70052 Abstract Background and Objective : The positivity principle states that students learn better from instructors who display positive rather than negative or neutral emotions in multimedia lessons (Lawson et al. 2021a). This study extends this work by exploring the role of affective and social cues displayed by feedback providers, such as their emotional tone and gender, on multimedia learning. Method : In this between-subject study, 160 college students received a five-section video lesson on human vision, with two practice questions inserted after each section. After each question, students received explanatory feedback videos presented by either a male or female feedback provider who displayed either positive or neutral emotion through gesture and voice. Results : Students who received feedback from providers with a positive emotional tone rated the provider higher on perceived positive emotion, supportiveness and competence, as well as on their own feelings of positivity. However, the emotional tone of the feedback provider did not impact posttest scores. Additionally, female feedback providers were perceived to be more negative, less supportive and less competent than male feedback providers, but the gender of feedback providers had no effect on posttest scores. Conclusion : This study expands the positivity principle (Horovitz and Mayer 2021) and the cognitive-affective model of elearning (Lawson et al. 2021a) by showing that positive emotional cues from feedback providers enhance learning, similar to the impact of the instructor's emotional cues in presenting the main lesson. These findings highlight the broader role of positivity in creating engaging and supportive multimedia learning environments across contexts. Summary What is already known about this topic ○ Feedback is one of the most powerful influences on learning and achievement. ○ The instructor's emotions impact learners' learning experiences and outcomes. ○ The instructor's gender can affect how students perceive and evaluate instructors. What this paper adds ○ This paper examines how feedback providers' emotional tone and gender affect learning. ○ The emotional tone strongly influences students' emotions and connection with providers. ○ The gender type affects students' negative emotions and connections with providers. Implications for practice and/or policy ○ Positive instructors are viewed as more supportive and competent. ○ More strategies are required to address gender biases related to female instructors.* ○ In-person learning settings are more effective than unsupervised online settings. * This has already been shown in multiple studies to be an issue for organisations that attempt to evaluate teacher quality via student opinion polls. They discriminate strongly in depressingly predictable ways!

ResponsesInList.Title: Research paper: Effects of Feedback Providers’ Positive Emotional Tone and Gender on Learning From a Multimedia Lesson
ResponsesInList.Text: Re: "○ In-person learning settings are more effective than unsupervised online settings." - At least on the affective dimension, there's an interesting workaround for asynchronous feedback on students' work; The teacher makes a video screen recording of themselves reviewing the work & narrating their assessment of it as they go. Any notes that the teacher makes on the document during the recording can also be viewed by the student when the document is returned as part of the feedback, e.g. in the Assignment module. Students reported that they felt it was like having their teacher leaning over their shoulder & speaking to them while giving the formative assessment. Studies have also shown greater uptake of feedback, e.g. more likely to redraft & resubmit, & more engaged in subsequent assignments. However, few studies measured the difference in effect from screen recorded feedback vs traditional written feedback (Typical written corrective feedback has many issues & that's another important topic for discussion*). Those that did returned barely significant effects so, in short, great for engagement but little evidence of effects on grades. *I suspect that if combined with more evidence-informed (i.e. effective) formative assessment practices, there could be a measurable, perhaps even worthwhile, effect size on students' learning & therefore future academic performance.

ResponsesInList.Title: Seeking Guidance: Tracking Attendance in SCORM with Embedded Streaming Video (HLS) – Without Forcing User Actions
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Moodle Community, I’m reaching out for help regarding an issue I’ve encountered with tracking attendance for videos inside SCORM when using HLS or embed stream links from a third-party video hosting service. The Issue I’ve noticed that if I embed a video stream link (HLS or iframe) from an external video hosting service (e.g., Bunny.net, Vimeo, AWS S3) inside a SCORM package, Moodle does not track whether the learner actually watched the video. The SCORM package seems to have no way of detecting: •If the video was played •If the learner watched the full video •If they skipped or fast-forwarded Since the video is hosted externally and not inside the SCORM package itself, SCORM only tracks whether the module was opened, not the video completion. ResponsesInList.Title: Seeking Guidance: Tracking Attendance in SCORM with Embedded Streaming Video (HLS) – Without Forcing User Actions
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Makseem Mak! Tracking video completion inside a SCORM package with external streaming can be tricky, but nothing that a good technical adjustment can't solve! If you want to keep the video inside SCORM, the most effective solution is to create logic that listens to playback events from the video player. Some players allow triggering JavaScript events when the video starts, pauses, or ends. With this, you can send these events to SCORM using `SCORM 1.2` or `SCORM 2004 API` ( `setValue('cmi.core.lesson_status', 'completed')` ). This approach requires the video player to support this JavaScript communication. On the other hand, if you don’t need the video to be inside SCORM, I recommend using the SuperVideo plugin ( https://moodle.org/plugins/mod_supervideo ). It allows for more efficient control over student progress, ensuring that the video is watched before unlocking the next content. SuperVideo offers advanced options, such as mandatory full viewing, progress blocking, and integration with detailed reports within Moodle itself. This way, you keep the experience smooth without compromising LMS performance! If you need any more help, we’re here for that! 🚀 Eduardo Kraus Innovation and new products

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tracking the number of posts a user has in the forum
ResponsesInList.Text:
Would a report built with the Configurable reports block work? I found one in the Moodle Docs page 'Ad-hoc contributed reports' that I tweaked for your question. If you'd build this as a 'global report', your teachers would be able to see a course level report of number of posts in forums for each student. The SQL query would look something like this: 
```text
SELECT
CONCAT(u.firstname ,' ',u.lastname) AS Participant,

(SELECT COUNT( m.name ) AS COUNT FROM
prefix_course_modules AS cm
JOIN prefix_modules AS m ON cm.module = m.id
WHERE cm.course = %%COURSEID%% AND m.name LIKE '%forum%') AS forums,

COUNT(*) AS Posts

FROM prefix_forum_posts AS fp
JOIN prefix_forum_discussions AS fd ON fp.discussion = fd.id
JOIN prefix_forum AS f ON f.id = fd.forum
JOIN prefix_user AS u ON u.id = fp.userid

WHERE fp.userid =
(
select distinct prefix_user.id
from prefix_user
join prefix_role_assignments as ra on ra.userid = prefix_user.id
where ra.roleid = 5
and userid = fp.userid
limit 1
)

GROUP BY u.id
```

ResponsesInList.Title: Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning
ResponsesInList.Text: Interesting paper on a small study (n=710) of an unintended effect of a (fairly?) common practice with multiple choice questions, i.e. asking students to rate their confidence in each answer they select: Abstract Recent evidence has shown that eliciting confidence ratings can affect cognitive performance– a so-called reactivity effect. Several mechanisms have been proposed to account for reactivity, but currently there is only indirect evidence about why confidence ratings are reactive. Here, we explore the strategic changes in cognitive processes that occur in response to confidence ratings. Using a category learning paradigm that distinguishes between memorization and rule learning, in a large-sample (N = 710) pre-registered study, we show that eliciting confidence ratings caused a reduction in rule-based learning, even when compared to participants who made judgments of learning that asked them to reflect on their learning during the task as a whole. We argue that confidence ratings promote changes in the strategies participants adopt, driven by a more conservative approach that prioritizes performance over mastery and ultimately hinders rule-based learning and knowledge transfer. Ref: Double, K. S., Goldwater, M. B., & Birney, D. P. (2025). Reactivity to confidence ratings: Evidence of impaired rule-learning. Metacognition and Learning , 20 (1), 8. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09413-5

ResponsesInList.Title: Comparing the effects of ChatGPT and automated writing evaluation on students’ writing and ideal L2 writing self
ResponsesInList.Text:
Small #OpenAccess 11-week study reports that students receiving detailed, specific feedback on their writing, generated by ChatGPT, made better improvements than an established automated feedback system but the students felt worse about it. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09588221.2025.2454541?mi=5fx7dw#abstract Abstract The affordances of ChatGPT in language learning and teaching have gained
increasing traction. While studies began to investigate the potential
of ChatGPT as a feedback provider, little attention was given to
ChatGPT’s potential impact on students’ writing performance and the
ideal L2 writing self vis-à-vis the established automated writing
evaluation systems (AWE). To address these gaps, a sequential
explanatory mixed methods design was adopted. One hundred and fifty
second-year university students from three writing classes in a Chinese
public university were recruited and randomly divided into a ChatGPT
group, an AWE group, and a control group. After an eleven-week
intervention, the ANCOVA results showed that while the ChatGPT group
scored significantly higher than the AWE group and the control group in
post-writing performance as measured by their writing score, in terms of
students’ ideal L2 writing self, the ChatGPT group performed
significantly lower than the AWE group with a medium effect size.
Qualitative analysis of students’ reflection papers revealed students’
(over)reliance on the tool and the accompanying loss of creativity and
agency. Pedagogical implications as well as directions for future
research are also discussed.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Comparing the effects of ChatGPT and automated writing evaluation on students’ writing and ideal L2 writing self
ResponsesInList.Text: AFAIK , the whole issue of the efficacy of explicit form-focused directive & epistemic feedback is still contentious even though nobody has yet provided good evidence that it improves writing accuracy in subsequent writing, i.e. not just a redraft. See the many articles by John Truscott on this, e.g.Truscott, J. (2019). The Effectiveness of Error Correction: Why Do Meta-analytic Reviews Produce Such Different Answers? In Epoch making in English teaching and learning: A special monograph for celebration of ETA-ROC’s 25th anniversary (pp. 129–141). https://www.researchgate.net/publication/335106040_The_Effectiveness_of_Error_Correction_Why_Do_Meta-analytic_Reviews_Produce_Such_Different_Answers I very much doubt that the effects of explicit form-focused directive & epistemic feedback could account for an effect size of d .7, so I suspect that something else is happening between the students receiving what are essentially GPT LLM generated "recasts" of their compositions. Is it that they get to read & cast an analytical eye over high-quality versions of their previously expressed ideas & arguments & that it encourages linguistic uptake in some way? I'm very curious about how they got to those large effect sizes!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Groups in Groups (double post, sorry)
ResponsesInList.Text: Okay, let me focus on the "sections" first. I would create two "groups." You can name them whatever you want, such as Section A and Section B. Sometimes it's a little awkward when I do this because I think you create the Grouping first, then create the teams. I'll let you experiment on your own because this will give you good practice. One advantage of having these Teams is that you can create discussion forums for each team to share ideas, and the other teams can be excluded from seeing individual team discussions. So each team can have "private" discussions, yet you can see what they are discussing and even participate. I haven't used group "Assignments" (meaning submittals), but you will want to explore this on your own to better understand how it works. I also haven't used "group" quizzes. I don't know if this would work. Others here on Moodle.org might provide other approaches to your situation. I do want to warn you that Groups and Grouping are pretty powerful features in Moodle, perhaps an advanced topic, so make sure to practice with your bogus course and bogus students. Sometimes, you will have to log in as a specific student (not switching to a student as admin or teacher) to see how your Moodle really behaves. Many of Moodle's Activities and Resources provide group features. Here's a suggestion for your end-of-semester team presentations.  Use the Pecha Kucha method and limit each presentation to 6:40 minutes.  Use voice-on-PowerPoint, and have students upload their presentations.  Then create a discussion forum and require the other teams to view and comment on each teams presentation.  This is all done asynchronously, so give students a week or so for the final discussion.  I know I have overloaded you with this idea, but I have had great success with it.  I would even convert their voice-on-PowerPoint to 6:40-minute videos.

ResponsesInList.Text: Rick OK, if our idle thoughts are possibly to be converted into action, how about re-designing an Activity Completion report format? Please add improvements etc to my ideas below. (I should be marking the final set of students' submissions.) My experience is based solely on the simple course I wrote 20 years ago, with assessment only by quizzes (all including essay responses) and assignments. There are 4 teachers, including me. This course (with its Moodle processes) is one small part of my life, about 1 week/month mostly marking. Activity Completion report Starting with the existing good points: It is an efficient, compact, overview of students' activities. It is restricted to a single course (unlike say the Activity Report) Its coverage can be from the complete course cohort to a single student (unlike the Complete report or logs). What it doesn't do: It isn't logically consistent, even the title is misleading. Its definition of completion is idiosyncratic. It doesn't include the all of the significant or potential activities and resources. It doesn't include all user types, just students (e.g. not teachers, nor groups) 1. Data sources for filling the table and their assumptions. The definition(s) of completion needs to be as similar as possible across the data fields. Completion can have different meanings depending on where in the process the work unit has arrived. For graded work (quiz/ assignment etc): i. A student completes an activity when it is submitted. ii. A teacher completes an activity when marking, resulting in a grade being determined. iii. The grading of an activity is completed when added to the grade book. For non-graded work (resources: feedback files, background reading etc): In practice, the student completes by i. opening the link to the file/ website etc, ii. confirming it has been read. As I am responsible for the course management, I should like to have a handle on whether each of these completions is happening, at an individual student and/or activity level, and any pattern developing across the cohort. So all the potential Activity completion settings for each activity should be as similar as possible to each other. At the moment, it is impossible to ask that the Activity Completion report includes submitted but not marked quizzes, and it is impossible to ask that the Activity Completion report includes submitted AND marked assignments - separate from just submitted. 2. Activity Completion report page "Include : All activities and resources" I run a chemistry course. I want to ensure/check that the students at least open the link to the periodic table - it is one of the essential resources on the home page of the course. But this does not appear on the list of activities and resources. On the dropdown menu the only options are assignments and files (but not resources). Every url/heading on the home page, from introduction to course feedback, should be shown in the dropdown as available to be displayed, probably clustered into activity types (resources, assignments etc). This list should be inclusive with an option to opt out. I have just realised that the default for being displayed in the report is to set an activity completion option in each individual activity. Interestingly, that is not the default for assignments or feedback files connected to assignments. The default should be consistent. Applying that change to existing courses would be disruptive. Could the revised option/default be applied just to that view? It would be useful to have an option to look at individual teacher's performance, i.e. a comparison between 1i and 1ii. In the top line of options, it should be possible to choose (or order) by group or teacher. Occassionally, a teacher (mostly PhD students around the world) misses marking an activity, which the student may not notice for a week or two after the deadline, with all the bureaucratic fuss and loss of confidence to correct the delay. So it would be useful if there were two lines for each student, confirming a) submission, b) graded. Alternatively, the activity could be ticked red- submission, blue- graded. This could also apply to resources, red-when viewed, blue-confirmation of reading. The table heading links to the student profile and activity are useful. When the mouse hovers over an assignment entry, the time/date of the submission (1i completion) are given, but not for the grading (1iii completion). The former and latter information is available on the Complete Report, but only the former available on the All logs. The data available through Moodle is really good, but gathering the dots to create a picture is an exercise in pointillist painting. It has taken me years to discover the tool and now work out its underlying logic. A link to a help page from the Reports menu item ( explaining the purpose of each report) and from the Activity Completion page (explaining the data processing) might have shortened my learning curve. Thank you

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Creating entire course via text (with links to hidden but available activites)
ResponsesInList.Text: Instead of using stealth activities, you can choose 'Show one section per page' option in the course settings under course format. If you add activities to the sections, they will not appear on the course landing page, but the section descriptions are displayed on the main page. If you edit the names into section description for the activities in that section and turn on auto linking, you will have links to the activities. If students want more detail, they can click on the section link to see the actual activities in more detail.

ResponsesInList.Text:
I think this is well worth a read: The Educational Hazards of Generative AI provides a basic scientific overview of how large-language models
(LLMs) work and connects this knowledge to practical implications for
educators. This document is intended as a resource for teachers,
principals, school district administrators, parents, students,
policymakers, and anyone else thinking about using generative AI for
educational purposes. The
widespread commercial deployment of LLMs, also referred to as
"chatbots," has generated a tremendous amount of excitement, including
in education. Already, teachers and administrators report using chatbots
with increasing frequency. There is no shortage of hype about how LLMs
will "revolutionize" education. But although
there are promising use cases for LLMs in education, there are also
potential educational hazards involved with using them. Chatbots are
tools and, as with any tool, the failure to understand how they work may
result in using them for purposes they are not well-suited for. This
document highlights areas of concern where misconceptions about how LLMs
function may lead to ineffective or even harmful educational practices. The Educational Hazards of Generative AI is intended as an introductory overview and is far from comprehensive.
As a technology product, LLMs are continually being updated by the
companies that deploy them, and our scientific understanding of how they
function continues to evolve. That notwithstanding, and because
educators are the professionals who bear the ultimate responsibility for
instruction and student learning, we hope that this document is helpful
in making decisions about whether or how to use generative AI in
education today. This document
was co-authored by Benjamin Riley (Cognitive Resonance) and Paul Bruno
(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign). We are grateful to Amber
Willis, Blake Harvard, Dan Willingham, Dylan Kane, Efrat Furst, Geoff
Vaughan, Jane Rosenzweig, Jasmine Lane, Michael Pershan, Peter Greene,
Sarah Oberle, Sean Trott, and Tom Mullaney for providing feedback on
pre-publication drafts, along with other anonymous reviewers. Citation: Riley, B., & Bruno, P. (2024). Education hazards of generative AI . Cognitive Resonance. https://www.cognitiveresonance.net

A presentation by Tim Hunt as part of our series of workshop on "All about conducting on-line tests with Moodle" [1], 15 November 2023 (21 min) video1936226816.mp4 Abstract 1. As teachers, we cannot do the student's learning for them. All we can do is to provide scaffolding and feedback to help them. Online quizzes let you do both. 2. I want to talk about the two fundamentally different types of online questions: Selected response questions - like multiple choice - the student need only recognise the right answer in the possibilities given. Constructed response questions - like short-answer or formulas - the student must work out the answer without hints, but are harder to mark. 3. Different ways to use questions, like exams or practice. I think you covered this in a previous session, but I want to say it again. In this section, I will probably demonstrate our embedded question plugins. I will probably also highlight interactive with multiple tries behaviour. 4. Finally, I will talk a bit about academic integrity - which will start to move in the direction of what you will cover. Note that the above home for the video is temporary. Once the work finds a permanent home for the talk, we'll publish the new link here. Irrespective of that you are allowed, and encouraged, to download it and use it respecting the open license below. CC BY Attribute to Tim Hunt and EduNET@LEARN [1] https://edunet.learn.ac.lk/course/view.php?id=19 (Edited by Mary Cooch - original submission Friday, 22 December 2023, 1:20 AM)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Adding a search field within a course
ResponsesInList.Text: A pragmatic approach would be to use tagged activities and the Tags block, because these are features generally available in Moodle. ResponsesInList.Title: 'Not Set' - permissions
ResponsesInList.Text: What does 'not set' mean in permissions? Is that like a parent saying, 'I haven't decided yet if you have permission to do that?'

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: 'Not Set' - permissions
ResponsesInList.Text: If a permission is not set in a given role, a user with that role in a certain context , can't perform the related action... unless another role contains the same permission at a higher level context. I could spend the afternoon writing an essay on how all this works, but the Moodle Docs contain all the information you may need for this: https://docs.moodle.org/404/en/Permissions

ResponsesInList.Title: Reusing Course Sections Beyond Duplication?
ResponsesInList.Text: I've asked this question before in here , but I'm still curious if anyone has implemented a similar feature for course reuse, especially for Moodle teachers and admins. If so, and if it's not through course duplication, how did you go about reusing the sections ? I have a Moodle course titled " Database Design," which includes several sections delivered on different dates throughout the year. Each section can be delivered online or face-to-face, with content remaining largely the same but varying in delivery date and location. For example, the course " Database Design" consists of the following sections: Section 1: Prework Section 2: Database Training 1 Section 3: Self-Learning Pathway Section 4: Database Training 2 Each section is scheduled for various times and locations depending on the delivery date. For instance, Section 2 (Database Training 1) has multiple scheduled deliveries: one on July 1st in Lecture Theater 1 and another on August 5th in Lecture Theater 3. Students are assigned to specific deliveries based on their enrollment. Students A, B, and C are enrolled in the July 1st delivery. Students D, E, and F are enrolled in the August 1st delivery. Question: How can I configure Moodle to achieve the following? Title/Content Customization: In the Moodle user interface, display the title of Section 2 as "Database Training 1 on July 1st, Lecture Theater 1" for students enrolled in that delivery (Students A, B, and C). For students enrolled in the August 5th delivery, display the title as "Database Training 1 on August 5th, Lecture Theater 3" (Students D, E, and F). Although the content will be largely the same, there may be updates over time, so I want to enable teachers to make changes to the content as needed. Visibility Control: Ensure that each section is only visible to the students assigned to the corresponding delivery date. For example, the July 1st delivery section should be visible only to Students A, B, and C, while the August 5th delivery section should be visible only to Students D, E, and F. Important Constraints: I want to avoid duplicating or backup the entire course for each delivery. Rather than creating a new course for each delivery date, I prefer a solution where Moodle can automatically create an instance of each delivery within the existing course structure. The goal is to reuse the course without duplicating it, accommodating different dates, locations, and student groups efficiently. Eventually there will just be one course but multiple instances of sections with different dates and locations. No duplication or backup needed. Considerations: Although the course content for each section is generally consistent, it still could be updated over time, and the title and visibility could be different based on the delivery date and location. Utilize Moodle’s features to manage section visibility and customize titles based on user roles or groups, ensuring that students see only the content relevant to their enrolled session. Look for ways to automate the creation of instances for each delivery to streamline course management and avoid manual duplication. Currently course copy creates a duplication of the course: But I don't want to have a copy every time when I rerun the same course (with different students). It is very hard for admin to maintain.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Reusing Course Sections Beyond Duplication?
ResponsesInList.Text: My recommendation would be to explore the Groups and Groupings feature, combined with the separate and visible group modes. If you use these in conjunction with the restrict access rules, you’d have one and the same course with a delivery for each new group of participants. Tip: Create an Archived grouping , to move older student groups to, after they have completed their course.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Reusing Course Sections Beyond Duplication?
ResponsesInList.Text: During a given semester, I have dozens of learners all on differing learning plans with differing start/end and due dates with usually no more than half a dozen working on the same tasks at the same time. Groups and groupings is how we manage assignments with group (and sometimes user) overrides for dates. The filter codes plugin lets you customise text and titles. Learning materials are sometimes in a separate course connected via a meta enrolment, for example, a generic programming competency that is language agnostic, but learning materials for different languages in their own course. It works for us, but is a bit of a pain to set up. Having relative dates working for all actives and not just an experimental feature for some would go a long way. It may be enough for your use case?

The setup is that learners will have done an in-person training session; we then want them to do a formative self-directed reflection activity. They will be given prompts and info, and then have to type their reflective answers into text boxes. As some questions build on previous ones, we'd like users to be able to get instant feedback (a mix of text and diagrams) as they complete each question. Their answers won't be graded in any way, but as the end we ask them to revise them as necessary and copy them into their professional portfolio record (hosted off-site). The issue I'm having is that - as far as I can see - in a Moodle quiz there's no way to give instant feedback to an essay question. I could potentially split each section into its own quiz, so that feedback appears at the end of each section, but that feels clunky. As it's not graded, I could also try embedding (e.g.) H5P activities into a Book, but I can't find anything suitable that will preserve user text and allow me to give text and image feedback; I looked at H5P questionnaires, but they didn't seem to do everything I needed. The OU's embed questions plugin might be a solution here, but I would have to try and get the site admins to agree to install it. Alternately, if there's a way to add arbitrary input text boxes and click-to-reveal content to a book page, then I could just do that - or would it lose the input text on forward/back navigation? ResponsesInList.Title: Can I get your advice about choosing a course structure?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello, I am preparing a 14-hour course in Moodle. I have learned about the resource Book and wonder whether to use Pages/Quizes/Assignments or Books instead. Could anyone share their feedback on these two alternatives? With using Pages, Quizes, Glossary, and Assignments Currently, I have the following course outline that looks a bit like the following (I won't repeat the lessons, but there are 10 lessons). Module: Course introduction Page: Welcome to this course Page: Learning objectives Page: Most asked questions Glossary: Terms you will read about Module: Lesson 1: XXX Page: What you will learn in this lesson Page: Introduction to X Page: History of X Page: How to use in practice Quiz: Test your knowledge Assignment: Put X in practice (The lessons repeat 9 more times) Module: Course closing Page: What you have learned Page: Next steps Quiz: Final quiz Page: Course certificate With using Books The same course structure could look something like the following when using Books. Module: Course introduction Book: Chapter for (Welcome to this course; Learning objectives; Most asked questions) Glossary: Terms you will read about Module: Lesson 1: XXX Book: Chapter for (What you will learn in this lesson; Introduction to X; History of X; How to use in practice) Quiz: Test your knowledge Assignment: Put X in practice (The lessons repeat 9 more times) Module: Course closing Book: Chapter for (What you have learned; Next steps) Quiz: Final quiz Page: Course certificate Could anyone share their feedback about structuring courses, also when deciding between using the Book resource? How would you structure the courses? Thank you !

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Can I get your advice about choosing a course structure?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Jessica, I would recommend you to follow the guidelines provided by ABC Learning Design. Details are available in this introductory course . I think your plan may cover 3 of the 6 recommended types of activity. At the moment your course looks like it is lacking opportunities for the students to collaborate, do their own research and to discuss the material.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Can I get your advice about choosing a course structure?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi John, Thanks for your reply. I will have a look at the ABC Learning Design. More globally, would you recommend to use the Book resource, or multiple pages (Page resource) with Quizes and Assignment resources instead?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Can I get your advice about choosing a course structure?
ResponsesInList.Text: I think the choice between Book or Page resources will depend on the context and what your students might want to do with the material. In both cases, you will use the built-in moodle editor to add audio-visual elements or H5P exercises. But, for example, the book has an easy way for students to take the whole text and print it out. From the point of view of ABC learning design, "book" or "page" are both ways for students to ACQUIRE content... that is only one of the . six types of learning activity.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Can I get your advice about choosing a course structure?
ResponsesInList.Text: I'd say it depends on the nature of the intended learning outcomes (ILOs) & the tasks you use to achieve them. For example, why impose the additional overhead (& cognitive load) of online collaboration, as well as the assessment issues that such tasks raise, when the ILOs can be achieved more quickly & efficiently with quizzes & assignments? However, there may be advantages to including social elements, such as shared tasks on discussion forums, for example to reduce the perceived social distance among cohorts of learners, improve teacher presence, & to improve course completion rates. For a course that is intended to last 14 hours, I doubt that there'd be much time for effective "community building" & it's unlikely that the students would feel that it's worthwhile unless the course is part of a larger programme in which whole cohorts are studying together. Even for "Carnegie unit" courses (i.e. 12-14 weeks), community building tends to be brief, shallow, & not all that beneficial in terms of students acting as useful resources for each other, e.g. recommending useful resources & helping each other with academic issues. Just my 0.02€!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Can I get your advice about choosing a course structure?
ResponsesInList.Text: Books have the advantage of grouping related material in the single resource; it makes the overall course outline easier to grasp. The corollary is that if students have to go back and find information, if the books are large it might be harder to zero in. If you're using activity completion, individual pages will give you greater granularity in terms of seeing who has looked at what. This often isn't necessary. You can have your cake and eat it though-- using Activity names auto linking allows you to refer to linked pages (like an SOP or reference document) within a book, while having it as a separate resource as well.

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Muareen, I don't use Moodle Outcomes much. They're essentially a more general version of rubrics but are more flexible. I was referring to intended learning outcomes (ILOs) that curriculum developers typically define during the course design/development process & which may or may not be communicated to students, i.e. the ILOs should be implicit in the course assessments anyway. The main drawback of ILOs is that they're, by nature, quite abstract & difficult for students to interpret. When I have the choice, I prefer to use "success criteria," which are examples or models that demonstrate expected performance/products from students by the end of the course or instructional sequence. John Hattie has re-popularised success criteria in recent years.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Text Block, Page, Book or Something Else?
ResponsesInList.Text: As mentioned by Mary, Books are very useful. Before I retired from teaching, I had somewhere close to four-hundred written tutorials regarding Computer Applications, which were all based on the Moodle Book resource. I learned the hard way NOT to use Wiki's. Books take care of linking all the pages together, the wiki does not, which makes the Book an excellent option for presenting content. To keep from having to make multiple copies of a book throughout my site, I placed tutorials in a bunch of different courses based on the subject content. e.g. A course for spreadsheets, another course for presentations, etc. In an active course, I would just provide a link to the tutorials as needed, which would take the student to the course which was set to automatically enroll them when they clicked the link in their normal course. Just before I retired, I started using the Content Pages (iContent) activity. It allowed for creating what essentially looked like a slide presentation with a few additions. A user could enter public or private notes to each page. A user could enter doubts/questions on each page. The teacher could add essay, matching, multiple choice, or true/false questions to each page. Users could like and/or reply to other user notes allowing for interaction based on the subject matter. Note that iContent is listed as compatible only up to Moodle 3.8. However, I just recently got added as an additional maintainer and I am close to having a release for Moodle 4.0 thru 4.3. If you are interested, a stable, work-in-progress version is available at https://github.com/drachels/moodle-mod_icontent/tree/MOODLE_1071_STABLE .

ResponsesInList.Title: Rubrics with an n/a criterion
ResponsesInList.Text: I have the following situation: Students complete several practical clinical sessions each term. They are assessed in each session on a range of criteria. A student may be assessed on different criteria for different sessions. Also, in the same session, diffierent students may be being assessed on different criteria. I want to create a Moodle Assignment for each clinical session, and to use a rubric that contains all the possible criteria for grading. I want the instructor to be able to grade students in the session using the rubric, but only using the relevant criteria. However, Moodle expects an entry for every criterion in the rubric. If I enter a 0 for criteria that are not being assessed, this will affect the final grade for the student. So, ideally I'd like to be able to mark some criteria in the rubric as 'not applicable' when grading a student, so that I can ignore these and just grade the student based on what was assessed in the session. Is there a way to do this?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Rubrics with an n/a criterion
ResponsesInList.Text: Rubrics allow multiple outcomes for each criteria. If, for example you required 100% for a pass, you could have each criteria have criteria - Not Competent=0, Competent=1, N/A=1 But this won't work if you need a certain percentage to pass, since the number of criteria relevant to the particular assignment will affect the range of scores achievable. In general I think it work better if the rubric has all and only the criteria relevant to the assignment-- it's easier for the assessor too, since they don't need to know what is/isn't applicable to each assignment.

ResponsesInList.Text: This is just an advice question. I appreciate all thoughts on the pros and cons. I have a yearly event with lots of volunteers. We train these volunteers with a series of videos contained in a Moodle course. Love it, provides tracking, competition etc. Every year, some number of the videos get updated and need to be viewed again. Of course, there are a lot of volunteers that come back each year, but we always have those that are no longer active and those that are new. So the question is, would you create a new (duplicate) course with the still current and new videos, or would you just update the videos in the current course? If you suggest the latter, would you make a new activity for the new videos, or just update the video in the current activity and use the update student notification, to alert them of the new content? This brings up another question, which admittedly I have not researched. If I update the content of a video what happens to the "completion" flag? Does it get reset to off, is that something I get to do myself? Thanks for providing any thoughts you might have on this. Just working thru how I want to update the course content for this coming year and years ahead. Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Yearly course, same people. Update content or new course?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Ken - There are different ways to approach a solution, and I think this is how I would do it: I would set up a group in the course for each annual group of volunteers. I would make the videos available to the current group of volunteers using the restrict access feature . Once the current group has gone through the videos and the volunteering work has ended, I would download the activity completion report and any other relevant data for this group. Then I would remove access to the videos for this group. I would then update the videos and any other course materials -- whatever I have to do -- before the next group of volunteers signs up. I would give access to the updated videos to the new group. This group may have people who have volunteered previously, but that's not a problem. All volunteers in the current group can access only the up-to-date materials. With this approach, I wouldn't have to maintain multiple copies of videos on the course homepage, keeping the course layout light and manageable, and there's no risk of current volunteers accessing old videos. However, past volunteers won't have access to the videos they once saw. If you want past volunteers to have access to the old videos, you'll need to use a different process. Anyway, with groups and the restrict access feature, you can do a lot of creative things.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Sharing completed assignments with Tutors

ResponsesInList.Title: Scaffolding content: increasing complexity/detail of this information each user's visit
ResponsesInList.Text: I had an idea for scaffolding learning of technical 'content' that leverages some of the advantages of online learning platforms (such as Moodle). Basically, I am thinking that each time a student reads some written information it automatically updates (replaces) the information (next time they read this topic's information) to a higher level of complexity/detail/etc. Does anyone have any research evidence of something similar being more effective (than student-written notes of this content, for example) that they can point me to? For more practical context I'm an amateur 'dev' looking to develop content, centred around 'computational science'. I'm happy to dive into Moodle's source-code to achieve this.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Scaffolding content: increasing complexity/detail of this information each user's visit
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Nick. I understand what you are getting at but I don't think it's a good idea to automatically update (replace) the information to a higher level of complexity - what if they didn't understand it the first time? What if they want to go back later and read it again? What if they had to stop reading it half way through? I suppose you could *add* some extra text at a higher level of complexity under the original text if you wanted to - but then you might end up with very long amounts of information, rather than smaller 'chunks' people apparently prefer now. Also - Moodle's standard Restrict access and Activity completion features already allow teachers to release other materials based on completion of previous ones, as you will know. So a student could read some text, manually mark it complete when they feel they have digested it, and then it will open up automatically the information at a higher level of complexity. I think that's a more acceptable way of doing it. BUT.. I am neither a researcher nor a developer, so let's see what others think😉

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Scaffolding content: increasing complexity/detail of this information each user's visit
ResponsesInList.Text: I agree with Mary on this. Even on really interactive learning platforms teaching programming such as Codeacademy, students get the opportunity to scroll back to the beginning of their course, to see what they missed or want to review. And that's for good reasons: review, repeat, retry are crucial learning processes you'd want to facilitate when designing your learning materials. Recommendation from my side would be to do the following: 1 course with all materials for a described level (maybe beginner level 0 to level 11, intermediate level 11 to level 20, advanced level 21 to level 30, expert level 31 to level ...) Use the course sections to contain all materials and activities for a specific level, restricting access and hiding to subsequent levels based on completion of previous levels linearly Allow 'free browsing' mode for students to go through the materials in a more open world kind of approach.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Organize modules conveniently
ResponsesInList.Text: Perhaps this can be done by using Moodle's file system, but this is not how I do it. I prefer to use "web pages" outside of Moodle for these common pages. Then, in Moodle, I display these web pages using a " URL " resource. When I update content on one of these web pages, I don't need to do anything in Moodle. There are pros and cons to my methods, as with any method. But this has worked for me since 1998. One advantage is that these web pages are easy to reference anywhere. For example, I could easily share my Business Analytics syllabus .  And since this syllabus was created with a powerful web-creation tool, I can do more within it than Moodle provides.  Using a website for course content used to be supported by many schools back in the late 1990's.  Somehow, we have gotten away from that concept. I once gave a presentation about my method. It may help guide you to solving your problem. MoodleMoot2018 (Spain and Mountain), "Managing Course Content Using a “Personal Repository”

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Organize modules conveniently
ResponsesInList.Text: I do something similar to what Rick does, except I do it in Moodle. I create a tutorial/documentation/explanation category with specific courses, in which I enroll everyone. Since I manually enroll everyone via a CSV file, this is easy to do. I then use the specific courses to sort related subject matter in to appropriate courses. I initially thought about using Wiki's for all the explanation pages, but dropped that like a hot rock when I realized what a nightmare it was going to be to create and maintain all the links within individual wiki's, especially when wanting to add or delete information. I settled on using Books as it handles all the internal links to the various pages, automatically. All I had to do was in each actual course, 1, 2, 3, etc., was provide the initial link to the subject matter with an explanation of what was going on with the links. EDIT: Oh, forgot to mention, I also had Moodle bookmark capability setup, and taught them how to use it to keep track of where they were at at the end of each day. (I used to teach in a face-to-face computer lab.)

So, I restricted my alerts with "must be complete with a fail grade": However, learners are seeing the alert after they fail the first attempt. Is there any other way I could set this up? ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Alert after failing assignment twice
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Inês! As the Assignment activity doesn't have completion condition for 'All attempts completed', the only option I can come up with is: Assignment 1st round -> Completion with passing grade Assignment Resit -> Completion with passing grade, restrict access to only become available once 1st round is completed with a grade < passing grade Label for notification of failure to pass 1st round and resit --> Restrict access to become available once Resit is completed with a grade < passing grade This also separates your students' attempts into 1st rounds and resits and clarifies how these are distributed in your reports. I'd only allow multiple attempts in an Assignment if it has been set up to be truly formative in nature (oriented to providing feedback on learner progress).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Cheating
ResponsesInList.Text:
Taken broadly, say valid for the whole world, there are no universal answers. What you are looking for is perhaps, what applies your case. But then nobody here knows your case better than you! Here is what a participant from a university in South Easy Asia wrote in a workshop on on-line testing with Moodle. I am unable to elaborate, I'm just quoting: We are conducting both quizzes and paper based online exams for our undergraduates as their end semester examinations. Online Quizzes Each
batch of our faculty has about 700 students. Our students do the quizzes
inside our computer labs (divide into small groups) as well as doing at
homes (all at once). One of the major problems is exchanging answers
between them during the examination. To avoid that situation we do the followings 1. Create large question banks. 2. Create questions under different categories (to cover all sections ). Online Paper based Exams Students are divided into small groups (around 30) and assigned an invigilator for each group. Each group has a separate zoom link and students are required to switch on their cameras during the exam time period. The folder resource is used to upload the question paper and prevent access until a specified date and time. Each group has a separate assignment drop box to upload the softcopy of student's answer script.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Games in moodle for making learning fun
ResponsesInList.Text: I understand where you're coming from, looking for games to make learning fun... but the games in themselves don't make learning fun: it's the underlying mechanics of games that make them more foun to experience. But you could learn from how these games have been constructed and apply those lessons in your learning design, by incorporating: - provide scaffolding for your participants -> support their learning, and gradually decrease their need to rely on this support, as to increase their independence. - meaningful learning activities (there's a purpose to doing this, and this is clear to the participant) - adequate and timely feedback a participant can actually use to improve - failing an activity in itself is not an issue -> failing at something is an opportunity to receive feedback on how to improve - a good storyline makes doing the activities more appealing - create a flow channel (Flow: Psychology of Optimal Experience, Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi) -> provide a mix of activities with varying levels of difficulty, some harder, some easier to guide your participants to their learning objectives The activity modules in Moodle don't generally come with learning content, but provide some means to create those learning activities. If Level Up doesn't work: check your cron tasks

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What are some best practices for creating engaging online quizzes on Moodle
ResponsesInList.Text: First of all, write interesting, relevant questions! Next, use the setting "How questions behave: Ineractive with multiple tries". Also, consider building your quiz with a few variants of each question, picked at random, so if students want more practice, there is some benefit in attempting the quizzes again. https://docs.moodle.org/402/en/Effective_quiz_practices#Robust_testing_with_random_variants

ResponsesInList.Title: Advanced quiz attempt and question analysis
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi all, I've recently received a question from our faculty if we would be able to provide the same analysis tools for quiz attempts and questions as they have in dedicated platforms for eAssessment. So far, I've covered most of their questions, but there are a few things that  remain unclear or impossible: p-value This is supposed to represent the degree of difficulty of a question, and is calculated as the overall average score for any given question. Is that the same as the Facility index calculated in Moodle? Rit and Rir These are Pearson product moment correlation coefficient values, but somewhat different from the way Moodle uses that. Rit represents the result for a specific question in relation to the quiz result as a whole (including the specific question), Rir represents the result for a specific question in relation to the rest of the questions in the same quiz. This kind of sounds like the Discrimination Index calculation, but with a twist. a-value This represents the quality of each distractor expressed as a value between 0 and 1 (or a percentage) for how many of the participants selected that distractor in their quiz/question attempt. E.g. if a question has option B set as the only correct distractor of 4 options, and 38% of the participants selected it, the a-value for this distractor would be 0.38. The sum of the a-values for the other 3 distractors would be 1 - 0.38 = 0.62. Rat and Rar Similar to Rit and Rir, but used to analyse distractors in closed questions. These would return values for each distractor. This is an option I haven't yet found in Moodle. Most of this information can somehow be collected from the Moodle database , but I haven't found a tool to aggregate all these into a nice and user friendly report.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Advanced quiz attempt and question analysis
ResponsesInList.Text: Details of the calculations that Moodle uses are on https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Quiz_statistics_calculations and https://docs.moodle.org/dev/Quiz_statistics_calculations_in_practice . p-value sounds ilke Facility index to me. I am sceptical that there would be any practical difference in usefulness between Rit and Rir, and Moodles Decrimination index. a-value is not computed as such, but you can get it form the Response analysis and a bit of work.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Advanced quiz attempt and question analysis
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Tim, Thank you for confirming the bit about the p-value / Facility index. Strangely enough, we have people who struggle to see the relation between a 0.38 and 38 % value, which to me is exactly the same thing. They're also quite particular about the way these values are named: in their literature terminology from my original post is commonly used, whereas Moodle uses more 'user-friendly' labelling to know what a value represents. Some 'translation' from technical term to common sense description is then required. Other eAssessment platforms just stick to the technical terms, because that's what Assessment Specialists here are used to. I found the documentation you shared, and will forward this to my colleagues.

ResponsesInList.Text: When I saw the topic of your post, I immediately thought "this person is coming from Canvas." Yes, Canvas has a "syllabus" feature. However, this is Canvas' view of what a syllabus looks like to them (and maybe more like what I would call a table of contents). At my school, no instructor used this Canvas "syllabus" because it never match any "traditional" view of what a college syllabus should look like. Well, be that as it may, it's Canvas. No, Moodle doesn't have that kind of feature. In my case, I kind of do the #3 suggestion. However, my syllabus is in HTML, as a web page. My school always wanted syllabi to be MS Word files, but I argued that an HTML file was better for many reasons, so I went against the wave. Students never complained, either. Also, since it is a web page, I don't have to worry about how students will open it; it just appears on a new tab. ResponsesInList.Title: Setting a deadline for multiple activities
ResponsesInList.Text: My course has 4 monthly Parts, each of which has a deadline at the end of the month. Each Part has both quizzes and assignments ca.9 in each. The course runs 3 times a year. I should like to set the 4 separate deadlines for each Part at the start of each interation of the course.  E.g. for the course starting 12th January, deadlines for Parts 1, 2, 3, 4 at 12th February, 12th March, 12th April, 12th May, respectively, at midnight.  At the moment, I can do this only activity by activity.  It is currently not possible to define that submissions are reviewable after a quiz is closed until the quiz is first closed, i.e. after the deadline has passed. There are a couple (or more?) potential methods. Set up the "master" course with the separate deadlines for each Part after 1, 2, 3, 4 elapsed months from the starting date, which is chosen when the iteration is activated. Or less efficiently when the course has been made available to students, bulk edit the deadlines of each activity in a Part to the appropriate date and time. Are either of these possibilities available for Moodle 3.9?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Setting a deadline for multiple activities
ResponsesInList.Text: The "Subcourse" plugin can help you organize your course into separate Parts while managing deadlines more efficiently. With this plugin, you can create a "master" course for each Part, and then link them as subcourses in a main course. The deadlines for each Part can be managed individually within their respective "master" courses. Here's how to set it up: Install and enable the Subcourse plugin in your Moodle site if you haven't already. You can download it from the Moodle plugin directory: https://moodle.org/plugins/mod_subcourse Create a "master" course for each Part of your main course (4 courses in total). Set deadlines for activities within each "master" course. You can use either the "Restrict access" method or the "Dates report" method described in the previous answer to set deadlines more efficiently. Create your main course where students will enroll, and divide it into 4 sections corresponding to the 4 Parts. In each section of the main course, add a Subcourse activity and link it to the corresponding part Repeat step 5 for all 4 Parts. Now, when you start a new iteration of the course, you only need to update the deadlines in the respective "master" courses. The main course will automatically reflect these changes, as it pulls the content and deadlines from the linked subcourses. Note that the Subcourse plugin only helps in organizing the course structure and linking content and deadlines. It does not provide a direct way to set deadlines based on a variable starting date. You still need to manually update the deadlines in the "master" courses for each iteration. HTH

ResponsesInList.Title: Best course format when using Moodle for VILT
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi all, looking for a recommendation or opinions on the best course format for using Moodle to register learners for a Zoom VILT session. These are single compliance-type training sessions that learners take every couple of years. Previously this had been done in Cvent, but our LMS has been used (for well over a decade now) for a wide variety of asynchronous eLearning and video-based training, while instructor-led training, virtual or otherwise has been managed separately. It makes sense to move this into the LMS, but while there are a variety of ways I could accomplish this, I'd like opinions on people's experiences with what has worked "best" in these situations. I'm testing doing these each as a standalone lesson with links to the Zoom session and two related PDFs, though this is just me experimenting. I'm sure there are better options. I'm using the enrollment message to send the course information, as well as having the same info in the lesson page when they enroll. The targeted learners will receive the enrollment key via email from their supervisors, and though the key will work on any session, there is a limit of 30 per session. The intent is not to have the learners return to the LMS once enrolled, if not necessary. This is the only course most of them need to take, and it's semi-annual. There will be 20 sessions to choose from. I'm sure I could use the calendar in some way for this, and I would like to be able to generate an ICS for this. I'm currently using Moodle 3.11, and would like to avoid using a plugin for this. This LMS has existed in one form or another since 2007, and using plugins has been problematic when they cease to be supported.

ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Michael, I would suggest this course format - https://moodle.org/plugins/format_designer . Best, Vardaan

This Moodle instance has existed for a long time and I've had plugins I've had to stop using over the years when the cease being updated. The other challenge with plugins is that I'm always a Moodle version or two behind as plugins often can't be released quickly or regularly enough to keep up with Moodle releases. For example, I love using configurable reports plugin and have been using it since 2012, but it's currently at 3.11, so that's the version of Moodle we're currently at. I may have to stop using it entirely when I need to upgrade to 4.0. Perhaps I should have titled this, "the best non-plugin course format for VILT."

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: notification in course
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Lisa - Do you mean that an email notification doesn't go out when a student submits their work in an Assignment activity ? If you have enabled notifications in your Assignment activity settings but teachers are not getting notifications: 1. Have you set up outgoing email for your site ? 2. Have you checked that cron is working?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: notification in course
ResponsesInList.Text: In addition to Ravi's comments: Lesson (mod_lesson) doesn't provide other notifications than 'notify student of marked/graded submission in essay question'. There are no Lesson module notifications a teacher can set up other than maybe setting up an event monitoring rule (but I wouldn't recommend that). Assignment has a variety of notification settings, which include 'notify when work submitted' and 'notify when work submitted late'. For all things related to receiving notifications, the cron maintenance script should be up and running and an SMTP server should be set up. If you don't have direct access to those settings, please consult your Moodle's administrator. If both are working correctly, be sure that the mail server isn't treated as a source of spam mails and that there aren't any thresholds (max number of emails) getting in the way of processing the notifications.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Selecting the next block of tasks from several
ResponsesInList.Text: We've used the 3rd party groupselect plugin for this https://moodle.org/plugins/mod_groupselect -- create a group for each choice of final activity, and restrict the sections to members of that group, then let people choose their group in topic 2. Using core moodle you could probably create 3 choice activities , each with 1 choice of final topic. Set activity completion on the choice activities to trigger when a choice is made, and set restrict access on the choice to be available only when neither of the other 2 are marked completed.
