ResponsesInList.Title: Multiple group assignments with different roles in each: possible?
ResponsesInList.Text: I think the answer is no, unfortunately. Here's my use case: I have a course hundreds of people are taking every year, each for different reasons, usually because I or someone in my agency requires the completion. Usually the only groups are internal for me (or the people who requires those people to complete). For example: anyone who works on project A has to complete. Anyone certified in project B has to complete. Completers in Project A and Project B can work for the same school district, university or company, so you might be in Group A and Group B or just A or B. But things have changed. Now, some of our school districts are requiring all their staff to complete this course and would like a way to see their staff have completed outside of asking me (which is a rabbit hole I would also prefer to avoid). Easy, I add all of them to a new group (call it group C) and give someone non-editing teacher permission (tech director/superintendent, etc). Except sometimes that person also completes because they are a member of Group A or B. The new permission allows them to see everyone in their district group AND the other group(s) they are part of. Which is no bueno. Is there a way to assign a permission in the group not in the course? or a way to link the group to the permission? I think there isn't but I'm hoping someone has found a workaround. The only solution I can think of is to assign groupings (can you filter activities /completions by groupings?) but for this case, it would be super manual and I don't love that.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Multiple group assignments with different roles in each: possible?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hmm... interesting take, this one... You know every user in Moodle starts out as being an 'authenticated user' after logging in, and their role assignments normally only come into play once they're enrolled in a course (as a participant or instructor)? The double roles (manager at category or course level, while also being a participant) have a few challenges: the highest permission level determines what they see and are able to do (like altering results or checking for the correct answer in a quiz) generally, people forget to switch roles to the student/participant one before starting a course The only reason in your case for having a double role, is that some of those people should also be able to see a group level report after completing the course? The easiest way to get that bit done, would be to require them to use two accounts (e.g. john.student@email.example and john.supervisor@email.example). The latter user account would then be assigned the reporting role.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Multiple group assignments with different roles in each: possible?
ResponsesInList.Text: My non-editing don't have all group access but the issue is they are in a group for me to track (everyone who takes the course because of X) and a group so they can track their employees (because they require their staff to complete for totally different reasons). ResponsesInList.Title: how to assign random piece of info to students
ResponsesInList.Text: Case: For the practical exam, each students need to get assigned a random IP range to use in their virtual lab setup (I teach computer networking). In the exam instructions published on Moodle, it says "use the randomly assigned IP range to you". So now I wanted to create a quiz with just 1 random question of type "description". I created tons of these description questions, each with another IP range mentioned in it. But that is not working, questions of that type cannot be randomly included in a quiz. I tried a multiple choice question where the IP range is in the question, and where there is only 1 answer option (= "I understood, and will use this IP range"), but question type multiple choice requires at least two answers. I would prefer that student does not need to type or click anything as answer, since I do not need an answer from them. I just need a way to assign them a random piece of info that they need to use in their lab. I tried the essay question type, but also an answer IS required (either text or an attachment) I tried the Cloze question type without any answers, but that is also not accepted by Moodle. I do not have site admin rights to add new activities to our exam Moodle. Otherwise I could try to create groups (their names would be the different IP ranges) and assign students randomly to those groups and use the group choice activity to show them their assigned IP range. But that group choice activity is not present in out exam Moodle. Who has any suggestions to achieve what I am trying to do????

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: how to assign random piece of info to students
ResponsesInList.Text: So the IP range is just a bit of 'text' (e.g., 127.0.0.1) each user should see based on some randomisation? How about doing the following: Go to Participants > Groups and use the Auto-create groups feature to randomly create groups of 1 student each Create a new section in your course Add a Text and media zone (Label up to Moodle 4.0) that contains 1 IP address, until you have distributed al IP addresses Restrict each of these Text and media zones to only be available to 1 of the groups of one and set them to hidden otherwise It's still a lot of work, but it should be doable!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: how to assign random piece of info to students
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Joost, I had thought of that already, but with a very large group of students that is an awful lot of clicking to set up. It would then be easier to just hand each student a piece of paper with the IP range they should use for their exam when they enter the auditorium. I am of the opinion that a platform such as Moodle should make life easier on lecturers, not more complicated by draining away extra time in setting up stuff like this. I found another workaround: as a teacher I only have a limited set of activities that hae some kind of random function built-in. Such as the generation of groups and assigning members to these. But there is also a random aspect to the question types formula and calculated multiple choice. I have solved my dilemma (although not as elegant as I would like) by creating 1 calculated multiple choice question with the variables x and y in them in the following string which has the same font color as the background (ergo white): 172.{x}.{y}.0 The question also contains the text (in black): Below you can find the IP range you have to use during this exam. Please check that you have been informed of this IP range. Answer option 1 is then set to: 172.{x}.{y}.0 with mask /24 (incorrect answer) Answer option is set to: I have been informed that my IP range is 172.{x}.{y}.0 with mask /24 (correct answer) And I have set the variable x and y so that is x randomized between 16 and 31 and y between 1 and 254 I then created a quiz with this 1 calculated multiple choice question with the display name "click here to know the IP range that needs to be used". Thanks for thinking along with me. It is appreciated.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: how to assign random piece of info to students
ResponsesInList.Text: > set the variable x and y so that is x randomized between 16 and 31 and y between 1 and 254 So these "strings" (the IP ranges) don't have to be unique?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: how to assign random piece of info to students
ResponsesInList.Text: By doing this randomization of x and y between those values, I can generate a dataset with that one question that contains over 4000 unique IP ranges. When 100 students take the exam, there is indeed a small chance that two student will get the same IP range assigned by Moodle. But they would need to know that of each other, be able to see each others laptop screen, communicate with each other in some way for this to be a problem. So it serves my purpose of giving my students a range that is not hard coded on the exam instructions but is given on the spot by Moodle. Thus reducing the risk of fraude. I have other systems in place to, to make sure that each student has a unique set of configuration parameters for their virtualized network components. Each student a unique IP range for them alone would be nice, but is not necessary for my purposes.

ResponsesInList.Title: Unavailable activities: display or hide conditions?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi fellow teachers! I am currently creating a re-designed version of the original course I created and delivered to my Art History students back at the beginning of the 2000s.🙃 It was originally built using the ToolBook authoring language , now abandonned, and re-designed in Moodle mainly with H5P customized activities . I want to "enforce" a sequence of activities within my Moodle course, and have understood the various Access restrictions and Activity completion concepts. I just have a minor point on which I'd like to have opinions and real-case usage. When access to an activity is restricted, do you usually display or hide the  access conditions warning? Any justifications for your choice? Thanks! Joseph (once a teacher, always a teacher)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unavailable activities: display or hide conditions?
ResponsesInList.Text: I personally prefer to hide them but I know some teachers who with very good reason say that they show the conditions so that learners know exactly what they need to do in order to access the activity/resource. For me the problem comes when for example you have an end of course quiz which is dependent on twenty other activities being completed - I would prefer to state in its descriptoin that you have to do all the other activities and hide the criteria rather than clutter up the page. I would probably say on reflection that if you want to give your learners a clear picture of what they must do then it is probably better to display them, but  if you want an element of suprise , or to not overload them in advance, or for people doing any kind of gamification than hiding is obviously necessary. Mary (retired teacher but still a teacher)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unavailable activities: display or hide conditions?
ResponsesInList.Text: I had my restriction unhidden until I learned it confused the students who mis-understood what the restriction said. I then hidden all of them, in every course. I do however, in the course email notifications and course description page state that there are X number of activities in the ABC course and each activity must be completed in sequence. Kind Regards.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unavailable activities: display or hide conditions?
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unavailable activities: display or hide conditions?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unavailable activities: display or hide conditions?

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Davin, Many thanks for sharing your thoughts on this, it's really helpful for us! That's the question we want reply through this research. We shouldn't take for granted that students don't need this extra information, as our assumptions can be wrong, so we want to make sure before making a decision whether or not this information is useful for learners. The approach of 'less is more' is kind of a must/law in UX design, but there are exceptions that break the rule and in some cases, like this one, having a description for an icon can be quite helpful, especially in terms of accessibility . Please check Nielsen Norman Group documentation around this ( https://www.nngroup.com/articles/icon-usability/ ). The activity title can be self explanatory for learners and the label may not be necessary, but this is something we cannot assure as it's up to the content creator to give the activity a descriptive title. But first we need to understand what are the students needs around this. In the case that our research shows that activity type labels are useful for learners, we'll make sure that the solution we design is clean, subtle and doesn't add a big clutter to the screen. Please bear in mind that these design examples are just the starting point of the work, and based on all the teachers/content creators and the student feedback we get, I'll be refining, improving and changing the designs to better satisfy all user needs. At the moment, there will be one tutor grading these questions so I have set an email to notify her when an attempt is made. When I have more than one tutor grading these questions, how can I allocate quiz attempts to the tutors? I don't want more than one tutor trying to mark the same quiz at the same time. Ideally, I'd like quiz attempts to be distributed evenly, e.g. to Tutor A then Tutor B then Tutor A etc. But I don't think that willl be possible. Is it a case of enrolling students into groups and having one tutor per group? Any suggestions very welcome. Thanks in advance.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Allocated tutors to manually grade quizzes
ResponsesInList.Text: In quizzes it's not possible to assign submissions to grades like you can in assignments. There's no advanced grading workflow available, though that would be an excellent feature to add IMHO . What you can do, is the following: Divide the students taking the quizzes into groups and add a tutor to each group. If the tutor role is based on the non-editing teacher role (or has the permission moodle/site:accessallgroups NOT SET), they can only grade attempts of their own group's students.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Allocated tutors to manually grade quizzes

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Aggregate Quiz Grade -> Completion
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Drew, You can't directly set a minimum value in a specific grade category as a completion criteria. AFAIK , you can only require a minimum course grade value in Course completion. If these quizzes are the only graded activities in your course, the course grade would naturally reflect the aggregate of these grades. But an 80% average score over all quizzes is not the same as the 80% passing grade of each individual quiz. There may be another approach to this challenge, if you are willing to use the mod_checklist activity module ( https://moodle.org/plugins/mod_checklist ) in your course. With this, set up to record completions of associated activities, you can track the overall 80% completion of the course as well. And since this is a completion criteria in the Checklist activity you'd use, you're also able to have the its completion as a cource completion criteria: the course is completed once the Checklist activity has a grade value of 80% or higher.

ResponsesInList.Title: Why use Lessons instead of Pages/Quizzes
ResponsesInList.Text: Seems to me: anything you can do with the Lesson activity, you could also do with a series of pages and quizzes. What is the advantage of using Lessons?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why use Lessons instead of Pages/Quizzes
ResponsesInList.Text: It's up to personal preference really, but for example with Lessons you get better navigation than with Pages or Quizzes. With a Lesson you can direct people to a specific page depending on the result of a question, whereas Quiz navigation is not as (in standard Moodle) as customisable.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why use Lessons instead of Pages/Quizzes
ResponsesInList.Text: But quiz offers more question types, horses for courses.....

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why use Lessons instead of Pages/Quizzes
ResponsesInList.Text: An advantage of Lesson is the branching is already built in as simple settings: you can create complex branchings based on questions. You can do this with Pages and Quizzes, but you will need to build all the branching yourself using quiz grades/completions and access restrictions: and remember (or better, document) how it all works. Another advantage is you can easily Import / Backup / Restore a Lesson since it is a single integral activity. If you want to build template Lessons with the structure and branching already set up and then copy and share it around to other courses, it is pretty easy to do so.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Why use Lessons instead of Pages/Quizzes
ResponsesInList.Text: From the instructional design perspective, Lesson and Quiz are two completely different contexts: Lesson offers a guided learning experience with branching scenarios and a limited number of question type options, whereas Quiz is primarily an assessment tool with loads of interesting statistics and psychometric analysis on board. Of course, you could work with conditional questions in Quiz, and there are plenty of feedback options for your students when building a formative type Quiz. You can use Lesson in a dungeon type of activity, much like the first generation of computer role playing games, provided you have well designed scenarios. Such a dungeon type activity would be a lot harder to construct with Pages and Quizzes, if even possible. And it wouldn't be as appealing as in a Lesson. Also, the blue background for questions in Quiz may work in assessments, but isn't always as useful.

ResponsesInList.Title: Chat-like Forum activity - Help/advice?
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi fellow Moodlers!
First some background: I'm working on developing practice activities for English as a foreign language (EFL) students who are training to take a speaking exam (Trinity College London's Integrated Skills in English). They're blended learning courses, i.e. a mixture of regular f2f classes plus online practice & extension activities.
In one phase of the exam, the examiner poses a problem or dilemma to the candidate, e.g.

Examiner - "For the next part, I'll tell you something. Then, you have to ask me questions to find out more information and make comments. You need to keep the conversation going. After four minutes, I'll end the conversation. Are you ready?"
Candidate - "Yes."
Examiner - "I am thinking of changing my job so I have looked into various courses. Now I don't know which course to choose."
Candidate - [candidate responds] etc..

The students practice this phase of the exam in writing because it reduces the immediate pressure & gives them time to think & develop their ideas & strategies for responding to this kind of conversation.
The students will start their online conversations in class on their mobile devices, mostly phones, & continue them after class.
Eventually, they'll be given regular online only assignments that the teachers can monitor & grade (mostly participation & some formative feedback).
Most but not all will have the mobile app installed.
The conversations typically occur over several days & having app & email notifications is very useful.
The students practise in pairs, one playing the role of the examiner, the other the candidate.
I keep the pairings as flexible as possible (self-selected) so that the early starters don't have to wait for slower students to respond. They quickly learn who's responsive & who waits until the last minute!
So far, we've been using the Forum activity module but there's an issue: The minimum possible "time to edit" for Forum posts in 1 minute & it's after 1 minute that push & email notifications are sent out. Much of the time this is OK but when we're initiating the task in class & all the students are getting started, & when students are posting at the last minute, it'd be nice to have something more responsive & immediate, i.e. no 1 minute delay between submitting a comment & getting a notification.
I guess the functionality we're looking for is closer to Signal, WhatsApp, Telegram, etc., i.e. Post a comment & the receiver gets an alert immediately, but with the monitoring & feedback capabilities of the Forum module.
I think greater immediacy will also encourage students to write shorter responses which are more conversation-like than typical forum discussions.
For privacy, oversight, & GDPR reasons (We're in the EU), we can't require students to use 3rd party apps & this will be required coursework.
Has anyone had similar experiences with using Moodle like this?
What kinds of solutions/advice can you offer? TIA !

ResponsesInList.Title: Chat-like Forum activity - Help/advice?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Matt, Sounds like a good course to me 👍 Have you tried group messaging? That’s pretty close to WhatsApp actually and built right into moodle! Just put the pair of students into a group and direct them to the messaging and they can start right away. If you want to monitor (and grade) what’s happening in the group, just add the teacher as well and use an assignment activity (without submissions) for it. An alternative would be our social comments block. It’s actually built to allow students to comment on things, but can surely be used as well for your purposes. You can download it here: https://moodle.org/plugins/block_socialcomments or try it out here: https://labs.bdecent.de/course/view.php?id=415 (log in with demo/moodle or sign up for your own account if you want to see the email notifications) Please note that currently, students still need to refresh the page to see a new comment. We’re working on a solution for that. Another alternative would of course be moodles own chat activity. The messaging built into core seems to be the best solution to me, especially because it’s very nice when used with the mobile app, but maybe you want to check out the other solutions as well.

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Stefan, Thanks for the diverse range of suggestions! However, I can see it being useful as an option to try out & see how well it works! I'll check out the add-ons too Cheers!

ResponsesInList.Text: Why don't you just use the Chat module? You can have different sessions for different people and set it to allow others to see historical chats.

ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, in some cases, I can see chat being useful. It's the flexibility & additional features of the Forum activity that I'd like to exploit, e.g. in- context private & personalised feedback on specific posts/comments, post & comment management options, grading & rating.

Regular learners can enter an " Ask the Expert " style section on the course and ask a question. Any expert is able to view the question and reply to it. Learners cannot see each others' questions, or answers to other questions; only the ir own threads. ResponsesInList.Text: Vedant, Using Forum you can do this if you set it to use Separate Groups, then create a group for each student and add all the Experts to each student group. (You can use the Upload user tool to create and manage such groups . Have you looked in the plugins database for something like this? ResponsesInList.Title: Course activity to facilitate this unusual forum-like use case
ResponsesInList.Text: Use the database activity. The trick is to enable approval for entries, but never approve entries, because not approved entries are invisible for other students. Your experts could then use the comments feature to „answer”. If you need more detailed instructions or a proof of concept, let me know! Hope this helps! Stefan

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Course activity to facilitate this unusual forum-like use case
ResponsesInList.Text: Ah, also you could do something similar with Glossary: just never approve the entries but allow comments by teachers. Glossary does not have the ability to understand Groups. But if your Experts are all in the teacher role or have the relevant permissions, it would work... As long as they don't approve entries, which if they do, will be viewable by all the students. The advantage of Database for this is you can create the data structure you want, if you need to do that. The advantage of using Glossary is you can just use one of the predefined formats and structures it has already.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle 4.0 icons - where can I download them?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Rosemary, The icons for core Moodle activity modules are available in both .png and .svg files. They are a new 'monologo' type that can be easily added to the colored background you see in the picker and on the course page. AFAIK , they aren't part of a font type such as FontAwesome or anything, if you were expecting this. There are probably two or three ways to get these icons so you can use them in a manual of sorts: Screengrab them with your favorite clipping tool Download them from Github ( https://github.com/moodle/moodle ) under /mod/'activityshortname'/pix Download the install files locally and then follow the same route to get to each activity's /pix folder and grab either the .svg or .png file Be sure to rename the files, as they are all called 'monologo.png' or 'monologo.svg'. Also: be sure to use the correct licensing when reusing the activity icons. I doubt there's permission to 'modify' or 'alter' them in any way.

ResponsesInList.Title: Using a Scale and a Rubric for Grading
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, I use a scale instead of points with my rubric and have a question. My scale is "pass, fail, absent, excused" and I only want to use the scale for those students who have actually handed in something. The problem is that with this combination when I open an assignment to grade I only see the rubric and there is not way to choose from the scale, Moodle obviously chooses automatically from the scale. Is that the expected/ intended behavior? Is there any way to choose from the rubric (just the way I can when there is no rubric) AND still have the rubric? Thank you!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using a Scale and a Rubric for Grading
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Yves, That is expected and intended behaviour. If you're using an advanced grading method such as Rubric or Marking guide, the aggregated score will be as follows: points scored / points total. This leads to a percentage score, which in turn is translated to a scale value. Let's say your 'Pass, Fail, Absent, Excused' scale is being used, it'll work as follows: No score = 0/4 points Pass = 1/4 points (25%) Fail = 2/4 points (50%) Absent = 3/4 points (75%) Excused = 4/4 points (100%)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: ADDING CATEGORIES TO A COURSE
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Armando, The concept of Categories in Moodle is slightly different than you'd expect: A category is basically a part of a tree structure, a folder containing one or more courses. A course can only be part of one category at a time. If you're looking for another way to add attributes or metadata to your course, there are two main options: use Tags ( https://docs.moodle.org/311/en/Tags ) or Course Custom Fields ( https://docs.moodle.org/311/en/Course_settings#Course_custom_fields ). One advantage of the latter is that the information in these custom fields can be displayed in your category tree structure, when viewing a course before enrolling.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Use of scales and custom certificates
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Chrysanthi, Even though a Scale is used, in the background Moodle will interpret the scale values as a numerical grade, as can be read in the Moodle Docs here: https://docs.moodle.org/en/Scales#Example_scales . If you have a scale with 3 levels (Fail, Pass, Distinction), Moodle will award 0, 1 or 2 points respectively under any normal grade aggregation such as average / weighted average / simple weighted average. If you wish to restrict access to the certificate based on a grade in the assignment, you'll need to set the numerical value that corresponds with the minimum grade needed, e.g. the grade is equal to or higher than 1 (Pass). @Moderators: this question is likely to attract more input from the community in the Teaching with Moodle forum.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unable to import gift file: wrong file type (but is not!)
ResponsesInList.Text:
As far as I can tell Moodle relies on PHP's FileInfo extension to determine the MIME type. So it looks like: The file is uploaded by the browser in a POST request to the Moodle web server . Moodle's PHP source code writes the file and uses FileInfo to get its MIME type. Moodle adds an mdl_files row for the file with mimetype set accordingly. Exactly how FileInfo determines the MIME type could be affected by changes to the server
configuration, such as operating system files such as /usr/share/file/magic or PHP's configuration. But In my tests on both Fedora and Ubuntu your file is detected as
text/plain: when I upload your file named myfile.gift from my Fedora workstation to Moodle the question import works as expected. And that's what is returned if I use the attached test script to get the MIME type of that file. But you say that there is different behaviour depending on whether the browser is on a different operating system? Perhaps you could use your browser's developer tools to check that the POSTed file is the same in both systems. If it's exactly the same file that you're uploading in both cases (and remember Microsoft Windows text editors will use CRLF instead of Linux's LFs) then you could check to see whether the uploaded file has the same hash, for example: 
```text
SELECT filename, contenthash, mimetype FROM mdl_files WHERE filename = 'myfile.gift'; 


+-------------+------------------------------------------+------------+ 


| filename    | contenthash                              | mimetype   | 


+-------------+------------------------------------------+------------+ 


| myfile.gift | 9f0b7dd0fc4fd778306945d336364c6d86a3a406 | text/plain |


+-------------+------------------------------------------+------------+
```
 Also: file types can be overridden in config.php by setting $CFG->customfiletypes . Also: to determine Moodle's version from the source code check the $release value in version.php in the top-level of your Moodle source code folder.

ResponsesInList.Title: Put multiple quizzes in one assignemtn
ResponsesInList.Text: I am teaching a few course with lots of chapters and several quizzes in each chapter.  I want to be able to make one assignment and put all the quizzes and tests in one place.  Otherwise the course gets too long(vertical scrolling)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Put multiple quizzes in one assignemtn
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Walter, If these quizzes are all separate tasks, they can't really be merged into 1 activity / assignment, as each quiz will record its own attempts, scores, correct/incorrect answers, time spent, etc. Also, your participants won't be able to accurately determine which items are still open and due. Having said this, you could consider any of the following improvements: Use other activity completion settings than 'Manually mark as completed' so the 'Mark as done' button will disappear from the course page (use receive a grade, complete an attempt, view the quiz instead). This has three benefits: Your students won't be able to just click the button and be done with it ==> they'll have to do the work You will be better able to determine which students still have pending work through the Activity completion report The course page itself will have a more compact listing of work due. Use restricted access rules to only display the next activity once the previous has been completed (and hide the rule). Use stealth activities (set to hidden but available) and add the activity names to an unordered list. Also enable Activity name auto-linking filter to automatically create links where the activity names appear in text boxes. Use the 'one section at a time' display mode for Topics format.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Put multiple quizzes in one assignemtn
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Walter. There is a documentation page Streamline your course page which might give you some ideas.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Put multiple quizzes in one assignemtn
ResponsesInList.Text: One other plugin for doing this, that you might consider, is the Content Pages, (iContent), plugin. You do not mention your Moodle version, but this does work on Moodle 3.11 and lower, even though it says it works on Moodle 3.8 and lower. It works similar to a slide show for presenting lesson material, but it can also include some of the most common question types on any slide which allows you to include quizzes with your content. An added bonus is that it also allows students to keep notes and ask the teacher questions. This can be either private or public.

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi. A couple of quick thoughts: 1. Utilize "Restrict Access" and/or Completion to hide the quizzes that will come later.

ResponsesInList.Text: Yet another possible method, especially if your course is very long, is to use the Subcourse plugin. In that case, each long section or sections of activities would be in a separate course and then the main course pulls the grades from those into the main course. I've used this in cases where there were courses lasting 9-12 months containing on the order of 200-250 activities originally. The sub-courses then take the role of one or more large sections of content, with the main course having the start and finish of the total course. This can work in those situations. If you have say 80 or 100 activities and need to have it all in just one course, then many of the other suggestions here would probably be the better way to go.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Which additional plugins would you like in core? (was Re: Moodle core plugins review)
ResponsesInList.Text: No, I am familiar with the Workplace report, which is clearly modeled on the one that has been in Totara for at least five years now. It does a decent job at what it does, which is let someone with no coding experience pick and choose from a limited set of table and fields into a spreadsheet style report. It will be useful for basic reports missing for two decades now, such as reports across courses, Enrolment details, Course Completions, etc. But it is basically a limited sort of report builder we have been able to find in apps like MS Access since back in the early 1990s. But you can't do anything really interesting with it and nothing custom at all if you want things like calculations, have interesting questions (for example: how many suspended users still have both grades and badges but no certificates? What's the average enrolment size of child meta courses compared to the number of teaching assistants assigned to them via groups? Show me the Assignment marking guide comments from teachers newly employed in the last six months for countries other than their own...) And it can't handle third party plugins, either. If you depend on a Certificate mod, as in companies, that won't help you much (because Workplace certificates are core and work entirely differently than in Moodle). Of course, that stuff may come along in time with some api calls. I doubt that either the permissions for the reports - which are planned but there's no indication of progress on them yet - will be able to match the flexibility of the many ways that CR can allow reports to be seen and by whom. There's only going to be four types according to the tracker: All users Specific users Cohort members System role assignments So, none of the cool features like by user profile or even course roles or multiple conditions or ? At least there will be an API that could be expanded in the future, but we already have this in CR. Why not just put it in now? Likewise for mailing the reports: it's being planned, but will it be as good as, say, the Ad-hoc one? Will there be a template library? An export to xml function? A way to share reports? If it had a SQL panel just to input code and be able to use its formatting options - as Intelliboard does - then I would be interested in it. For those who have nothing, it will be a great improvement. To those used to rolling their own reports, it will be useful for making easy generic reports for users who can't or won't do their own. This will be a real time saver. But for anything sophisticated or custom, you will still need to have both CR and the Ad-hoc queries plugins. But, now you will have three tools, all of which work differently and look differently and have different features and limitations.  They say, "Don't look a gift horse in the mouth." But if you don't, you might end up with a donkey, a zebra, and a water buffalo.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Which additional plugins would you like in core? (was Re: Moodle core plugins review)
ResponsesInList.Text: Marcus, Apologies for my rant ;) The good news is that Workplace's Report Builder is a good tool with ongoing improvements: corporate customers demand competent and full featured reporting and Moodle will have to constantly deliver those improvements to them or else. The bad news is, of course, Moodle's track record of putting in a new feature and then letting it languish for years with little or no improvement. If this is a one time port from Workplace, then that would be disappointing, but not surprising. Meanwhile, if Report Builder could have as a counterpart a combination plugin of CR and Ad-hoc dq features combined into one plugin for the development and sharing of custom code, that would be an ideal one-two combination.

ResponsesInList.Text: I'd potentially take a different approach to a similar outcome. I'd quite like to see a wider range of plugins included in the code base - but have them all disabled by default. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Which additional plugins would you like in core? (was Re: Moodle core plugins review)
ResponsesInList.Text: David and Richard, Those are interesting ideas. My thoughts on this, pro and con are similar. It sounds rather a lot like the model that Wordpress has: a small(er) core with many, many plugins. It has a lot of advantages. Having a slimmer Moodle core set of tools would certainly be useful in many ways. There's any number of core plugins I would happily rip out if I could but every time I suggest this, I always get push back saying, "We want that in core." Well, if I don't want that in core, I am stuck with it and have to then deal with that. So, not only would it be useful to add in core tools later, but right now we can't even remove most of those: next update, it will give you a headache and try to reinstall them. Making core plugins truly pluggable like third party plugins would a definite improvement. Another advantage might be it would promote a bit more the abstraction of certain tools from core (eg Quiz and Gradebook) to allow them to have more potential competitors I know there's a lot of interdependence between certain features, but encouraging more tools to be pluggable is good. On the other hand.... having managed Wordpress sites, I can say that admins will end up spending much of their time and most of their frustrations managing plugins with the slim core model. To get a Wordpress site to do pretty much anything at all other than simple blog posts & pages, you have to spend a lot of time hunting for plugins, paying for plugins, and managing plugins. All those plugins have to play well together: that is sometimes a difficult challenge. It takes a lot more work to do that than the current Moodle approach. Right now, I think there's a couple challenges to getting this to work with Moodle: - The only thing that makes this tolerable in the Wordpress world is the ease with which updates and upgrades can happen. We only have part of that in Moodle. Updating plugins is light years better than it used to be - thanks in large part to the work of David. But we can't update Moodle itself this way and if we could, we would need a lot of logic to make sure versioning was good. Having all this info right on on admin panel like the one that WP has would be very useful: we don't really have a central place for this in Moodle due to the "our big core" versus other's plugins approach. Consolidating the Notifications page with the Plugins overview page would be needed too. - There's a lot of incentive in the WP world for plugin devs to build alternate versions of plugins: partly because it is easy to pay for them. We would really need a payment system for plugin developers so that we can avoid the common problem of orphaned plugins. I think the only successful place in Moodle where this sort of works now is with themes. An official plugin Marketplace is needed. - A recommendation system would be needed. I recall some time ago there was a project to get experienced Moodler users to write up reviews of plugins, but I don't recall it went very far. You would need something like that - and a way to prevent abuse of it (which is yet another frustration of the WP world: useless and fake and paid reviews for plugins are legion.) - For new sites, you need some sort of addition to the install process which lets new site admins pick from a set of key tools. First time installs by new admins can be a problem since they may not really know what plugins they should add, pedagogically. Having a couple of predefined packages of common plugins would be very useful, or even an install wizard that would lead them through choosing common plugins. I think this could give you both a slim core, but also have the ability to do an initial install of plugin sets at install type, disabled to start with, disabled to start with as Richard suggests. - A related issue is that we all know how this works in the real world: having made an initial choice, it means other tools that teachers may want to explore and try out will not be in the site at all. Teachers might just use what they have and not know there are other possibilities. For example, now many users would try out Lesson or Glossary or Badges if they were not already just sitting there to try? Being able to experiment and trying out new activities is important for teachers and course designers too. That would be gone and replaced by some sort of request to the admin to install something just to look at it. Having to install plugins instead of simply enable them does add friction to the process: neither admins nor teachers like friction. And installing a plugin is a lot more friction for admins - and an interruption for all users - than simply enabling one already installed. - Security is an concern too: installing a new plugin is much more potentially dangerous process that simply enabling an already installed plugin: right now there's some very important security that has to be be in place for the code. I can't just install a plugin without going to the server to open up some permissions temporarily. Again, you can say admins should know how to do that, but it is another raising of the bar for new adoptions. While in WP with its integrated admin panel, this is taken care of so there is a lot less interruption to users than Moodle has. I have to say that personally, I find the Moodle approach a lot less headache than the Wordpress approach to plugins: I mean, almost NO Wordpress is usable these days out of the box. You always have to add plugins to to get anything useful. Back in the day, when blogging was new, this approach made sense: the only core tool you had posts. Of course, this is also true of Drupal (and to some extent Joomla) but that is the nature of those tools. However, in Moodle, I would certainly like to be able to remove certain core features and plugins and never have them in the site at all. So, perhaps these new approaches could encourage more of a fully pluggable architecture for core. And we could have our cake and eat it too

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Trả lời: Re: Trả lời: Re: 1-1 class
ResponsesInList.Text: I don't see the requirement to create separate topics for each user Without actually trying it, so more than happy for anyone to correct me, but I think what you would have to do is 1. make sure permissions to view participants lists are removed so users can't see each other (you'd only have to do this once) 2. Add each user to their own group - in the course Groups settings there is an option to auto create groups which can be done by number of users in a group, set that to 1. If you get new users in later you may have to redo that, or add indivuals to their own group manually. 3. create your course with all resources and activities 3a. resources such as labels, files, pages, etc do not need to be restricted, they are the same for everyone - if you need to personalise the content, consider using a plugin such as Generico which allows you to create content using variables such as user names 3b. activities can be set with groups as Separate Groups, so that each group can only see their own content on the activity. Create each activity once and set the group mode. There's no need to duplicate the activity (or whole topic section) for each user. I believe that's it. No need for multiple topics. You can use the access restrictions as well if some content needs to be further restricted, but making use of the separate groups feature should enable what your original post asked about. Richard

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle core plugins review

Please see MDL-72046 for the plugins we are working on removing. We'd like to hear from you if you are using any of the plugins listed below and think that the plugin should remain in core; also if you have any suggestions for more plugins which should be considered for possible removal. Quiz results block (block_quiz_results) Flickr block (block_tag_flickr) Examview question import/export format (qformat_examview) Algebra notation filter (filter_algebra) HTML tidy filter (filter_tidy) Box repository (repository_boxnet) Legacy course files repository (repository_coursefiles) Equella repository (repository_equella) Flickr repository (repository_flickr) Flickr public repository (repository_flickr_public) Merlot.org repository (repository_merlot) URL downloader repository (repository_url) Box portfolio (portfolio_boxnet) Flickr portfolio (portfolio_flickr) Mahara ePortfolio (portfolio_mahara) Survey activity (mod_survey)

They really should not be using legacy files as a shared files repository - better to use something designed for that purpose e.g. SharePoint or whatever solution is recommended by their institution. Legacy files are not secure in the sense that anyone (including students) who has access to a course can potentially access a file within the legacy files repository. ResponsesInList.Title: (Workplace) Certifications and Programs
ResponsesInList.Text: Happy Monday!! I'm a bit confused by how Certifications are working and am hoping that someone can explain this to me. To me, a Program is a group of related courses that all need to be completed in order to get credit.  For instance, a Cyber Security Awareness program that consists of 10 different courses on varying topics.  There may or may not be a certification involved, but the key is there are 10 different courses required. To me, a Certification can be either one course that needs to be taken at some cadence like yearly or a program.  I'd like clarification on one course needing yearly certification.  It could be a HIPAA course that changes and/or you want to make a new version that is more engaging.  In order for the user to be updated on changes, they need to re-take or re-certify every year.  I don't understand how this is a program. In order to set up a certification, you must create a program.  So, can a program have one course in it?  I assume so.  Then, how do you add the new version of the course for the next year? (Edited by Mary Cooch to clarify Moodle Workplace - original submission Monday, 19 April 2021, 3:10 PM)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: (Workplace) Certifications and Programs
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Jackie, Certifications in Workplace are recurring programs, they could be a one-off thing or they might need to be taken at some cadence. If your Certification only requires one course to be completed, then you'll need to create a program with a single course. With Recertification , you can configure the cadence and also choose a different program for the recertification. Let me illustrate with an example. Let's say you have a Health and Safety Certification you want your staff to take every year, to be certified for the first time they'll need to take the full program but to renew/retake the certification they will only be required to take the "refresher" course (with legislation changes, etc.) In Workplace, you would two programs: Health and Safety: full program with all courses Health and Safety refresher: program with the "refresher" course only. The refresher course would be updated every year And a single certification, selecting: Certification program = Health and Safety Expiry date = configure accordingly Require recertification = Yes Select a different program = Yes (Health and Safety refresher) Expiry date (recertification) = configure accordingly Hope it helps. Cheers, Emilio

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: (Workplace) Certifications and Programs
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks so much, Emilio. So, Program is/are the recurring courses and Certification is like the wrapper that sets up the cadence, etc.?? I'm assuming I can have just a Program without a Certification if it were a one-time set of courses to be taken.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: (Workplace) Certifications and Programs
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Jackie, That's it. Yes, you can have just a program for one-time set of courses to be taken, and you can also have a one-off certification if you need it. Cadence in Certifications is optional. Possibilities are endless, for example you could define a shared program (Program in the Shared Space) and then create certifications in different tenants pointing to the same program but overriding dates or having their own dynamic rules (i.e. issuing a certificate upon completion). You would end up having different configurations for the same set of courses with a single source of truth. How cool is that? 😉 Cheers, Emilio

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Course Completion Block set as a default
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Jackie, An additional answer to the points you raise: As Moodle defines the following context levels (Site, Category, Course, Activity, User), a block with a context level 'Course' cannot be added to the context level 'Category'. In this case, from a developer's point of view, it makes no sense to collect completion status info on courses in a specific category, as that data does not exist in that context. From a user's point of view, I kind of understand where you're coming from: if a user would be browsing the course catalogue (through the categories), it would be nice to see your completion status for courses in a specific category. This, however, is not how Moodle works... The best place to aggregate this kind of completion data would be on a user's Dashboard in the course overview block. Here, you have your progress bars for courses tracking progress, and in WP you'd even be able to track progress at program level ( AFAIK ). If you'd make sure user enrolment is correctly provisioned, and the courses track progress correctly, there would be no need to show completion statuses other than on the Dashboard and in the courses.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Motivating Students
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Tim, I believe that rather than looking at technical tips regarding engaging students, it's best to look at the humans present. Having taught and designed online courses since the '90s, I understand that the keys to student engagement mirrors what happens in successful face-to-face classrooms; it comes down to what the instructor does interacting and communicating with students, along with promoting peer interactions. Fun and dynamic activities will promote student interest; however, when students work remotely/independently, and perhaps without a keen interest in the subject matter, it will be the conversations and the recognition of the individuals present that draws them in. Some of the steadfast tools such as discussion forums, the workshop module, wikis, et cetera, promote visibility and voice. I start my Moodle courses with activities that ensure students participate and define who they are by uploading a representative profile picture and participating in a "Who's here?" introductory forum. The instructors' diligence in reaching out to the silent and acknowledging the efforts of those present are the most important behind the scenes endeavors which are key to student engagement. I would choose instructor initiated interventions to student inactivity over automated (impersonal) cron job initiated reminders, etc. Moodle integrates in its design features that will illuminate which students are active or not, and what they are doing on their course. Simply clicking on the 'Last access to course' column heading link in the Participants page will reveal who's been active. Reaching out to inactive students can then be initiated by the teacher (a person) to address the concern. Solicitating feedback from the participants using the "Feedback" and "Choice" modules will reveal general design deficiencies which can be dynamically addressed. Instructor engagement = student engagement . 👍

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Motivating Students
ResponsesInList.Text: Thank you Tim for this discussion. You open a lot of possible avenues for further exploration. You are in an envious situation, being able to pilot different modes of delivery in your nascent program. I too like Matt's idea to incorporate weekly synchronous sessions using an external platform (ZOOM; MS Teams; Google Meet, etc.). It will give students an opportunity to connect and hear how their classmates are experiencing the program. The power of peer collaboration and assessment is too often overlooked in distributed learning programs. In face-to-face classes, much of the teaching/learning is fed by the students themselves. Students will hear perspectives from classmates that they might not have considered or perhaps have been timid to ask. The power of these invaluable learning opportunities is too often lost in course design for distributed settings. I believe that in practice, self-paced , learn anytime , anywhere makes for great catchphrases but impoverished learning environments. The self-paced model does serve certain learners very well; namely highly disciplined, task driven and motivated learners. If that description fits your learner base then this should be a highly effective model. In my experience, learners from grammar school to post-secondary need the scaffolds of timely pacing to motivate their attention and progress. What's missing in online environments is the process of meeting at a scheduled location to receive instruction with an expectation to complete related work and submit it in a timely fashion. For most of us, learn anytime means "I will do it later" which transitions to not at all . With your program just beginning, I wonder if you are able to pilot both models. For instance, you might offer a self-paced track for students who are unable to maintain a directed schedule, and an alternate choice for those participates who prefer more peer interactive learning. Personally, I would offer the self-paced option to students anytime they find they are unable to keep pace with the scheduled class. The self-paced model would be available for those who need it. You asked if users were allowed to message between themselves in the platform. They are, as it promotes interaction. Privacy is maintained by instructing students to to select " Hide my email address from non-privileged users " in their profile settings. Consequently, only instructors and course managers can see this information. You are considering using Whatsapp for the instructor to announce "every couple of days a link to an activity or some other content". I find that the "Announcements" forum adequately serves this purpose. It is a one-way broadcast which e-mails students specific information from the course instructor. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Motivating Students
ResponsesInList.Text: I second that points that David has made. Personal relationships are key to successful online cohorts in courses/programmes that last longer than a couple of weeks. I also use Moodle for language learning & have had to deal with the exact issues that you're describing. Yes, it's a good idea to send students timely reminders of up-coming events & activities to encourage them to stay on schedule but I've found that Moodle generated messages aren't as effective as messages written by the teachers. It's also good to schedule regular whole cohort emails that introduce or summarise the week's &/or next weeks learning activities, what the general strengths & weaknesses have been & how you're going to help them to improve, for example. It may also be useful to set up a feedback or Q&A forum & link to it from the email so that you can get a conversation going & allow students to have some degree of influence over how the course progresses. However, if you do this it's important to be responsive & accommodate students' requests are far as possible (set expectations beforehand). Students will more than likely hold teachers' feet to the fire if they feel they aren't being listened to! For example, if the T:S ratio is high, then it could be a good idea to hold one or more syncronous sessions on a webinar platform, e.g. BBB, Zoom, Teams, Meet,  or whatever. You could use it so that the learners get to put a face & voice to the teacher & maybe each other. This can go a long way to creating stronger connections between people & you may well see more active participation in discussion forums as a result. It needs a practical, learning-oriented premise though, so that students have a strong, academic reason for the potential inconvenience to them to attend. This could be something like demonstrating the process of writing assignments &/or best practices to ensure fewer issues &/or better grades, for example. You can use it to introduce the first writing assignment so that they're all set up, have organised their ideas, & are all set up to start writing by the end of it, much the same as it works in the face-to-face classroom, i.e. How to get more students to put more effort into their writing assignments & not leave it to the last minute. Make sure it's as dialogic & participatory as possible so students are listened & rsponded to & that it feels like it was worth attending (as opposed to a lengthy monologic presentation). Just some ideas. I hope this helps!

ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi Moodlers, I'm looking for advice, suggestions, solutions for a learning activity I'm trying to design. I'm working on a way for students to identify the different types of information in a given text. Here's an example: The text below contains the following types of information: Topic sentence Claim Background/explanation Example Call to action Click
on the eight parts of the text that make claims . (To show you what I mean, I've put the sections of text that are correct answers in bold . The students should just see a normal, unmarked text.) In my recent book, I discuss the subject of
routine and the effects it has on our lives. Actually,
my original idea was to look at the working methods of successful
creative people like writers and artists to see if there were any
helpful lessons to be drawn. The more people I examined, the clearer
it became that there was one thing the vast majority of them had in
common: they had a regular working
routine and stuck to it strictly, even obsessively. // Their habits
and routines often ended up being more like rituals. To
take one example, the composer Beethoven apparently used to start
each day with a cup of strong coffee made with exactly 60 coffee
beans, which he insisted on counting out personally. And that’s by
no means the oddest ritual I discovered. Obviously we don’t all
have to behave like that, but it does appear that routine
is something most of us need. Most humans function
better when they have some kind
of structure to their lives. In fact,
without routines for day-to-day activities , nothing much would get
done. Transport wouldn’t run on time,
schools and workplaces would be in a permanent state of chaos, and so
on. So, society as a whole seems to favour, or even require, people
with regular lifestyles. But
there’s a growing body of research suggesting that too
much routine is bad
for personal well-being , and it’s this
aspect that much of the book is concerned with. Breaking
up your routine and doing something new, it appears, increases your
happiness . It’s not just a case of
getting bored: routine also increases
our sense of time passing by too quickly . When
nothing new is happening, we’re not so conscious of events and
simply don’t notice the days and weeks slipping away. There’s also an interesting connection
between time and memory, or more exactly two kinds of connection.
Firstly, a lot of what people accept as
naturally increasing forgetfulness as they get older is actually more
to do with their lives becoming predictable . It’s
not so much that they forget things that have happened but that they
didn’t really notice them in the first place because they’d
become so automatic. The other thing that strikes a chord with me as
I get older is the explanation for why childhood memories seem so
vivid. When you’re young, everything is new and your brain is
working overtime to take everything in, so your impressions of events
are much more memorable. What we need to do is to try and
recapture that sense of newness by disrupting routines and actively
seeking out new experiences. What I'd like students to do is to click on sections of text that correspond to the information type, in this case claims. In my original design, I have the topic sentence, claims, background/explanation, example, & call to action information all pre-identified/labelled so that students can get specific feedback after they've clicked on or after they submitted their choice(s). The learning outcome that I'm after is that students can identify & categorise small sections of a text in context so that they can become more proficient at note-taking & summarising. However, the status continues to show 'not graded' when only the feedback form is used. It only changes to 'graded' when I add a numeric grade. I'm hoping that there is a simple workaround that I have missed and would appreciate any advice. With thanks, Kathy

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Assignment showing 'Not graded' with only feedback
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Kathy, It may be stating the obvious, but in order for a status to change from not graded to graded, a participant should receive a grade. There are ways to work around this, if your aim is to have a more formative assessment, as I gather from your task description. In that case, I'd recommend setting up a course scale, with a small number of scale options such as (-, Continue your work) or (-, Seen). Of course, in the background, such scale values would be numerical in nature, but to your student, it'll appear as a formative 'Green Light' or 'Go ahead' whilst also sending notification of your feedback to him or her. Set your assignment up to use this scale instead of entering a numerical grade, save and proceed. Good luck!

ResponsesInList.Title: Giving each teacher their own space
ResponsesInList.Text: This is quite hard to explain and even harder to search for, so forgive me if this has been dealt with before, and also for what might become a long post! I am frequently in a position where there might be, say, four teachers on a course. They might always have different students to each other, or it might be the same students learning different things. Moodle does a great job to allow activities , communication, etc. to take place without annoying everyone else who isn't involved. However, I have often been in a position where I have wanted to add a specific activity relating to a specific group on the course that is not relevant to any other teacher or student. For example, in the summer I was doing an activity involving Padlet, and a large proportion of my students couldn't work with it. I suspect there was a mixture of issues with OS, browser, VPN, country, IT ability etc. It didn't matter, I needed them to be able to respond to the activity, so I set up an assignment activity in the course. This is fine and dandy, but over a 10-week course, if this happens now and again involving multiple teachers, you end up with an awful mess on the course page. The same thing can happen in the forums. Some of these things may need to stay there for weeks, although some will be able to be removed or at least made invisible quite quickly. So, is there any way in Moodle to allow each teacher an area that doesn't make the course page bigger, longer, messier where they can add activities etc. as they see fit over the length of the course or is Moodle simply not designed that way. Having different courses for each teacher isn't an option. FWIW I have just upgraded to Moodle version 3.10 and the latest version of the Boost theme.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Giving each teacher their own space
ResponsesInList.Text: Kevin, It appear that you are currently using Groups to provide teachers with access to their students. We currently have courses that have over 50 teachers working with over a 1000 students. So these courses activities Groups mode to be separate mode. That way when teachers access the course they see their students only. Of course we have modified the Teacher role for those courses that teachers only have permission to see their group only. This way it is easier than selecting from a list of groups. Of course another Moodle function that will help is activity restriction. Teachers can create an activity and then restrict an activity, resource or topic to their particular group. That way the other students and teachers will not see those in their own courses. We have teachers that use this functionality for students that are on IEPs so that that only those students have access to the materials that is appropriate for that group of students.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Giving each teacher their own space
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for your response Dave. However, I am unclear how this stops the course page from getting clogged up with activities. For example, if I find I need to add a forum, do other teachers not see that forum? Same with a poll, for example.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Giving each teacher their own space
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes - that is if teachers role permission has been adjusted to limit teachers to only view the groups that they are enrolled. Below is one of the permissions that we have changed so that teachers do not have access to all the groups. So it is important to make sure that the teachers are assigned to groups. Along with making sure that the activity mode for those activities that the teachers want for their groups only to have the activity restriction to be viewed by their student group only when creating individual activities for them. Also all other activities that students need access should not have any restrictions, but it is nice to change the activity mode to separate groups. That way the teacher will only have access to their student group scores instead of every group in the course.

ResponsesInList.Title: Course Version Control, Course Runs & Program Management
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi everyone, I have hit some road blocks and was hoping to get some help in creating courses. I teach Course A, which runs every quarter. Q1 Is there a way to create one course i.e. Course A and have 4 runs of the same course and enrol 4 totally different batches of learners. Q2 In addition, these 4 runs could have minor changes i.e. some topics/ contents are updated and outdated as time passes . Any suggestions on how to do version control? One of the solution to the above 2 problems will be to create 4 independent courses. However, it wasn't so desirable since I still deem the learners from the 4 runs having completed the same courses. Any ideas on how else I could configure them? Q3 Lastly, if we have course A, B, C & D, is there a way to sequence & bundle them together and create a Programme/ Curriculum X out of it? These courses could also be part of other Programmes/ Curriculum Y, Z etc

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Course Version Control, Course Runs & Program Management
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi I face the same issues. You can duplicate courses, and choose whether to copy user data to the new course (you wouldn't). You could name the first course "Course A - Q1 - 2020" and then duplicate for Q2. In the Q2 course, make your changes. Duplicate Q2 to make Q3 etc. Students will be associated with the course that they did, and their grades will be linked to that course. "I still deem the learners from the 4 runs having completed the same courses" You could create a course called "Course A - Master". Students who complete Course A - Q1 etc are then enrolled in Course A - Master using a plugin. You then manually enter their grade for their Q1 course as their grade for Course A - Master. Over time, all students who complete Course A will be listed in Master with their final grade. The details of their participation will still be accessible in the course that they did. Programming a learning path and dependencies can be done using plugins, but the viability strongly depends on how much automation you hope to achieve, and the logic of how students flow from one course to another. You'll have to be really clear about your workflows and rules, and then investigate using plugins. Regards Brendon

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Course Content Vs Different Classes
ResponsesInList.Text: The way I handle this situation, is to make a full backup at the end of a course. For extra assurance, I download a copy of the backup to my local hard drive. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using groups in forums (Moodle 3.8.3)
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello there. Please test these steps and see if they work for you: In your course settings, make sure you have it set to Groups (let's say separate) You don't have to 'force' it unless you want to. You probably don't need groupings. Make sure you have created groups and added students to the groups. In your forum, set the forum to Separate groups. As a teacher, if you want students to be able to answer your posts (rather than just reading them and seeing the permalink) then you must make sure you tick the "post a copy to all groups" box underneath the post. This will then duplicate your post so that it will display a separate copy for each group, to which they can reply. The documentation Using Forum has a section on using groups with forums which might be useful to you.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Workshop Activity - Can each student be assigned a difrent task?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Jack, this is an interesting collaborative activity. I haven't used the Workshop for years and never for such a sophisticated scenario like the one you describe, so here is a possible workaround: You could create groups (2-3) who will work together the whole semester and create the definitions. The advantage I see is that it increases the possibility that a definition is accurate since it already undergoes a peer-review process. If you see a group has a high level. If the workshop doesn't work for you, I'd give the Wiki a try. Create a page for each term or a page for each letter of the alphabet. This way, there is no possibility of avoiding difficult terms, because a group should work only on "empty" concepts. It also forces groups to start early on the definitions so that they can pick their preferred ones. Once the definitions are worded, you can copy+paste the texts and create some quiz questions. I think the wiki would reduce your correction and grading time, but I don't know if it's a substantial reduction.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Filling activity by teacher
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Vahid, here are some ways to achieve that: teachers create an Assignment in a course and disable all Submission types. Hide it and disable any notifications for it (if you don't want students to see this activity or know about the comments) teachers grade and comment on it. It can include the kind of feedback you want to give to grade the activity. This item is included in the Grades section. You can edit the Grades to calculate only this item or several items. You can also add the item directly in the Grades section and skip the previous steps. However, the best assessment is a transparent and objective one, which allows a student to understand the reason for his/her grade and to work to improve it.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle for private music lessons?
ResponsesInList.Text: I'd like to share how I solved the problem I described in the original post: that Moodle isn't really optimized to let teachers distribute individualized content to each student enrolled in a course. I would love to see the functions I described above incorporated into Moodle. It is so jam packed with amazing features... it's really like a wonderland... but in this one area I see room for lots of development: tools for anyone who educates one-one-one: tutors, private music teachers, personal trainers, etc. Here's what I'm doing right now (there are perhaps better ways, or other plugins that do this, but this is what I was able to put up quickly and without a huge learning curve): 1) I still use the Google Sheet assignment lists (see my other post in this thread for an example). I have one for each student. It tells them exactly what their individual assignments are for the week. The nice thing about this is that Sheets are accessible even outside of Moodle... the student can simply bookmark it in their browser if they like. 2) I hunted through plugins and found the one that would solve my problem: Links ( https://moodle.org/plugins/block_links ). After installing and reading its documentation, I opened its Settings. (I don't remember if the Settings automatically opened the first time? But it's always accessible from Site Administration > Plugins > Plugins Overview > Additional Plugins > LInks > Settings .) The Title is of course whatever you choose; I titled it My Personal Data , because I told my students, "This is where you'll find YOUR stuff. No one else sees what you see here." The Profile Field is defaulted to Institution . That was fine with me because I don't use that field for anything else. You can choose another option if you need to. Link Target, your choice. I like New Window, but whatever. Then of course, Save Changes. 3) One at a time, I opened the Edit Profile page for each student. I headed to the bottom and twirled down Optional. At the Institution field (since that's what I chose in Step 2), I gave each student a unique value in that field. Do whatever works for you: perhaps just their FirstLast name, or a student ID number, etc. To state the obvious: if you changed from the default Institution field in Step 2, you'll need to enter the identifier in that field instead. (OF COURSE, this entire step is much easier done ahead of time by simply uploading users with a CSV file (they could all be done at once), but I didn't know I would be doing this. So... I did it... one... at... a... time.) 4) With Editing on, I added the Links block to the Site Home (pick whatever page you like). There it was: a block called "My Personal Data". And because of my admin role, I also saw "Add/Edit Links" in the bottom of the block. 5) I clicked on "Add/Edit Links"... then "Add a new link." In the "Link text" field, I entered (Name)'s assignments (for the first student). In the URL field, I pasted the Share URL to the Google Sheet assignment list for that student. I usually just ignore "additional text" and leave "show by default" as is. Do whatever you like with those. Here's the important part: Clicking Additional Settings > Category shows a drop-down list of all the unique identifiers that appear in any student's Profile: Institution (or whatever you chose). Here, I chose the Institution value for that first student. This guarantees that only the user whose Profile: Institution matches that "category" will see that link in the block when logged in. 6) Repeat Step 5... one... at... a... time... for each... individual... student. Yes, very tedious. I'm just a single man operation (private piano) so it's not like I have hundreds, but since I'm full time, it's still a lot for one guy. I only had to do it once, though, and it has made my Moodle run like a machine for me ever since. The Links plugin is great, and a real life saver for people like me. I can see how useful it can be for lots of other uses besides mine. I just have to hope that it never gets abandoned, because that function isn't in Moodle Core and I would be up a creek. The only drawback is the one at a time thing. For someone like me, you just power through them, and get them done. If someone had similar needs to me, but hundreds or thousands of accounts to set up, yikes. I guess they would also have the staff for it. It would be cool to see this plugin make it possible to add multiple links for different users all on one screen. That's just for convenience; it does its job well already. What I REALLY would love is to see Moodle itself support use cases like mine: the need to distribute individualized content (not just links, but assignments, announcements, activities, etc.) to individual students, even though they're all enrolled in one course together. Someday? EVEN BETTER: I would LOVE to discover that I'm wrong !!! and that Moodle can do all this, but I just don't know how. That would be a joyous discovery.
