ResponsesInList.Title: Re: QCA, e-assessments, e-portfolios
ResponsesInList.Text:
I attended a working forum/conference in April last year, where vendors, researchers and various
stakeholders of ePortfolios met. I have a couple of pages of notes, a sort of checklist of things to consider
when deciding on ePortfolio packages that I adapted from a brochure that was circulated at the conference. It is available here: http://mysandbox.net/ePortfolios.pdf . ( There's a link to the full brochure at the top of the document. ) I am using an
open source content and course management system called Segue which I link to as a resource from inside of moodle. Segue is an open source platform that supports both the creation and management of courseware and personal ePortfolios. Segue software empowers individuals with little to no HTML experience to produce impressive, personalized ePortfolios.
After looking at a
number of vendor and open source products, we found that
most of these tended to be overly determined with rigid or unadaptable
categories. One thing is certain, your learners and faculty will be
less
likely to embrace ePortfolios if they are unable to modify or
personalize
them to an extent. They really need to make them their own rather than simply
another
assessment activity. I saw a number of products that were promising but
it
became evident that teachers would feel uncomfortable with the
comlexities
of use, training and management of these products.
The Segue open source product seems to have the right balance of easy
to use
tools and adaptability or user defined arrangment and catagorization of
content. You can get a general understanding of how it works here: http://segue.middlebury.edu/index.php?&action=site&site=help If you would like to try out the one I have setup on my server, you can go to my site and register yourself as a Vistor: http://mysandbox.net/eportfolio . As a vistor you are given immediate access to the site through your email confirmation but you will need to email me to change your access level so that you can create your own portfolio: leblanc@mysandbox.net Although the system is quite intuitive, I have compiled some instructions . I found that new users often overlook the various features when they don't use the instructions. Seque uses php and mysql .

I am sure there are quite a few different interpretations of the nature of ePortfolios. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: QCA, e-assessments, e-portfolios
ResponsesInList.Text: Our approach to portfolios & eportfolios is that learners can choose whatever tool that suits them. If the portfolio project at Moodle takes sufficient shape, I will certainly introduce it to my learners. This is the same way that I have introduced Segue. It's available as an optional tool for those learners who want to use it. Some of our learners are highly skilled with Web based technologies and prefer to express themselves using their own tools. It's been a real struggle working out with instructors what portfolios are and everyone's role with regard to assessment, etc. (ex: Who owns the portfolio ) Instructors are confused that they will not actually assess primary artefacts (products) but rather the learners' reflections (process). Instructors look at the evidence learners present and more particularly the accompanying reflection learners have written to support why any given artefact fulfills the assessment criteria. I have presented Segue to my colleagues as an option that should alleviate fears some might have regarding privacy. Segue allows the user to choose who has access to their portfolio and what parts they can see, comment on, or even give edit access to others. Any artefact can also be accompanied by a threaded discussion that the portfolio user establishes. All that the instructors need to track is that the assessment criteria that has been completed and the grade accorded. Dr. Helen Barrett has an international reputation for her research in portfolios. Her Website has a multitude of links and resources: electronicportfolios.org

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle strategies to nurture social learning environment
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi all! I'm writing for two reasons, the first which is most relevant to this topic: 1) What moodle-strategies are people using to nurture a social learning environment in the classroom? I'm not sure how clear that is, so i'll provide an example from my own classroom environment. I have been using the Moodle's Topic view. Generally my topics are as follows: Each topic usually begins (as expected) with a relevant attention-grabbing activity/discussion of some sort designed to get people interested and focussed on the topic (This can be a simple HTML resource with links to interesting web-info). This is almost always followed by an HTML Resource containing the proposed learning outcomes for the topic (can be modified on the go if participants have other ideas for the topic). I usually follow this with a single-post forum containing some background questions related to the topic. Participants are required to reply to this post with their answers as well as links to where they found their information (sometimes this research is done in pairs). Hopefully this encourages participants' research skills. We then come together as a group and briefly outline the results of our research (I have the moodle forum projected at the front of the room). There is almost always a number of HTML Resources (or uploaded files) containing hands-on exercises for participants to learn the basics of the new skills in a number of different forms. This usually works towards apply the skills to our own projects. Sometimes the topic ends with a journal entry. Othertimes, it ends with a Workshop (if the learning can not be easily assessed in the major project). Very rarely I've included a choice (poll) but this is only because I often have difficulty creating decent questions to poll on. We always go over the Learning Outcomes again at the end to evaluate how we are going. Apart from the HTML Resource, I've found the Forum and Workshop activities to be extremely useful for nurturing a social learning environment, followed (quite a way behind) by the Journal and Choice activities. Bear in mind that i've only been using Moodle for 4 months, and I'm only just begining to learn about social constructivism ... Perhaps you can provide examples from your own experience demonstrating how you best use Moodle to nurture a social learning environment...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle strategies to nurture social learning environment
ResponsesInList.Text: Here is the fundamental barrier in a classroom - face to face talk. So you need activities that make them commit to a forum etc. instead of chatting. Some recent activities that worked fairly well in a classroom: Music technology: post an image (a spectagram, scrolling image showing the frequency distribution in music sample) in the start of a discussion with some open questions; asks students to comment (actually working in pairs on 1 workstation). Comment and question other postings. Computing: normalise a database (3 step process of making a database more efficient): work in pairs to do each step, post solution on forum, comment on other's answers, make relevant changes and move onto next step. Actually very reluctant to perform the peer assessment. [Would probably have done this one as a wiki task, but wiki only got installed a few days ago.Next time a set a group/research project, it will definitely use the wiki feature.] General: work in pairs to write very detailed glossary definitions. In fact, get thye students to contribute glossary contributions on a weekly basis- at the end of the course, they have a relevant dictionary for revision. Encourage comments, corrections and ratings. Seed each glossary with a few examples. If a student asks a question orally, ask him/her to post it instead. Journals: seed the journal with open questions, particularly related to progress or project management. I'm now getting some students being more honest through this medium about problems with the course than face to face. Use it for target setting. Is this the kind of specific thing that you mean? Looking back on it, the social comes from working in pairs, the activities are constructivist and constructionist . Cheers, Andy D

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle strategies to nurture social learning environment
ResponsesInList.Text: Gday Andy, Yep that's exactly the kind of specific thing that I was after! I had begun the semester (when I first started using Moodle), with Journal entries at the end of each topic, and tried to use the glossary too, but had not found them so useful! For the Journals, I think i'd based the open question around the subject matter, and this was my problem. When reading peoples entries I always thought: "hey, this should be a forum so everyone else can see what we've each written". I will try relating the journal questions to learner progress instead. As for the Glossary entries, I think I made it seem just like a task that students had to do... maybe I should try encouraging the comments, corrections and ratings. I think that working on the Glossary as an activity would be an excellent revision task now anyway, so I might try that! I am quite surprised that you see face2face talk as a fundamental barrier in the classroom... at first I thought you were joking, but then you said later that if a student asks a question orally, to get them to post it instead. I find that face 2 face talk is invaluable before, during and after activities. I try to ensure that the bulk of the information that learners develop is recorded within moodle (forums, journals, workshops etc), but not at the expense of face 2 face talking as a group. Can you clarify exactly what you mean? For example, in what situations do you find f2f talking beneficial, and in what situations would you point learners back to moodle? Thanks for all your ideas Andy! -Michael

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle strategies to nurture social learning environment
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, I think I understand Andy's comment on f2f barrier. Perhaps UK is more alike "continental" Europe than to Australia. I teach Biochemistry to first year university students. The main problem is getting them engaged. If you let a question on the air, in the classroom, you get all faces down, seeking for something on the floor. It's not Biochemistry, other topics suffer the same behavioral response from the learners. It's a combination of shame and shyness. If they ask something, that's a prove they don't know it. And if they answer, they fear been evaluated on it. So, students are quite reluctant to talk with the teacher in a teaching enviroment (they do talk about cinema or sports), just the opposite of what would be good for their learning. There is today, yet, a feeling of "class-fight" between teachers and students. The distance of the net let their fears relax in someway, and they do become more participative on-line than in the actual classroom, the f2f barrier is over. - Enrique Castro -

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle strategies to nurture social learning environment
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Michael, I've been trying to find some activities that involve students researching information for the larger group.  Individual forums can be organized so that students are going out into the world and gathering weblinks, etc., around specific topics...  I find this is a simple assignment that truly supports group learning.  Don't forget the power of Moodle's custom scales.  You can elicit feedback from peers on these posts by using the scales and making them visible or invisible, according to your purpose. But my favorite tool that you haven't mentioned is the glossary.  In our lit courses, I ask students to post concepts that they are discovering in their texts.  Someone might write about "forgiveness" in Hamlet.  The students are required to provide a quotation from the text that sets the concept in context , and then 2-3 sentences of literary analysis.  It takes absolutely no time for a class to create a healthy glossary of really significant ideas from the text.  These, too, can be rated by peers in terms of accuracy, helpfulness, etc..  The beauty of the hyperlinked glossary is that the concepts become part of all of the other course activities--so good ideas are not left behind. best, Tom

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Tom! Yeah, I love using the Single discussion forum as an intro to each topic to get learners researching info for the larger group... found this sort of thing invaluable. But again, maybe I've been jumping back to a classroom discussion of our findings too quickly? (I've just had a play with the custom scales.... very helpful!! Thanks for pointing me in the right direction.. i'll give the ratings a go today!) And as I replied to Andy, I'll give the glossaries a bit more effort too! So it sounds that people find the following tasks helpful for encouraging social constructivism in the classroom: Investigation activities (Single simple discussion forum where learners can work in pairs to reply with the results of their investigation, including links). Ratings are useful here. Journal activities for feedback on individual learner progress and feedback on the course itself. Also useful for setting goals or learning contracts. Glossary activities, again with comments and ratings being very useful. Workshops activities for with peer assessment (find this one invaluable myself), for encouraging formal feedback between peers as well as learning from each others work. Would anyone add any others? (Perhaps using choices, lessons, quizes?) Thanks again for your feedback, Andy and Tom!

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle is a very good Classroom-Assistant for traditional classes also
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, folks Moodle is a very good classroom-assistant (web-enchancement) for traditional classes, too.  I have 5 traditional classes using Moodle for web-enhanced activities , watching online videos, filing reports about the videos, and general discussions.  Students are rating each others' reports about the movies they've watched online. Classes had a 1st major test.  I have the Moodle-classroom-assistant scores.  So, I did a correlation of 1st test scores to classroom-assistant scores.  In 3 sections , some 80 people or so, the correlation coefficient was .29 (p < .06).  While just missing statistical signficance by a hair, the data show a positive correlation coefficient meaning that as classroom assistant grades increase, test grades increase.  This is hard data indicating that Moodle is doing the job well as the web-enhanced "classroom assistant" in helping students to learn the material. Just thought you would like to know there's hard data supporting the use of Moodle in a web-enhanced traditional classroom.  Certainly the content has bearing on this correlation but, without Moodle, there would be no content to engage students in further learning. It would be an interesting PhD dissertation to see 5 different platforms employed as classroom assistants, each with the same content, correlated to grades on reliable alternate tests or even same tests to discern the power of the platform to improve scores.  I would hazard to guess that Moodle, being so engaging and fun as compared to the clunky proprietary non-pedagogical platforms, would show itself to be statistically significantly better in improving students' grades. Somebody go do that dissertation, please.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: registration key
ResponsesInList.Text: The idea of the registration key is to only allow students on the course that you know should be on the course and you need to give them the key before they enrol. If you want anyone to enrol, leave that field blank

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: registration key
ResponsesInList.Text: You can only use the registration key if you have contact with your students in real life. I'm a teacher and have many classes. I make a registration key for every class and give him to my students at school. They write him in their agenda and can enroll to that course.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: registration key
ResponsesInList.Text: For some of our classes, we have used the registration/enrollment key the other way round, so to speak: We first let the students join the course (without any enrollment key required), and once all of the students have "arrived," we activate the enrollment key, preventing "guests" from joining the course. In the worst case, the teacher would have to unenroll any unauthorized student manually. This way the students need not bother with the enrollment key, they can't "lose" it, nor can they start "sharing" the key.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: registration key
ResponsesInList.Text: Markus, Another way of controlling access is to use the course "enrolment period."  Simply set a period of time that your course will accept enrolments after which students cannot join. This in conjunction with your activation of an enrolment key should work fine! Jeff

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Examples of Moodle's Social Constructionism?
ResponsesInList.Text: To boil down lots of books and papers into two sentences, my take is this: Social constructivism is about the internal process of constructing knowledge within a social environment and through social interactions. Social constructionism focuses on the learning power of constructing artifacts for (and with) others in a social environment. For a slightly longer exposition, see Moodle Philosophy .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Examples of Moodle's Social Constructionism?
ResponsesInList.Text: As I understand it [0], Social ConstructioNism builds on Social ConstructiVism, but emphasises the importance of building something together. Social constructivism is about building internal knowledge structures in a social context based on one's prior understanding; constructionism is about building external artefacts as a means to more effectively build the inner knowledge structures. From "Situating Constructionism", Papert and Harel: ( http://www.papert.org/articles/SituatingConstructionism.html ) Constructionism--the N word as opposed to the V word--shares constructivism's connotation of learning as "building knowledge structures" irrespective of the circumstances of the learning. It then adds the idea that this happens especially felicitously in a context where the learner is consciously engaged in constructing a public entity, whether it's a sand castle on the beach or a theory of the universe. Regards, Cormac. [0] Disclaimer: I am not an authority on this, I've only recently begun reading about social constructionism, although I'm looking forward to discovering more and putting it into practice in the forthcoming academic year.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Examples of Moodle's Social Constructionism?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi: Frankly, my own sense of the constructi v e - ism versus the constructio n - ism discussion, is that this is a particular moodle-like distinction.  In fact, this discussion itself is part of the process of engaging in the social construction of knowledge.  A key publication in setting out this idea of the social construction of knowledge is the book: Berger and Luckmann's The Social Construction of Reality (1966).  If you want to go to one of the sources of contemporary theorizing on this topic, that would be a good resource.  I am not suggesting that it is an easy resource to read, but if you want a seminal work, that would be one. A more 'quick and dirty' summary -- in the context of collaborative learning --  might be a paper by Arthur Warmoth .  I am not suggesting this paper is the definitive source; but it is a source which seems to be substantive and authoritative. Hope this is of some help. Don

ResponsesInList.Text: From the tone of the article, I think too much was expected of the medium of elearning in facilitating interaction, and less attention was paid to the role of teachers and students themselves in facilitating interaction. I haven't started teaching with Moodle yet, but in my previous online teaching (which was an adult education class for personal enrichment where interaction was the only "activity" in the course beside perusing the course material) we used an email discussion list for interaction. One thing I did that helped to get the ball rolling for discussion was to post a few "suggested discussion topics" with each unit. Students would post their thoughts on those topics, and also opened topics of their own. Also, there is the issue of intimidation. If not properly controlled, some students can dominate the conversation and make other students feel put off. On my email list, students were allowed to post only one message a day. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Best Practice
ResponsesInList.Text: This can definitely be done online!   Here's a few tips for one style of teaching I found successful: The teacher needs to firstly take an interest in actually teaching. Read the help documentation on reading , writing , questions etc Teacher and others should seek to find about each other using the profiles and other reports in Moodle.  Try some of the surveys, they do really work.  Set up an "Each user" forum and ask everyone to introduce themselves with a new discussion, then ask them to respond at least twice to other people. Now present resources that are relevant to the goals of the course, but ALSO relevant to the background of your students. After each burst of content, think of activities for students to express what they've learned and to talk it through.  Emphasise direct relevance to students.  Use a journal with your personal feedback, then follow up with an open forum, or try a glossary building exercise.  You may want to have a small assignment in there.Try forums with and without ratings - think up different interesting scales for students to rate each other on. Make a regular chat time for live sychronous connections (or face to face if possible), it can really make a difference to the asynchronous stuff. Continually revise future weeks of the course based on the feedback you are getting from the activities. Keep it relevant, keep it active. Check on individual students (activity report) and try to think of ways to motivate individuals who are having problems. As you can see, my ideal style of teaching is not drill and grill.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Best Practice
ResponsesInList.Text: I've found that discussion boards can be either the most productive tool in an online course, or the worst use of time and energy. It all has to do with how carefully the discussions are planned and monitored, and how well the activity fits with the learning goals. I've taken, designed, and taught quite a few courses, have a master's in online teaching & learning, and find discussion boards in general to be the least well planned element of many online courses. Often discussion forums are added to a course just because people think they should be there. I disagree. They should be there if they are creatively used and contribute to the learning. They should be absent if the only assignments are "please read and post what you think". This is boring and overdone. Some courses lend themselves beautifully to creative uses of discussion boards, like debates, role playing, editorials, you name it. I teach several courses that are designed to teach specific skills (e.g., web design in Dreamweaver). I don't use discussion boards in this way in those courses, because I don't find it useful. I do use them as Q&A Boards in these kinds of courses. In either case, we can be much more creative than 10 assignments in a semester of "post what you think and respond to one".

ResponsesInList.Title: Hitler Youth Instructional Unit
ResponsesInList.Text: Okay, our third-year German students will read two novels this coming year in which the Hitler Youth organization plays a significant role ( Die weisse Rose and Damals war es Friedrich ). We would, of course, be speaking and writing in German (well, 99% of the time). We know how we would develop our traditional instructional unit, but how would we begin to make the unit more constructivist ? Here's the begining of our thinking of what such an instructional unit might look like (very tentative!): Topic: Hitler Youth Objectives: Upon completion of this unit, the learner will be able to: * discuss the structure and objectives of the Hitler Youth in Nazi Germany * discuss the advantages and disadvantages of belonging to the Hitler Youth * discuss both postive and negative aspects of group membership in society in general Extension: If students wished to do so, we could take a trip to the Holocaust Museum in Washington, DC. This is unlikely, though. This seems like a pretty traditional unit to us. (It would take a three weeks, by the way.) But it does require students to construct things for one another, collaboratively creating a small culture of shared artifacts with shared meanings [ link ], doesn't it? What do you guys think? (Go ahead, be honest. We can take it.) -- Art

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Hitler Youth Instructional Unit
ResponsesInList.Text: Art, I am a social studies teacher and the unit looks like something I would do in class.  You might also want to discuss why someone would be attracted to a group, what the group does for self esteem and belonging.  Also, maybe talk about nationalism, as the Hitler Youth was a nationalistic organization. Are the Boy Scouts of America nationalistic, and if so, what is the difference? A neat activity might be to break them up into groups... 1, 2, 3, 4 and have all the 1's research and write about a certain aspect of the book or the Hitler Youth... all the 2's do another aspect and so on... Then, have each group break down further... 1a, 1b, 1c, 2a, 2b, 2c... and have all the A's get together, all the B's, all the C's.  Each group would have an "expert" in their field, who would teach the others what they have learned. Nice collaborative/cooperative learning activity. As far as grading, giving a grade for the items you create, like the posters, or the discussion forums and powerpoint presentaions would be a more authentic assessment.  How about creating a Web Museum of the Hitler Youth.  You could create a new class in Moodle that would serve to teach others about what you students learned.  You could find sound bites, pictures, texts, include your own forum discussions, create a glossary of terms,... lots of cool stuff. I always wanted to do colloborative things with the English teachers in my old school, but they were not interested.  But, nothing teaches history better than contemporary literature... in any language!! Nice looking unit. Jeff

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Hitler Youth Instructional Unit
ResponsesInList.Text: Wow, Tom, that really is an interesting resource. A colleague and I have talked several times about the need for educational role playing games (Internet-based RPG's), but we have never really done more than talk. I could imagine making use of the hot seating technique described in the paper: Hot-seating is a form of a role play, in which students take roles of historical persons and prepare themselves for the interview in front of the classroom. I find this activity very useful. Each student in the class is an expert of one historical person and he or she shares the knowledge of this person with the whole class. The rest of the class are advised to ask relevant questions from the student in the hot seat. By using this method, students understand that the same historical event might have very different interpretations. For example, if students are asked to take roles of historical persons who witnessed the destruction of the Spanish Armada in 1688 the results of the class discussion could be interesting. The roles and questions could be: Spanish sailor: Why did he join the Armada? Spanish soldier: Why did he want to take part in the invasion of England? King Philip II of Spain: Why did he disliked Elizabeth I and why did he want to invade England? Duke of Parma (Commander of the Spanish fleet): Why was he sure that the Spanish Armada would be victorious? Francis Drake: Why did the Spanish hate him? Elizabeth I: Why she did not want to marry Philip II of Spain and why she think that a war with Spain was inevitable? English sailor: Why did he think that the English would defeat the Spanish Armada? Hot-seating enables students to think about the notion of historical truth and by listening to the different subjective stories about the history of the Spanish Armadas invasion of England, students learn the skills of historical interpretation. Of course, I would really have to think a lot about how to use this technique. But it certainly might be a useful exercise! -- Art

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Hitler Youth Instructional Unit
ResponsesInList.Text: Dear Ralf, I think there is a theme that runs through our instruction here: that individuals, groups and even societies sometimes descend into something like evil and that the consequences can be unspeakable. When our students read Conrad's Heart of Darkness , they are confronted with a story of a man who goes over to the dark side. When they read Goldings Lord of the Flies , they must try to make a sense of a group of school boys who do the same. And when they read a simplified version of Sophie Scholl's The White Rose , they must consider what happens when an entire country does so. (Conrad's and Goldings' stories are fiction, I know, but I think that most or many teenagers are sophisticated enough to understand that there is truth in the premise that in the absence of normal social constraints, things can go horribly awry.) I am sure that it is true that the Nazis were unique in many ways, but I am never comfortable saying so. There are so many examples of inhumanity thoughout history, I just don't know. I see it in the world today, too. And teachers have to find a way to deal with even uncomfortable topics like this one. Frankly, I find it much easier to talk about the dative case and possessive adjectives. -- Art

Then, students could research specific Stalinist policies to determine how well they worked for the Soviet Union, and the people as a whole. Here is a chart I did for another project that is a simple explanation of the different economic systems. Economic Systems Market Based upon Supply and Demand Usually focus on consumer goods Little government control Command Controlled by strong, centralized government Usually focuses on industrial goods Little attention paid to agriculture and consumer goods Mixed Combination of Market and Command economic systems Market forces control most consumer goods Government directs industry in need areas. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Instructional Design Issues
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Abdul, IMHO the priority list for an e-learning course design: 1. Robust 2. intuiative navigation 3. Design around what students are going to DO rather than what content you want to deliver 4. Whizzy things I would therefore go for '2' in your option list if I have to choose:  streaming stuff leads to complications (suddenly not robust).  Number 1 sounds as if you are thinking how to deliver content to them and are a bit vague about what they will 'do' (hotpot tests', '..go through lecture'). Can I suggest another approach?  Since this is about writing you could really do some great things with forum work, e.g. give students some text to edit, have them post their different versions in a forum.  When they are used to this do the exercise with another bit of writing and, publish thier edits and then get them to assess each others edits.  This is a very powerful teaching technique - you will have to police their feedback carefully though - make sure they know how to feedback politely to each otherwise you could have some flaming wars on your hands. The advantages of the above:  Forums are v robust and simple, students will engage carefully with the 'doing', you should get some interesting results which can be further discussed with the students.  For further reading Gilly Salmons books should be of use. I hope I've understood you well enough for that to be of use All the best Richard

ResponsesInList.Title: Need advice on online teaching strategies
ResponsesInList.Text: I teach computer information systems courses at a community college (Intro to Programming with VB.NET, Advanced VB.NET, and Database Design). Our courses lead to a two-year degree in Computer Information Systems with concentrations in Software Development, Networking, or E-Business. I have taught the same courses both in the classroom and online and have found that teaching online is much more difficult and time consuming than in the classroom. As this semester nears an end, I have had my first chance to take a breath and start to realize the stress that online teaching has caused me. In the past, much of my stress could be attributed to the rattletrap LMS our school was using. But, since I jumped ship and started to run my courses on my own Moodle site, that stressor has vanished .   I am left with the realization that I must be doing one or more things wrong in the way I am administering my courses. Perhaps if I explain how I teach my online courses, some of you out there can see where I can make improvements to both save me time and effort as well as help my students improve their chances for success. Using my Intro to Programming with VB.NET course as an example, here is what I do: Students have about 1 programming project to turn in per week. I download these, unzip them, and bring them up in the VB.NET IDE to test their function and examine the students coding. This is, of course, very time consuming, but I have yet to figure out how a student can learn computer programming without actually writing computer programs . Students post in the forums if they need help. I respond as often as I can and encourage other students to help out as well. I do not award any credit for other students helping out in the forums (I can't seem to figure out a fair model for awarding points or I would try). Answering questions in the forums really takes a huge amount of time for me. We have many displaced workers as well as other students who have marginal academic skills. There are sometimes some gems, but most struggle and need lots and lots of attention to help them have a shot at grasping the material. I really work hard to help my students succeed, but there have been several times I have taught the course where I have had upwards of a 50% withdrawal rate by the 12th week of the 16 week semester. I provide downloadable as well as streaming video of "lectures" that I create with Camtasia and convert into .wmvs. This helps the students a lot, but I would like to find the time to make more for them to watch. I have two hands-on "tests" each term in which the students complete several small programming project in a fixed amount of time. They complete these tests at their home and upload them to me in the same way as a regular programming assignment. These also take quite a bit of time to grade. I have one 10-20 questions timed multiple-choice quiz each week. These are taken with the Quiz feature in Moodle so I do not have to spend time grading these. Now, what could I do to streamline all of this so that I am not online or grading all the time? We are adopting new texts (I got to pick them out, so they fit my teaching philosophy) so now is an excellent time for me to radically change how I administer my courses. Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated. Thanks Paul Norrod

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Need advice on online teaching strategies
ResponsesInList.Text: I found that my learners gain much more by working collaboratively on programming assignments in pairs or small groups. This cuts down on the amount of marking I must complete each week and puts the onus on the learners to coordinate their efforts and engage in activities . I am teaching Java which also has some advantages with the abiity to extend code. I generally will post a simplified or base level program. The learners then take my code or someone else's posted code and extend it. This way, everyone learns from everyone else. I have been using a combination of moodle and FLE to run my class. FLE has something called a Jamming session which supports course participants to publically view and post artefacts, in this case programs and screen shots of program runs. Naturally, this generates a good deal of peer-to-peer discussion. I find that learners are encouraged to build upon what others know and do, and a very supportive atmosphere is engendered. In fact, I sometimes am able to sit back since questions are often answered by fellow students before I've had a chance to respond. Instead of the tutor/instructor being solely responsible or being the 'authority' for the students learning, they have, for the most part, taken on this role themselves.

ResponsesInList.Text: Well done David; that's the whole idea of collaborative online learning. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Need advice on online teaching strategies
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Paul, You've got me on my favourite soapbox with this question:  'The importance of teaching design and skills in online learning': Firstly, your retention is better than you think.  On an introduction to computing course we regularly lost 65% of students and they were not 'needy' students like yours and many of them had done multiple (paper based) distance learning courses before. Suggestions: 1. Cut back on some of the content of your course.  No one likes doing this ('cutting the legs off my baby' is how a colleague once put it.) but if you do you will create some space in which I would explicitly teach 'how to communicate in moodle' skills.  The skills should be assessed.  Your justification in doing this is that programmers can get a lot of advice for free by using various forums and they need to know how to get help and what help they can expect from such a source. To teach communication skills get students to take part in a warm up exercise so they get the technical skills of posting and replying and, more importantly start thinking of themselves as a group.  I can refer you to some texts for this if you want.  Then get them to practise posting replies to discussions in a supportive manner.  I would guess your students tend to be technical, separate learners.  You want them to do things like acknowledge, criticise constructively, invite replies.  eg instead of: 'that code was dumb.  You can't use that variable in VBNet, look at your text book', you want 'Hi Pete, you've done some good work on this code, its put together pretty well.  I spotted an error, I think you've used an illegal variable on line 20.  Am I right?  Hope this has been useful - John'. Once you have got them used to these skills you can test them.  I would assign a small mark (5 -10% of overall grade) and just skim read 3 of their messages to see that they've got the point.  Mark high as a way of avoiding them complaining.  Marking such things is open to interpretation and your using the assessment as a way of getting them to engage rather than to really grade them (hence small % of overall grade). 2.  Now you've got them with the skills to communicate well, you need to use the 'golden silence'.  This is counter intuative but I've seen it work spectacularly well - you want to facilitate them answering each others questions and you do this..... ....by not answering their questions . I'll explain: Your student support should be heavily wieghted towards the first few weeks of the course - I guess this is when you lose most students?  Answer their queries quickly and praise any student supporting any other student.  You may also want to phone them up for a 15 minute 'welcome to the course, how are you finding it conversation'.  This is very time consuming but it pays divedends because students feel supported and as David noted once they feel part of a group and not anxious hopefully they will begin to support each other. As they start to help each other out you should withdraw from the forums (leave a question unanswered for more and more time), this will encourage them to help each other out.  Eventually you should watch what is going on in the forums (be gentle on people giving wrong advice and do it via email, allow them to correct their error in the forums) and only post if someone speciffically calls on you to answer a question in a forum. When it works you will be amazed how much they help each other, they come to think of the forum not as a place where you post answers but their space to help each other - they may even forget you are looking in. Note I say 'hopefully'.  Groups differ, you almost have to have a core of 3 great students who want to be supportive to each other to genererate a supportive group and sometimes you just don't get them. You also may just have a very needy set of students from what you say so this advice may not be that helpful. Be explicit in explaining to them that they should be supportive of each other.  I'm not sure it needs grading but you can explain to them that in answering questions they are learning more themselves. 3.  I think you may be able to cut down on assessment.  Davids solution of getting them to work in pairs is good, I'd let them do an assignment on their own then get them to work in pairs and only produce one assignment between them.  This may cause problems if one person ducks out of the work though. Another way is to invest time in replacing some of the assignments with multiple choice tests, cleverly written MCQs can test a lot of the skills of coding without having students do coding.  I certainly think an assignment and an MCQ per week is too much. You can also use Davids advice about producing a bit of code and ask them to improve it in specific ways, again, this can be used to test their coding skills but it will hugely cut down on marking time because 20 coding projects from scratch will have a huge variation in structure. However, you are absolutely right that they have to produce code and IMHO at least a third of your assignments should be 'produce code to do this from scratch'. 4.  Your online lectures sound like they are a useful learning tool, I wonder though if you could develop different multimedia resources that are quicker to produce and as effective.  To comment on this you'd have to let me see one of your lectures. Phew! I've spouted a lot of stuff here assuming all kinds of things, if you want to flag which could be useful I could expand further and in a more focussed way. Richard

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: FrontPage Course - Feedback Invited!
ResponsesInList.Text: David, First, you should get familiar with course properties as they pertain to Group mode .  If you click Settings on the course homepage you will bring up the properties window. The Group mode property allows you to make one of three selections for how Groups will behave. In my illustration I have selected "Separate groups" and enabled Force so that the feature is active within the course. Next, you will want to to click the Group icon on the course homepage to establish members for each group you will define.  Unless you have clicked the "Turn editing on" button, you will not see anything when you enter the Group setup window.  When you have done this, you will see a list of all users that are enrolled in the course in the left column, teachers and students alike. Groups does not care what status a user has.  There are three columns: People not in a group Groups Members of selected group In the center column (Groups) you have an option to "Add new group" names.  Do this for whatever groups you wish to create (e.g., Tutor Jones, Tutor Smith etc.).  Next, simply assign each user to a particular group, INCLUDING the tutor, displayed in the left column by first highlighting the group you have created and then using the "Add selected to group" button.  Experiment with this, you really cannot screw up anything as you add/delete in your practice setup. A few things to consider :  When you add teacher/tutors to a course by clicking the "Teacher" (or whatever name assigned in course properties) link in the Administration panel on the course homepage, you have an option when making a user a teacher as to whether they will have "Editing" permissions.  Generally, the teacher who is the course creator is the only user who should be given Editing permissions. These permissions allow the teacher to alter the course itself, something that will effect all groups.  Therefore, assign this permission with oversite.  Finally, although isolated in their own group, tutors are able to view certain activities (Forums etc.) in other groups if they wish (birds-eye view). This will become evident as you explore the feature and determine what settings will work for you. Hope this has been helpful. Bryan

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to set up extra credit?
ResponsesInList.Text: The way I do extra credit is as follows. (1) Set up an assignment called Extra Credit .  Make it worth 1 point, and give every student 1 point on that assignment.  This way, no penalty.  Every student starts with 100% on this "assignment", and you have nothing to explain to the students. (2)  When you want to give a student Extra Credit, modify the assignment to be worth, say 100 points temporarily. (3) ADD the number of extra credit points into this "assignment" for each student.  Don't forget to leave them the 1 point they already had.  So if they just earned 10 extra points, they now have 11 Extra Credit points  (10 plus the 1 "default" point). (I know... this is silly... about as silly as Moodle not having Extra Credit in my opinion.) (4) MODIFY the assignment BACK to being out of 1 points possible. The end... Hopefully, once Gustav's new calculated grade module is part of the general distribution, we can all forget this Extra Credit nonsense Dan

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: I don't mean to sound flippant by saying that I do my best to collapse the three Moodles that you have described into one. But I think I hear your question. You wonder how a student's ideas (written into a forum or journal) might match words that are stored in an out-of-sight glossary? I believe the process is the same as those people in this forum who write their posts, save them, and while reviewing for edits, recognize that there is a glossary link available to them. True, the author might not have chosen "the right words" that trigger such a connection, but that is ok. I never intend for Moodle to make the primary connections between ideas (that's why classmates respond to each other and why the teacher stays involved). But, for certain, more secondary connections are happening in Moodle because of forums and glossaries then on any student's pad of paper. Another good activity is to have students regularly rate the various glossary definitions. 1) it helps the writer become clearer; and 2) it gets the class thinking about whether the concepts in the glossary adequately "cover" the ideas posed in the class. This activity increases the chances that a student will adopt some of the terminology used by others in the course. -Tom

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: One excample of Moodle supporting the learning theories of "sosial constructivism ": Lets say one person makes this post into a Moodle discussion forum: "Can anybody support the opinion that Moodle supports social constructionist pedagogy?" That person might experiece that he is able to find out a whole lot about "sosial contructivism" by himself alone, but still he find it interresting to to make this post to optain som answers and comments from other "moodlers". Lets imagine there is i practical "learning zone" between what this person are able to find out allone byhimself and what he might be able to find out working together with and optaining some help from people in his environment. This difference between what a person is able to find out allone and what this person is able to find out or learn cooperation with orthers is by by Lev Vygotsky called  "the zone of proximal development ". But back to the definitions of the moodle web page: <Quote> This extends the above ideas into a social group constructing things for one another, collaboratively creating a small culture of shared artifacts with shared meanings. When one is immersed within a culture like this, one is learning all the time about how to be a part of that culture, on many levels. <Unquote> But why should it be only "constructing things for one other" ? I think the learning situation will require 3 or 4 elements: 1. "The learning object", the "problem area" or that "the learner" are working against, while "constructing" his knowlege as a result og the interactive "dialog" against his "learning environment". (Examples: electrical engines mathematical tasks or german grammar) 2. The "learner" or the "student" himself. 3. The teacher. 4. The other "learners" much in the same role as the teacher. According my point of view "the learner" is more constructing his knowledge on basis on his interactions with the learning environment, using the help from "the other", not as a primarly result of explaining the things for "the others". Of cource he might learn even more also from explaining his new obtained knowledge for "the others" but this will, as I would see it be the secondary learning effect. The primiry learning prosess will be learning by interacting directely against a "physical or technical" learning environmant, beeing in "the zone of proximal development", learning even more, using the help from "the others". " S ocial constructionist pedagogy" that is a method of learning. Moodle that is a tool for teaching and learning. The tool does not neccesarly make a method, and a method do not neccesarely require one certain tool, as I would see it. I think that Moodle is a very flexible tool for teaching and learning. I think it actually would be possible to adapt Moodle as a "learning tool" to nearly any method of teaching and learning. It actually support, as I would see it, the typical "functions" and "dataflows" you would find in any general learning environment independent of learning method. I also think that Moodle as a tool has functions and potensials that will fit very well for a learning environment based at "sosial constructivism" as a learning method . By the way - if Lev Vygotsky is considered not to be "sosial contructivism in the Moddle way" I would be interested to know. Best reg Arne.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text:
May I ask us to pause and reflect a little on our reflections? First, Dimitris poses a question about the philosophy of Moodle's educational methodology. How does Moodle support social constructivist pedagogy? (I also notice that Dimitris appears not subscribed to this forum or even a member of this course. So we are kind of like whispering behind his back, aren't we? This feels a little funny to me--a problem of collaboration?--must we *force* problem posers to continue in the collaboration? If a problem poser disappears for a while, it maybe feels like a teacher giving us a task to do, then let us muddle around (moodle around?) til we have an answer to report back (and maybe get a warm pat on the back). I guess that process is not so "funny" after all, but rather typical. Then, Martin invites Dimitris to ask more specific questions. He asks Dimitris to tell us more about himself. Martin, ever polite and pleasent, does not take offense at the abruptness and possible skepticism of Dimitris' posting. Surprisingly, he asks about Dimitris' background. What does that have to do with the question? Is this a touchy-feely personality style? Or is it a part of social constructivism, that to begin learning together we must know the context from which each member of our little learning group is coming from? Next, Tom gives some examples of how he sees Moodle supporting social constructivism. The glossary in particular. Tom shows his sincerity to answer Dimitris' request for examples, giving details on how a glossary project would be collaborative and constructivist. I feel hungry for more examples. Besides student-generated glossaries, what else is constructivist? Arne joins in and widens the discussion to some of the theoretical concerns of Vygotsky. He points out that Moodle actually supports "...the typical 'functions' and 'dataflows' you would find in any general learning environment..." He concludes that Moodle is a tool, not necessarily constructivist. I am beginning to like this topic, as I have to think about these theories for a paper I am writing. Now I decide to read and join in soon. He annoyingly keeps spelling "sosial", but that causes me to think--maybe there is more than one way to spell a word? Maybe in Norwegian English, that is convention. Maybe, there is always more than one right answer--even in seemingly objective worlds such as spelling. Or maybe it simply means the Norwegian keyboard does not have a "c". Ger picks up on the questions of a zone of proximal development and adds... Didn't you just KNOW that Ger would join this discussion? The question is, why did it take him so long? Arne returns and adds more comments about Vygotsky. Now I am really interested. Arne is clearly not so interested in the initial task--answering a visitor's question--as Martin and Tom tried to do.  He is taking charge of the dialogue to move in directions he is interested in. He has changed the learning task of our group to deal with a broader issue--the core of Moodle's educational philosophy and method. I think about this and wonder if maybe I should begin adding my own points. But I decide not to, and instead ask a bunch of questions. What is going here? Is this an example of social constructivist education? Why the colors? What do they mean? What of the above dialogue was constructivist and what was not? How does Moodle support constructivim and how does it not? What is my own goal for this learning group? The original question or the latest one? What do I want from this discussion? Should I facilitate the others' needs? Or push my own questions? Next, Don shares thoughts on these questions. What is going here? Is this an example of social constructivist education? Yes, I think so. For me at least, the dialogue helped me understand something I could not realize by my own individual study. My own individual study was tested, questioned, and then I felt compelled to construct an interpretation of what five people were talking about. I reflected on the role I wanted to take and risked myself by taking a new role I was unsure of. Why the colors? What do they mean? They are meant to show the functional role of different kinds of comments in the dialogue. Black=analytic summary Blue=subjective reflection Brown=interpretative questions Green=my own answers to those questions Colors also broaden the educational input to appeal to more learning styles. What of the above dialogue was constructivist and what was not? Yes,
I believe this was constructivist dialogue because not everyone was forced to join this topic--only those for whom it was interesting or compelling. Also, the problem was changed by the needs or wants of the members. Third, there is reflection and summarizing in the dialogue. Fourth, I integrated the knowledge into my own thinking and I played around with it. How does Moodle support constructivim and how does it not? Moodle did support it by
providing a forum tool, an HTML editor that allowed coloring and
emoticons, and face photos so that I could begin to know my classmates
and talk in a more intimate manner. However, almost any forum software
can do this. The constructivist dialogue that happened here was through intervention by members
who employed there own conscious/unconscious teaching/facilitating
strategies. The role-taking, summarizing, reflecting was not encouraged, prompted nor forced by Moodle. Moodle simply did not get in the way. However, for Moodle to suggest it is uniquely constructivist or supports constructivist pedagogy better than others is probably wrong (but true in the case of comparisons to our arch-enemies WebCT and Blackboard --chorus of boos in the background). Moodle the community is constructivist, not Moodle the software. Let me shout that: * Moodle the community is constructivist *. Why? Because its facilitators facilitate that way. It's the same as in face-to-face classrooms. Some classrooms are collaborative and many are not. What is my own goal for this learning group? The original question or the latest one? What do I want from this discussion? Should I facilitate the others' needs? Or push my own questions? OK, I think I am going to push some of my questions and points. First, I want Moodle the software to become more constructivist. I want the forums tool go beyond serial listings to have prompting mechanisms to summarize, reflect, archive, prune, rearrange, and formulate a library of group knowledge. Already it is doing that with threading of replies, searchable keywords, group-work options, etc, etc (so it is unfair and exaggerating for me to say Moodle is not constructivist). But bear with me on this point. I do not have specific designs in mind, but I will think about that and collaborate on that this year. I will ask more questions to Ger, Arne, Tom, Martin and Dimitris about about Activity Theory, Social Constructivist Theory and other thoughts they have. I want to discuss task definition and design as well. Martin said somewhere that he likes IMS as a standard because, like Moodle, it approaches education as a sequence of tasks. I really want to think about that--especially as we map out version 2.0. So Dimitris, Martin, Tom, and Ger... Would you agree with Arne's suggestion that Moodle is an empty tool, a general learning environment, that could be constructivist if used that way? Would you agree with my suggestion that Moodle can be more constructivist if given more development of processes that force various levels of reflection and collaboration? And finally, should we spend more effort reflecting and summarizing our dialogue? Is it merely sensitivity training or is this a useful pattern to create consciousness of consciousness in discussions? Special thanks to Kierkegaard, whom I believe was involved in the original design of Moodle...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: Why did it take him so long... I try to read more of your writings and to write less.. ..and only testing all the new stuff in Moodle and giving it a good place in our local view on a good integrated educational setting is very time-consuming. This special way of using the "zone" by Arne triggered me. (Reconsidering it now, I must say that Arne extended the use of the zone in a clever way: people are part of that zone, so, yes in theory he is right ) Lets state things more clear, just for the discussion: It is interesting to know that Martin started to build Moodle because he could not find a tool that filled his SC-needs. For me that becomes part of the Myths around Moodle, like the fact that the designer of the Mac "stole" this idea during a bus-trip-visit to the Xerox-labs, or that Bill Gates bought the draft for MSDOS in a dark garage from a previous friend.) It is more interesting to check if Martin was succesfull in his attempt, so check Moodle against a SC-benchmark. (SC-benchmark, tuned for eLearning?? Does anybody know one?) A tool is as bad/good as it's user: There are a lot of tools that bring limitations in the educational arena. With the best intentions we made in the past tools that prevented the users to do the wrong things and then we were surprised that nobody used these tools.. In the previous century Dutch Architects built for the working class houses with small windows. Why? Because these working class people where spending to much time with hanging out of the windows... SCORM limits learning to "learning on your own", that's why I do not like if people say that I ONLY may use SCORM. But also using SC in a to restricted way can elict limitations: The resistance of Martin against the Quizzes in the beginning (= "SC does not allow") and the long discussion about giving the quizz on one big sheet to give the student optimal control (= "SC prescribes that"), paying the price of a higher chance of sheeting. (Martin and others may fine tune this) New options in Moodle have their dangers: with the new lessons modul you can create great learning experiences like the TITANIC example, but you can also fallback in programmed instruction. From boring quizzes, teacher made glossaries and wrong use of dialogues you can say the same. Our discussion should go about the tricks we can built in to elict (NOT limit) the good use of these tools. For me the clearinghouse in glossary is one of these tricks. A good theory can help, but ten good theories can help better:  It helps you to see your educational construct from different point of views and with that wisdom you can improve your creation. So not only SC, but als "students in control of their own learning" (Dalton, Montessori, Freire, Rogers,Maslow, Bandura, Abelson, Clark, Gagne, Merrill, Romisowsky, Reighluth, van Merrienboer, fill in your own favorites...) What I hate the most is declaring the current educational system Old Fashioned: Old wine in new bottles. (What is against good old wine? Keep the good wine, improve your bottles, but do it step by step! Revolutions like Mindstorms in the past are doomed to fail. ) The good news about Moodle is that it is open and rich, but for "students in control" and "students building togheter their own knowledge constructs" we need moch more moduls and.... THE TUNABLE ROLES from Moodle version 2 (July 2004?!?!?)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: Would you agree with Arne's suggestion that Moodle is an empty tool, a general learning environment, that could be constructivist if used that way? Nope. I think it could only be considered an empty tool (and I suppose this might be possible in a really strange classroom), if a teacher never allowed or encouraged students to answer, amplify, or question each other's responses in forums (note the help links in the forum module--I don't see those in other bb's); or if a teacher never allowed forums to be rated by the class; or if a teacher refused to let students add to a glossary; or if the old information that went into forums would never be used, later, by students who were constructing responses to new questions (think of all the good work that is "saved" in Moodle, students working in notebooks do not build collaboratively). Would you agree with my suggestion that Moodle can be more constructivist if given more development of processes that force various levels of reflection and collaboration? I agree that role defining, etc., might help teachers and students recognize how their interaction puzzles together an atmosphere of learning and construction, but I would tend to recommend that Moodle increase the number of pop-up help menus that describe this kind of behavior, rather than using role-defining modules. True, if someone told me to be a father on Tuesday and a husband on Wednesday, I might be able to concentrate on those role-specific tasks, but I'm not aware of any particular week when anything is that cut and dry. Likewise, bringing these concerns to the attention of the students is helpful, but I believe that future updates of Moodle don't need such specific processes added to the interface, per se. And finally, should we spend more effort reflecting and summarizing our dialogue? Is it merely sensitivity training or is this a useful pattern to create consciousness of consciousness in discussions? I think to be able to "debrief" any activity is hugely important in a classroom. Even Outward Bound (a wilderness classroom) stops students (on the far side of a frozen river) to ask how the river-crossing went. What can be learned? What can be changed? Who deserves kudos and thanks? In "feature requests" in the bug-tracker, I've asked for debrief forums to be attached to any activity, but the fact is, debriefing probably doesn't need a special tool in Moodle -- you've already done it for us here and invited response -- what Moodle needs are teachers and students who pick up on some of these habits. Overall, I think Martin has been wise to be stubborn on issues like quizzes. He wants Moodle to be a really good tool for really good teaching. Sometimes really good teaching consists of intense dialogue and practice (journals, forums, assignments, workshops, dialogue) and only a small smattering of assessment (the quiz). I think invoking the names of educational philosophies in this forum is interesting insofar as we connect them to our habits as teachers. Maybe we can create a really good glossary filled with educational theorists, so that invoking their names brings up brief descriptions of their theories and practices. Only then (I think) will the community fully benefit from the individual wisdom that its participants bring to the table. -Tom
