ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: Suggestion of 3 different ways of using Moodle: Lets imagine that there is a City with 5 different villages around. The name of the villages could be village1, village2 etc. Some people living in this area want to take part in a one year training program in the subject A. And then lets look into tree ways of using Moodle for organizing a one year training program in subject A. Alternative A. Moodle as a tool for organizing planning and logging ordinary classroom training based on "Social constructivist theories". Alternative A. All students will have to move into the City to live there for a period of one year, while taking part in the training program. The training program is built up around a series of projects and training tasks. The students are working together in groups, communicating with each other and with teachers. When required and as necessary it is also arranged more traditional learning sessions when the students are not able to solve theoretical problems completely on their own. Such blackboard lessons will normally come up as ordered by the students. The use of Moodle will be to make the planning, to make the activity logging and to contain a library of e-books and other necessary information. There will be a discussion group or two, but these will be very little used because the students and the teachers normally will see each other practically every day. Almost none of the functions of Moodle that is related to interactive functions like discussion groups are in use because they are not required. Alternative B. Moodle as a tool for organizing, planning and making communication between "distributed classroom environments". The students dont move in to City. It is organized local classes in each village and all activities are organized from "the school" in "the city". The task of Moodle will be to perform course organization, activity logging, and to maintain communication as required between village study circles and between village study circles and "the school". In this case many of the more interactive parts of Moodle like discussion groups could be rather important. Alternative C. Moodle as a tool for organizing, planning and making communication between school and students in their home. The students dont move in to City. They perform all the training from their home and via internet. The task of Moodle will then be to perform course organization, activity logging, and to maintain all communication as required between students and between students and the teacher. In such a training environment Moodle will have to replace all of the primary communication means related to social constructivism as mentioned under alternative A.And now the interesting question which alternative A, B or C will fit best with the theories of "Social Constructivism" ? I think it is rather obvious that this will be alternative A, that alternative that make the less use of Moodles "social constructivism inspired functions" is that alternative that has the strongest relations to "social constructivism". Or said with some other words "communication via net can not replace and it is not better than real communications between real humans", if those two are the alternatives. On the other hand if the alternatives are "social constructivism alike communications via Moodle" and no communication at all, then Moodle can be a great tool for connecting people and ideas. I think alternative B is a rather interesting one. In alternative B, some kind of distributed classroom structures, I believe you could combine some of the best sides of both type of learning environment. You could be able to communicate and work together with real human beings, and still you will be able to learn over distance and connected to the learning environment in "the City". One other interesting side of alternative B is that the village will not have to be located 50 km away. If the other village should be 50.000 km away, one place on the other side of this planet, the situation should still be much the same. By the way why not build "world wide classes", that could mean to make "Moodle classes" consisting of a group of ordinary school classes, studying related subjects. In this way students and teachers could be a part of their ordinary group. In the same time they could also be a part of a world wide network of classes cooperating via Moodle. You might be working on a problem you can not solve, you only leave it to your classmates in Argentina or some other places in the world and vise versa. I think I can see at least a possible use of the "social course format". Lets hope that Dimitris that opened the question will look in one day .. Once more thanks for all the interesting comments ! Arne.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: Arne, For me the gold is in your phrase "maintain communication." If communicating is simply checking up on due dates, directions, assignments, etc., give me any old LMS and any old non-sc inspired function. Hey, give me a teacher-centered blog with comments... But if communicating means depending on the group to ask these questions of each other or to rate my post against whether I read the previous post carefully enough , then I'm going to want a tool with plenty of pedagogical reminders and functions. The pieces of Moodle that I've been harping on are the ones that don't let the learner forget that she is learning -- and that what she is learning (and how) is important to the educational health and wealth of the rest of the class. That's why I don't think Blackboard or WebCT are interested in student-built glossaries. Goodness, that Moodle thinks the student is almost as important as the teacher! I think I'm preaching to the choir ( ), but I liked your village metaphor. In fact, I've been using Moodle as an enhancement to regular classroom teaching. But I have held a magnifying glass to the work that goes on in the Moodle component. Teaching a student to write and think well is like preparing him for Alternative C -- he can't depend on knowing and seeing me (Alternative A) to get his point across. The words he sends to Moodle matter. SC would call the posts a kind of shared artifact. When the student sees that the village depends on (measures / honors) his words, his message becomes amazingly clearer. best, Tom

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: "For me the gold is in your phrase "maintain communication." Yes.. Arne stresses the effect of physical distance between you and the rest of the class. But it can also be psychological distance: As soon as you let students also work on their own in groups bigger then 25 and in rooms bigger then a classroom (= "study-landscapes") you have three new needs: How can I maintain the communication between me and my class BUT ALSO between the students. How can I as a teacher monitor what all these students are doing, so I can help who gots stuck How can I visualise for these students what they can choose/change to get good results in the long run and how far they are now "on this track of their choice". When we canceled 80% of the classroom-meetings at our local University (Faculty of educational technologies), some teachers said that they were glad to get rid of these "last rows" in the lectureroom with all these students talking about all kind of things except the lesson .. Then we said: "Look out! Yes they are talking about other things, but they also check if the other students started already to study for their exam. They ask their peer on the left, they ask their friend on the right and then decide to start also... tomorrow. If you loose this classroom, you loose also this external motivation effect, ending up with students getting far behind... (A big problem in personal paced distance learning..) Moodle compensates for this "information-from-the-last-row-loss" with the "show the activity in this course" That is one of the little things I like in Moodle. Martin (with his experience) forsees these future needs in us.. So the gold of Moodle is not in the first place in the comparison with other tools, but in what it has to offer EXTRA FOR NEW WAYS OF LEARNING SETTINGS (SC?)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Educational method philosophy documentation
ResponsesInList.Text: First of all thanks once more for a lot of interesting comments ! Actually I have tried all the tree basic ways of using learning management systems, as mentioned above, more or less, using two different kind of commercial learning management systems. I have tried to use method A and B mentioned above for a period of approx 4 years. The last two years I have been a part time student in a two years education program "information and communication system technology for teachers" in that is a part of the educational program of Stavanger University College. In this educational program we are basicly using a "computer and internet only" approach. On the other hand in my daily work and organizing of teaching for young people (18 years approx, some older) I try to use the alternative A approach. The commercial learning management system we are using for our study is from a Norwegian company it:solutions . The product is called "its-learning". For my lessons and for my students I just changed over to Moodle. I think the basic functionality of "Moodle" and for "its-learning" is quite much the same. I think the way both systems are made with "social constructivism" as a basic theory for development. As least the functions for communicating via the learning management system are pretty much the same. The design (visual design) of the commercial system looks a little bit "more developed" than the design Moodle I think On the other hand Moodle does support one basic function, that the commercial system strange enough, does not support in a direct way - a planning function. What ever kind of education or training program you are making, you will need some kind of planning. You will also need some kind of recording to keep a track of the things that really did happen. I think these "functions" are quite well covered in by the Moodle course "weekly format". Our commercial learning management system does not support neither planning or events recording directly. (Of course you could include a plan made in Word or Excel or something like that.) I actually think, as a more personal point of view that "the old" principles of "system analysis" for administrative software systems also can be used as a basic design principle for learning systems as well. A "learning system" could also be considered to be a complete learning environment consisting of information and technology related elements, and then non technical elements, as well. Like any "system" the "learning system" (if considered as that) can be divided into subsystems and "functions" and it is also possible to speak about "data flows" and tasks that should be maintained by the whole and complete "system". What "functions", which "tasks" and which "data flows" that is designed to be maintained within the "technical part" of the system and which similar "functions" that will be maintained by "non technical parts" of the whole "learning system", that wold be another discussion. If you want to educate a dentist or a house electrician I guess it would be possible to put all of the theoretical information into Moodle or some other learning management system. But you will not be able to repair peoples teeth or to make electrical installation in a house by reading on a PC monitor or by doing a number of quizzes via Moodle. If you want to be an electrician, a dentist or if you want to learn to speak Chinese it will not be enough to get the "social constructivist part" or the "constructive part" of your education via a PC, what ever that is inside or outside that PC. In this way, I believe that a learning management system like Moodle can be used in a lot of different ways depending on "the design" of the learning situation or the "learning system" as a whole. Like any use of technology I believe that learning management systems can be used for the better and for the worse. If politicians start saying something like: Let's not use so much money for education, let us rather close down those regular classes and let the young people rather learn alone by themselves and via Internet, I think this could be a development with a lot of negative consequences. (Actually we have started to hear this argumentation already.) If on the other hand learning management systems like Moodle are used for organizing and improving more traditional and more real social learning situations, the perspective might be a bit bether. So when you will prefer to use "real social constructivism" as a design for the learning situation or "virtual social constructivism" or to combine those two principles this will depend a bit of the design of the learning environment or "the learning system" as a whole. As I will see it the real strength of Moodle is that it is not dependent of one certain use or one kind of "educational philosophy". As it is designed Moodle can actually support or organize almost any kind of learning concepts. I think that the capability to organize and support more traditional classes where the main element of "social constructivism" is placed in the class and not via Moodle, is a rather good use of Moodle. Because of this I would believe it is more important to keep a central focus on the "basic educational functions" like planning and activity logging and organizing of material in pdf, sound and video format, rather than developing a lot of interactive tools for "computer only" teaching. After two years of being a student of a web based learning program, I would say something like: Yes this learning system ("it's learning" from it:solutions) is based on or developed from the theories of "social constructivism" but the functions and the functionality that can be carried out from such a web based system is not those that could be part of a "real social constructivism" oriented learning environment. (Communications via machines can not replace and, will not normally be better than the real communication between real persons.) "Virtual social constructivism" or possibly only "virtual constructivism" would possibly be a better word, I think. On the other hand, I think learning management systems like Moodle, can be used to improve the quality of more traditional learning environments and learning situations, based on "real social constructivism". Also the "virtual social constructivist aspect" of Moodle can be used for connecting groups and persons in different countries and at different places where the alternative would have been "no communication at all".

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Social Constructivism, Vygotsky, Piaget, Freire and Gardner.
ResponsesInList.Text: Arne, I really enjoyed reading your post. As your post indicates a lot of the themes of sociocultural theories overlap. My own research based on Vygotsky and Leontev's Activity Theory, directly aligns with the Constructionist theory which, according to Martin Dougiamas, was the theoretcal framework informing the development of moodle. What distinguishes these theories from cognitive theories is the belief that 'knowledge' is not seen as an object that can be passed from one person to another, rather understanding and meaning are constructed by learners through their interactions with others, while actively engaging in learning tasks. Learning does not take place within a vacuum, rather it is a process integrated within a social context . Knowlege is negotiated and constructed through a dialogical process. The real jewel of the moodle LMS is that it centres on learning activities rather than objective content . There is great support for social interaction and dialogue around learning materials. Moodle was built as a learning management or virtual learning system informed by social constructionist theories. Certainly, this theoretical framework is directed at how we learn in general, not particularly within computer mediated environments. In fact, no learning or communication media have ever shown significant improvements in learning outcomes. It's how these tools are used in teaching and learning situations where instructional benefits will accrue.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Social Constructivism, Vygotsky, Piaget, Freire and Gardner.
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks a lot David, for a very interesting comment ! My personal point of view is that "social constructivism" is not really dependent of the use of computers. My personal point of view is also that "sosial constructivism" vere not really "invented" by Lev Vygotsky or any other certain person. Actually I think the "social constructivism" vere a major didactic method already in the stone age. "centre on learning activities rather than objective content ." For sure they did not learn how to hunt the wild animals using overhead projectors. I use now use Moodle as a "tecnical part" of my lessons in secondary school (18 year old students). We also have an commersial LMS system that we can use as well. The "killer function" of the Moodle program, that the commersial LMS, strange enough do not have, is a system for planning and to make a log of the lessons and the projects that has been done. Very easy that can be done just using the Week format of Moodle to make the plan and then revice into the plan what really did happen as time and events pass by. As I am using the Moodle program at the moment I am mainly using it for the organization of ordinary lessons and projects that the studentas are working on. Also we use it for storing and organizing different kind of "key information" that the students are using for or in their projects. Actually we are using very few functions, but those few functions apear to be very helpfull and very useful. Even though we had tried use a commersial LMS for approx a half year first without much success, the students adaptet and started to use Moodle on regularly basis after just one week. So now "everybody" agree in that Moodle is something neccessary that we just have to use. My pont of view is that Moodle is designed in such a way that is very well suited to support the "social constructivism" as a way of teaching also when the "computer part" of the training is not the major media for training, but just one media of training among a other medias and means, like ordinary books, laboratory equipment, project works and so on. By the way, the commersial LMS has one rather usable function that the Moodle don't have (I think). When somebody issue som new content in one of your courses, you will imediately see a remark on a status panel. So you just click on that remark and then you can se the new content. In this way you do not have to send around or receive a lot of e-mails and you do not have to look around on different places to see the new content either. On the other hand, the planning and logging posibilities of Moodle makes Moodle to the best alternative for us. If it had something like a sentral status panel that could show something like "5 new messages in your cources" and then direct clickable access to those 5 messages, it would also had adopted the best part of our commersial LMS, as well.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Assessment by 'competency'
ResponsesInList.Text: Joyce, I'm new at Moodle, so if my answer somehow doesn't match the question, sorry! What "competency" are you trying to assess? My understanding is that in order to assess, you need the outcome you're looking for (what students know or are able to do as a result of the learning activity), the assessment method (observation, document, test, etc.), and the indicators of different levels of competence. Here's an example of a very simple rubric I'm trying out for assessment of the outcome "Students use learning strategies to complete assignments." I've reduced it to a single indicator for my course, but it still has 3 levels rather than 2: Indicators Minimal Developing Proficient Assignments are on time and meet instructor specifications Fewer than 50% of assignments meet instructor specifications and are turned in on time 50-80% of assignments meet instructor specifications and are turned in on time More than 80% of assignments meet instructor specifications and are turned in on time Does that help? Eileen

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Adding a comment or translation to single words in a PHP document
ResponsesInList.Text: For security, scripts (eg javascript) are stripped from forum messages and other places where students can write text. The reason is to stop cross-site scripting hacks that a student could use to gain, say, the admin password. The usual method for these XSS attacks is to attach scripts to Javascript triggers. The same limitations are applied to Moodle "Plain text" resources, but not to "HTML" resources (ie choose HTML from the menu when creating a resource) or to uploaded resources. So if you want to use scripting you need to use one of these last two methods. A useful little trick that works on most browsers (and in the forums!) is to attach a TITLE attribute to tags which makes a tooltip appear eg http://www.javascriptkit.com/howto/toolmsg.shtml (Hint: hover your mouse over the link and the word TITLE in the last paragraph)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Adding a comment or translation to single words in a PHP document
ResponsesInList.Text: XSS attacks have to be specially crafted for each case, eg when triggered by a user they might steal the session cookie from the environment and then pass it on to another site which is ready to collect it. Then the cracker would use that session cookie to assume the current session and thus get into the original site as that original user. So, yes, I suppose in theory all uploaded pages should be checked for possible bad scripts but in practice it's very unlikely to be a problem - the page itself would have to have been made by a malicious person who was a skilled programmer and knew the eventual context of the page.

ResponsesInList.Title: Getting students up to speed with Moodle
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm curious to hear what strategies and tactics folks are using to help their students use Moodle. Here are a couple of odds and ends I've found helpful (teaching in a college setting, using Moodle to support face-to-face classes): Make creating a user account and enrolling in the course (I use enrollment keys for security) the homework assignment for day 1 one of the class.  The idea is to establish from the very beginning that using Moodle for discussions, readings, and homework is going to be integral to the course. Require students to upload a picture to go along with their profile.  I find this a great way to help me learn student names in the class, and also because it seems to make online discussions more personal and social.  If students don't have a digital picture of thesmelves, I offer to scan a regular photograph of their choice or I just take a quick picture of them with my cell phone (has a camera built in) and send it to them.  (As an interesting alternative to this, one group of students that I'm hosting on Moodle, who are using it as a sort of groupware app for their teamwork and all have instructor access to their "class", used pictures of their favorite movie stars in their profiles as a kind of icebreaking exercise to get to know other group members.) During the first week or so of the class, give a homework assignment of submitting a paper (assignment) online.  The "paper" just needs to be a single sentance--"this is a test paper"--but that way I get to troubleshoot any students having problems with the interface before a significant assignment comes due. "Participation" is a grade in most of my courses, and I've told students that online discussion forums count toward that, just as much as speaking up in class does. John

ResponsesInList.Title: Student Work Journal: Could Use Some Advice

And they spend a lot of time working at their computers offline, of course: creating graphics, editing video, learning to use Flash, etc. Literally one half of the grade they earn for me comes not from any product that they generate, but rather from doing the above. Just "doing" valuable "tech stuff." I do not let them simply float about the WWW, but I also try very hard not to tell them what they must be doing every minute. We are almost never all doing the same thing at the same time: one student is investigating how to write for the WWW, while another is looking into how to use Photoshop, while another is learning how to best embed streaming video into a web page. I think you get it. (I know some people will have a problem with this sort of chaotic approach to classroom management, but I think it works quite well for us.) NOW, A QUESTION: Since this "participation component" is so important, I really want to (and have to, I suppose) keep track of what these seventeen kids are doing at their computers. So... Could they not in the last few minutes of each class post to a Moodle forum a brief description of what they have done in class and upload their history page from the browser for that day? ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Year N to N+1
ResponsesInList.Text: One of the important things that hasn't been implemented yet is a really easy way to "empty" courses of user data. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Year N to N+1

ResponsesInList.Title: International Language Project

My counterpart and I simply guide the students, prompting them to expand on their posts, to ask good questions, to think about the topics, etc. The students seem to like it and they get a lot of practice using the language. If you teach a language, you might want to try a little project like this one.

ResponsesInList.Title: Students Create Flash Resources
ResponsesInList.Text: This is not terribly sophisticated, but some may find it useful: 1. You create a forum in which you list vocabulary items related to a topic you're teaching. I teach German, so I could provide a list of words that can describe people, for example (nett = nice, freundlich = friendly, gemein = mean, laut = loud, and so on). 2. Have students go to http://www.spellmaster.com/ , where they may create simple, interactive vocabulary practice activities in Flash. 3. Students then upload their Flash activities to the forum, so that other students may access them. 4. Students may provide feedback in the forum about the activities. Of course, there are other modules that you might prefer to use for this. I just really like the forum module. At any rate, it's a fast, free, easy way for students to become content creators and for everyone to practice vocabulary.

ResponsesInList.Text: Someone explain the relationship between "Scales" and "Grades" if any?  And what is the difference between "Custom Scales" and "Standard" ? Thanks for any assistance, Ken Crabb

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Scales and Grades (Quiz Scores)
ResponsesInList.Text: If you mean the teacher's administration links, "Grades" is the gradebook which lists all grades of your students, while "Scales" allows you to create your own grading scales to be used in that gradebook. "Standard Scales" are server -wide, i.e. they are created by the site admin and applied to all courses. "Custom Scales" can be created by an individual teacher and they will only be applied in his/her course.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Question about making teacher announcement.
ResponsesInList.Text: Laura, Everything in Moodle is possible. ;) For specific courses, have the teacher edit (update) the course news forum, and then choose the "force subscribe" option from the pull-down menu. Everything posted in that forum will be sent to everyone. You might want to make it so that students cannot reply to a news item. In the course settings, you can also choose to have course news items appear in a window (you can even choose how many past items to automatically show). If you don't want to "force subscribe" students, you can at least encourage them to check that window frequently. 2. If you turn editing on from the main page (the admin might need to do this), you can create a news forum that appears like moodle.org. Depending on how you want to use it, the forum could be "force subscribed" to all users, but this might be overkill. -Tom

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New backup and restore feature
ResponsesInList.Text: To backup or restore courses you can select when to include "user data" in every module in the course. Also you can select when to include users or no, so: - Do a backup (with user data or without it). - Download , archive or whatever you want to do with the file. - Select "restore" in the FileManager (near "rename" and other options). - Select "without user data" in every module and "none" in "Restore Users". - Finish the restore process. - Now you should have a new course without user data at all. Backup individual course modules (individual activities ) is not supported in this version, although it can be done in two steps: - Create a backup of a course, containing only info from the module where your activity is in. - Restore that backup to a new course.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New backup and restore feature

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Ideas for demoing Moodle for faculty?
ResponsesInList.Text: Taking a page from the demo courses, what I did was create my own demo page for the faculty I was introducing Moodle to.  It was similar to the Moodle demo pages insofar as I tried to give examples of most of the features/options.  But I think making the pages a bit like mock ups of actual courses offered in the department helped. The university I teach at (adjunct) uses WebCT and the IT department has a regular series of workshops on it for faculty.  But despite that, I've gotten a slew of folks to switch over to Moodle.  It's probably because of what the unviersity does wrong in their training program: it's passive, requiring faculty to come to the IT department ot learning about it or how to use it ... getting faculty to use a new online resource involves a bit of evangelical nudging it's rigid -- faculty who want to take workshops all must start out in the most basic workshop and work there way up.  This quickly alienated folks who were bored stiff by and abandoned the webct 101 stuff--the very early adopters they needed. it's curriculum centered instead of learner centered.  I got the distinct impression that they could have a class of two people, with very specific learning interests, and they'd still plow through the same material. There's also the big one... Moodle is just friendlier.  The first time I ran Moodle I switched from WebCT mid semester, which you'd think would irk students to no end.  Nope.  They found it easier to use, despite the fact that many of them had prior experience using webct in other courses.  The same is true of faculty who have used Moodle. The good word of mouth has led other faculty to try Moodle because students have asked for it and they hear other profs complimenting it. And so I've been running a kind of wayward home for faculty who don't want to use WebCT.  This semester it's also expanding to faculty at a nearby university who are escaping their campus use of Blackboard. John

ResponsesInList.Text: Sorry if this is the wrong forum for this... My wife and I teach German I through German V at Aiken High School in Aiken, South Carolina, USA. Our students and we have been using Moodle for a little over a year. We are enthusiastic, active Moodlers. We were wondering if there were any other teachers of German as a second language out there who might want to build a little Moodle course with us. This course would most likely take the place of a traditional e-mail relationaship and would take advantage of some of Moodle's magical powers (forums, chat, collaboration, etc., in a safe, protected environment). Our main goal would simply be to provide an interesting, low-stress opportunity to use the language in an authentic way. Why not do this with native-speakers of German? Well, we have found that the disparities in language experience and ability are just too great and that our students become frustrated that their limited ability to communicate in German cannot compare with the German/Austrian/Swiss students' usually very advanced ability to communicate in English. Frankly, this makes them feel stupid. Obviously not the result we want. We are not looking for a huge project - just a little pilot program. ResponsesInList.Title: Do you save your instruction time via Moodle? (Experiment)
ResponsesInList.Text: Dear instructors: We are working on a project called: Saving Instructor Time Investment by Using Web-based Learner Support Tools. We found Moodle is a promising tool for us to experiment with and we would like to participants who are interested in testing its efficiency of their instruction. Following is the general description of our experiment setting, you are more than welcome show us your interest in participating in this experiment as well as discuss/suggest your ideas about the experimental setting. Goal : The goal of this project is to find out whether web-based learner support tools can save instructors time and make learning more efficient. Here we want to focus on the tools that provide peer-feedback (Moodle: peer graded assignment). Experiment : What we would like you to do with our experiment is to assign two groups of your students - one is an experimental group using Moodle, another one is a control group with instruction in your original way. We will need you to record your time for each instructional activity with an easy to fill-in form, and share your feelings of using this tool with us. We prefer a subject that is objective, easy to perform a test so that the result will be comparable. For example topics in science will do fine. As for installation, we will run the server as administrator and give you full access to Moodle to deliver your course and help you to tackle technical problems if you need that. Time frames: The experiment will take about 1 month. We estimate to take you a few hours of your extra time in this month. This includes: 1 hour for filling in time investment forms, and 2 hours to setup a peer-feedback assignment. Result: Our experiment will be an authentic case study of your instruction. The result of this experiment will help you to evaluate your efficiency of using Moodle. For Instructors who never use Moodle : You are very welcome to participate in our experiment, too. We will help you to use Moodle and tackle the technical problem. The result of this experiment will help you to evaluate whether you would like to use it or not. We hope to give you a brand-new web-based instructional experience and benefit from our experiment for your further instruction. Best regards, Dr. Koos Winnips Msc. Student Laura Lin University of Twente Faculty of Behavioural Sciences The Netherlands .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How do I set up a quiz?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Dianna, I just set up some quizzes and it took me a half hour of trial and error to figure out how to do it. The steps are not intuitive but since the quiz module is new, I am sure it will be cleaned up soon. Here is how... 1. After logging in as an administrator and entering your course that you are a teacher for, click the "turn editing on". 2. At the place you want to add the quiz (in my case, Week 5), click add Quiz. 3. Fill out the first screen of information for your quiz. Click "continue" and move to the second screen. 4. On the second screen you can create questions but there is no button saying "create questions". You must go to Category and change the value to "Default" and click "Show". Then you will see a new screen of question options and fields to fill in. 5. After creating questions, you have to "add" those questions to the quiz. 6. After adding questions, save the whole quiz. There are more details, but the above information should save you some time of fooling around. Don Hinkelman

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: integrating curriculum maps
ResponsesInList.Text: It sounds like an interesting approach, unfortunately I can't extract much information from those pages on how one would apply them in a real class! Can you tell us more about them? How have they been applied already at your school?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: integrating curriculum maps
ResponsesInList.Text: In a nutshell, curriculum mapping is a post-mortem journal of what was explored in a class month by month. Often, schools break the journal into categories: skills/content/assessments/resources/and essential questions. Schools that map are tossing out skill ladders and treatises that say "Johnny will do this by this date" and instead looking, month by month, when Johnny is introduced to ideas and when those ideas are followed up in the curriculum. All school meetings, in a mapping world, turn into map discussions: today we look at health curriculum in all of the maps cross-discipline; tomorrow we watch how and where revision skills are taught... Rather than putting teachers into lock-step, reading across maps makes certain that teachers can formulate good decisions about how to approach material. The review of the maps (using the various target criteria) lets good ideas radiate out and bad ones wither on the vine. This was my first year including an on-line component to my course...what I'm finding is that seeing the activities broken down into weeks is already a step towards mapping. Because mappers are motivated into articulating the essential questions for each activity, I want to make my maps more transparent and show the kids the questions that can start and perhaps guide our discussion (skill and content). ("How is the civil war still going on in the United States?"; "What do we learn about the success or lack of success of revenge in Homer's story?"; "Why might some element of a text yield richer material than another?"; "In Hamlet what do the dead have to say to the living?"; "When is it the time to act and when is it the time to think?"; "What strategies are available to those who grieve?", etc..) So I'm just trying to rearrange the furniture and find places to stick all of this information without allowing it to become overwhelming. Maybe I'll create maps for each unit (month, section), in a resource link, and then link to the resource from the "heading" of the topic-view of the course list.

ResponsesInList.Title: "Accidental" enrollment
ResponsesInList.Text: It seems like some of our students keeps accidentally enrolling in classes they are not actually in. This is what happens: The first time they access the system, they fill in the "New Account" form to enroll in their class. Later students often browse around in moodle, looking at the other classes. By doing this, they are (unknowingly) added by moodle as a participant in any new class they enter. This is confusing to the student, as they begin to receive Forum messages from the new class, etc. One way to prevent this kind of confusion would be to have a confirmation popping up before the student is enrolled in the new class, asking "Are you sure you want to enroll in name_of_class?" Has anyone else experienced this situation?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Reading List Course Format
ResponsesInList.Text: I think the topic format as it is would be very well suited for this - each 'topic' covers one or more readings, with associated forums, journals, assignments etc. There is a specific type of forum that might be useful - the "each person posts one discussion" forum, in which, funnily enough, each person starts one discussion. Your intro could specify that each person write a review of the reading to start a thread, and ask them to reply to several other discussions. Think of some focus questions as specific activities (eg "relate the reading to your own professional practice").

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Reading List Course Format
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes... I can see how that would work for a class of people all reading the same thing. But what if you wanted to customize reading lists for each person? I understand you could use a separate topic-based course for each individual, but then you'd lose the sense of a community of readers. I realize the flip-side of this is that if nobody read anything the same or overlapping, they'd probably not have too much to talk about! But there still seems to be some sort of middle ground. Particularly among audo-didacts, you find people designing their own courses for self-study, but then they want a forum or community of like-minded folks to discuss with. Maybe moodle simply wouldn't be the appropriate way to go in that situation... Tracy

ResponsesInList.Title: Customizing for individual students
ResponsesInList.Text: Or... thinking about it a little differently, what if you simply wanted to customize readings for students to bring in different perspectives? Or because you have a mixed class with different competency levels? You'd like to coordinate their work to some degree (they're still in the same course), but you need the flexibility to work with individual students on more of a one-to-one basis. Seminars and research-type courses might be another example of needing to customize and work with students individually. Just thoughts as I puzzle through. Tracy

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Customizing for individual students
ResponsesInList.Text: You bring in a good point: I was thinking of using the logbook for this purpose, but how to integrate the results there a little bit more automatatic...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Customizing for individual students
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, Just out of interest, I was wondering where the logbook is? Is it in a particular version of Moodle or is it something in the future? I would like to find out how to manually insert grades for students coming from another system (other than moodle)?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Customizing for individual students
ResponsesInList.Text: I think you do need to have at least some content commonality to encourage interaction. If students are VERY different you might consider running different classes. Something I've done in a course before is to have a core set of readings planned up front, but also to: a) modify later topics acording to how things went with the group in the earlier topics. b) have a set of optional readings stored in the last topic, and refer to these as needed to individual students from within the journal feedback.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Reading List Course Format
ResponsesInList.Text: Can you create a forum called "READING LIST" where you add a long list of topics which are simply the designated book titles? This way participants can respond (yes I read this, or a full-blown discussion) to the appropriate texts and you can do some easy analysis in the activity report as to whether individuals have been active in the reading list forum. You could also create a "porfolio" forum for each student (designated by student name) where she creates discussions ( blog -like) describing what she has been investigating. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: basic question add teacher
ResponsesInList.Text: Only Administrators can assign Teacher rights.  If you are logged-in as an Administrator, choose(click) 'Assign Teachers' from the Administration options (should appear in the relevant box to the bottom left of the Moodle front page ).  Choose the relevant course from the list and then select from the list of potential teachers which appears next.  Potential teachers must have already registered on your Moodle or they wont appear on the list.  To add the relevant person to the list of active teachers on that course, just click the little left arrow next to their name in the list and it will move from the 'Potential Teachers' list to the 'Existing Teachers' list.  Presto!  You have now added a teacher to a class. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: importing Quizes in text format
ResponsesInList.Text: No, not with the "missing word" format, unfortunately. That format was the result of a very specific request from someone who had thousands of questions in that format already. I'm not sure if it will make sense to extend it to become Moodle's "native" format. As yet Moodle doesn't have a standard format that supports all question types - the import capabilities are very new and "missing word" is really an example of how to write a custom import module for a specific purpose. It would make sense to adopt an existing standard as the standard format, but though IMS QTI is the frontrunner for this I've heard it's a nightmare to actually work with.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: importing Quizes in text format
ResponsesInList.Text: Part of improving the quality of Moodle is also improving the quality of tests. (open assignments is another subject.) When I saw the first draft of QTI, I was thrilled: just draw in your favorite elo-tool a map, do some QTI-scripting and then ask the user to click with the mouse on the city they think it is the Capitol of... And then export this quiz to another system and still they can point with the mouse! But then realizing how much work it was to get it in the standard-QTI-format and asking your self how much better this "pointing with the mouse" was then just a map (with marks a,b,c and d) and asking in a M.C: "what is the Capitol.. a,b,c or d). On that moment I was healed from QTI for the next two years at least. Of course, when the whole world delivers test-sets in QTI-format it becomes interesting to have a QTI-importfilter, Until that day a simple structure format is my wish. Another point is that teachers are asking for other things then these boring m.c.'s.. "Why not play the Hotpotatoes-blues inside Moodle?" Students want to taste variation in their brain-meals, is then the motivation. I accept this for the phase where teachers want to invite students to work with the resourses and use tests for monitoring these activities , but not for grading. (So yes please create lots of variations like the missing word, or matching or.. and yes make the design as simple as possible: the missing word is brillant in it's simplicity.) Coming to grading: How good is the test YOU just created as grading-tool: How fair are your weights? Are the (Wrong) alternatives in a question not too misleading? How to callibrate all this, ending up with a  test with realibilty or even predicting power.... Everything you can describe as a set of m.c.-questions (like the missing word) can you even with "common sense" evaluate against the scores of your students, but how to check the quality of more complicated tests like a matching(words)-test? For me the test problem has these parts: Creating m.c.-questions the most easy way AND question by question online AND with file in like this nice Missing-word-format Then organise in a database -table with a webfront the grouping and weights of questions in tests. (I think this interface-part is very nice done in PHPtest: http://www.resynthesize.com/code/phptest_info.php also the possibilty to give students debrief-information inside each question ) Next point is the handling of the tests inside your Moodle (AND MAYBE ALSO in a kind of course-independent test-center) If you collect all the results of your students the next years then having a tool for question-analysis and test-callibrating against your own local population would be nice: must this become part of Moodle? Well, a simple histogram for the cumulative answers over the years for each each question would be nice, the same on test-level: the results of a test against other gradings inside a student cohort. ... But calibrating a test against studentsucces inside your local schoolsystem? I have no idea

ResponsesInList.Text: I think the original reasoning was that otherwise: - student does quiz - student reviews quiz on one window - student copies correct answers into second attempt - student learns nothing This was before random quizzes etc so I'm not sure how current that reasoning is.

ResponsesInList.Text: I think even with randomization it is still a good idea to (optionally) prevent students from reviewing a quiz before it has expired. However, there is a small inconsistency here. Even though the students are not able to review the quiz before expiration date, they still get *full* feedback once they submit the quiz. Therefore they: - do the quiz - keep the feedback window open - start a second attempt in a new window

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: why review of quizzes after expiration?
ResponsesInList.Text: depends of the function of the test: if it is a diagnose at the start of a module, then retry the test would be ok. The presence of a feedback-field for every question, for example with references to " (web?)-book-pages" would be nice..

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: why review of quizzes after expiration?
ResponsesInList.Text: I totally agree. That's why one of the settings I suggested for "allow review" is "immediately". If this is selected, students will be able to view the results and feedback the very moment they have submitted the quiz.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: why review of quizzes after expiration?
ResponsesInList.Text: >However, there is a small inconsistency here. Even >though the students are not able to review the quiz >before expiration date, they still get *full* >feedback once they submit the quiz. Therefore they: >- do the quiz >- keep the feedback window open >- start a second attempt in a new window >- copy answers >- learn nothing Surely that depends on the extent of the feedback? The quizzes we have implemented so far give feedback for each question. But it is feedback that encourages and directs the student to go and search for the information...sending them to a particular book perhaps, or suggesting a particular line of enquiry...they still have to find or work out the answer themselves. The results so far show that this works well...by looking at the scores there have been *very* few, if any, of the "First Attempt 10%, Second attempt two minutes later 100%" variety. People have been taking notice of the feedback and making more use of the research skills that they have been taught...in many cases the little nudge from the feedback was all they needed. Most of the students that have taken the quizzes have had three (or sometimes four) attempts, and the verbal feedback I have had from the students about this approach has been very positive.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: why review of quizzes after expiration?
ResponsesInList.Text: I agree with Sean here, but that is perhaps because I have been approaching the quizzes slightly differently than many here. I give one-week timed multiple attempt/show all quizzes as preview for each class and encourage the students to come to class with 100% marks. Most of them have been doing the quizzes three or four times during the preview week. I believe this is preparing them for the weekly lectures in the somewhat controlled environment of the Moodle quiz and not just a means of testing their ability to cheat. These quizzes are based on about 80% from the textbook, and about 20% which requires that students do some research on their own outside of the main text. Once a month I give them a one-shot/no feedback recreated quiz of the main points I expect them to have learned. I am also giving them two assignments during the 15-week course which are also one-shot written assignments, but with feedback provided in the form of personal comments and a grade. I plan to give final grades as follows: Weekly Preview Quizzes -- 20% Monthly Quizzes -- 30% Assignments -- 40% Attendance (or baked cookies) -- 10% We are about half way through the course so I'll have to see what the final outcome is, but I'm happy with their progress at the moment. I believe they have also been happy with the way things are running. Cheers, ptervin

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is this Weird or Stupid?
ResponsesInList.Text: It is reassuring to me that nobody jumped in with any reason why this is a bad idea. I have to admit, though, I am a little insecure about the best way to go about this. Say that we wanted to design a mini-course built around Erlkönig , a beautiful, sad poem by Goethe in which a man is riding through the forest with his young son. The son tells the father that the Erlkönig , the fairy king, is threatening him, the father does not believe the boy, and the boy dies in his arms. Normally, you would talk about plot, character, tone, etc. You would address vocabulary and grammar as needed. This has been done a million times and there are many Erlkönig lesson plans available on the 'Net for anyone who wants them. My question is this: How do I best take advantage of Moodle's strengths (collaboration and reflection, I think) in designing a new Erlkönig mini-course? For third-year German students, let's say. My initial thought is that one of our activities would be for students to collaborate in small groups on a German-language role-play between the father and the rest of the dead boy's family. In addition to writing the role-play together, they could comment on what they liked about each group's role-play and tell what they thought was not so great. And I wonder if students should not write a journal entry about how they felt when the boy died... (Sad, I hope!) Do you think that this is on target? Is this the way that you would do it? I very much appreciate your taking the time to let me know what you think. And your honest, "undiluted" responses will NOT hurt my feelings, I assure you! (I asked, right?)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is this Weird or Stupid?
ResponsesInList.Text: Back after having some Italian food at a local restaurant. OK - you want the students to reflect upon and develop their thinking about the deeper meaning of der Erlkönig . I would have two different discussion boards and possibly a "quiz" with whether the different questions asked by the students should make it into the second board or not. This has the benefit of making the students not only think of der Erlkönig but also focus on what might be relevant questions to ask. Discussion group one is where the students can formulate questions and discuss the questions being asked. Second is the quiz where the students should vote for whether a question will make it into the second discussion group or not. Third is a discussion group where only replies are possible and the questions from the quiz are posted together with some text that further develop the question. The above (seen as a preparation) can then be extended with your role-play in small groups. Hope the above is clear enough - otherwise I'll happily answer any questions you might have, Parts of the above concept have been tested within the "principals education" here in Göteborg with success but I tried to take it one step further. Cheers

ResponsesInList.Title: Learning Erlkönig
ResponsesInList.Text: Great discussion, good to see! From what I've read here so far I can see two different (but overlapping) situations emerging: a) the course in which teachers discuss how to set up a course for students b) the course for the students itself Gunther's suggestion is excellent - it shows an example of how the teacher can plan a sequence of activities designed to help the class learn collaboratively about specific things, without dictating the content in detail. I also agree with Art about involving everyone in setting goals and assessment. Moodle's pedagogical support is nowhere at the level I dream it could be (there's been so much operational stuff to get sorted out first) ... there will be much more soon, though - for example there might be a wizard to help you make decisions about how you will set learning goals, and perhaps a specific interface for managing goals. However, even now, you as facilitator can stay involved in the course discussions, and use Moodle to continually re-construct upcoming activities in response to the direction that you see things going within the course. Keywords here are fluid, changing, responsive, reactive. In an environment like this you can give the learners/participants a chance to shine and teach YOU things about this poem you may never have thought of. One idea is to develop a simple "starter" course, then invite your teaching colleagues to role-play as students, and help them to collaboratively redesign the thing from the inside. I realise I may have overdosed on philosophy a little lately, but does this make practical sense in your two situations, Art?

It's not like we only know one way to say "to murder" in German. It would only need to be a paragraph, and at this point no one should need the whole class period to respond to a question if it's broad enough. Having us write the sentences is also a good way for us to show what we know about writing German sentences. The vocabulary isn't going to do us much good if we can't form a sentence or thought with them. Hopefully everyone knows how to do that. It's not like the essays have to be strictly graded either, like 5 points off for not putting the correct ending on one of the adjectives. It could be more lenient since it is at the end of the test and be more like if you miss one adjective ending then that's ok but if you continually miss them then take a few points off. ResponsesInList.Text: It's been a long and busy day... Many of the posts focus on the form rather than seeing the quiz as another learning opportunity. This is a probably a worldwide disease among students, injected in them from early school years. It is very hard to give any advice but you did the right thing asking them clarifying questions. I don't know if the students knew your view on quizzes before this discussion. If not then that would probably have been valuable. Students tend to adjust to the expectations of the teacher. Cheers

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Learning Erlkönig
ResponsesInList.Text: Follow-up: I created choices based upon the student suggestions and the students voted on them. That went well. (But a couple of times when they voted, I could see their vote, but from the student view, it was as though their vote had not been added to the database . I watched them vote, and they did not seem to be doing anything wrong.) I was very pleased to see that one of my quietest students really asserted herself at one point. I did not know that she had such strong feelings about essay-writing and creativity! I obviously still need to learn a lot more about creating and administering this sort of learning activity, but I am sure that we will keep working at it in my classes. Thanks!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Is this Weird or Stupid?
ResponsesInList.Text: Try to NOT suggest a couple of topics as a starter. In fact, don't suggest any topics! Leave that to the students as much as possible right from the beginning. If you feel that the students come up with topics that aren't particularily good or they seem to have difficulties finding topics then you can moderate the topics discussion. Cheers

A few years ago, though, it would have been almost impossible for me to relinquish control like that, but I could do it now. A little older, a little wiser, I guess. Thanks!

ResponsesInList.Title: How do I move/copy a quiz to another course?
ResponsesInList.Text: I have set up quizzes in one course (one quiz per week) and would like to copy the quizzes to two other identical courses (different students using the same text). How do I do that? It appears I have to reenter all the data again. Thanks for any advice. Don Hinkelman Sapporo Gakuin University - English as a Foreign Language

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How do I move/copy a quiz to another course?
ResponsesInList.Text: Go into "Edit Categories" and you can then "Publish" your categories. You (or other teachers) will then be able to access that category (and the questions in it) from any other course (it appears in their category list). You will have to build the quiz itself again but at least you won't have to re-enter the questions.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How do I move/copy a quiz to another course?
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks! I got it. You get another speed record for problem-responding, too By the way, I agree with your earlier comments that forums and journals should be given priority over quizzes in education. In my field, ESL, we need to recycle a lot of information, such as vocabulary, as well as reflect and construct ideas. Quizzes are good for that as long as they aren't taken too seriously. In addition, I find that a well built quiz gives so much immediate feedback, students get excited and more enthusiastic for the topic and further communication.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: "whether or not educational technology is an independent discipline"
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks Gunther, Re: Teaching Online with Moodle and Low-end media, Most excellent article! Your articles and links are very informative and thought provoking. My son received a Playstation 3 years ago as a gift and I wasn't happy about it. One day I decided to just sit with him and watch him play to try and see what was so attractive about the exercise for him. It was the challenge of trying to figure it out and then win. I hadn't realized that there was so much reading and thinking involved in good videogames. I began to wonder how a kid could be in school all day and come home ready to be seriously challenged by a game. Was it because he wasn't being challenged at school? This quote from the article referred to in your post says what I've been trying to say in the low-end media thread: [ quote ] It has been observed that formal education systems are not keeping up with the new kinds of thinking that emerge as technology explodes. In a recent Wired magazine article, James Paul Gee asks How did videogames become such successful models of effective learning? Game coders aren't trained as cognitive scientists. It's a simple case of free-market economics: If a title doesn't teach players how to play it well, it won't sell well. Source: http://www.wired.com/wired/archive/11.05/view.html?pg=1 If Learning Science is to be a true integration of wisdom resources, there's a need for the incorporation of more than just existing academic/educational 'disciplines.' Technology is blossoming much faster than unified bodies of theory can characterize it. Some kinds of learning are happening without educational input. [ end quote ] I do hope that the article mentioned above and all of the related material on this subject is reaching the educators. I'm sure that many students today wonder why their teachers can't, or won't, find a way to connect with them in a more relevant way. I think their lessons need to be packaged and delivered in a way that makes them believe that we have some understanding of their new reality. Then, I hope, they will begin to believe that we care enough to teach them what we think is important. And teach them in a language they understand. Does that make any sense. I'll get to the other sites as time permits. john captain

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: "whether or not educational technology is an independent discipline"
ResponsesInList.Text: Our daughter also got her PS2 several years ago. It has been a rich learning tool. We play Dark Cloud and Final Fantasy X and Kingdom Hearts. She learns strategy as she moves to the goal. We collect information about the various parts of the game and enter them into databases and then use the information like an inventory management system to plan how we will level up weapons. We play civilization games and learn that if you don't feed your people, they die. She also looks up information about the Hanging Garden of Babylon or a trireme. How many of us played the Pokemon card game? Playing required reading skills and learning some complex rules before you could play. And the kids loved learning to play without thinking they may be learning skills they could use elsewhere. I find using games a great way to learn. And as you pointed out John, it teaches them in a language they understand.

ResponsesInList.Title: Easy formatting of material
ResponsesInList.Text: Maybe another one for the developer forum... Our big problem at the moment is how to allow non-technical users to edit course materials that will end up on line. We took the decision *not* to simply put up Microsoft Word documents onto a site, however we always receive material in Word format. What we have tried is manually converting the Word document to a custom XML format, and then processing it using XSLT to HTML and XSL-FO to a PDF file for printing. This helps the technical people, but the original writers don't want to edit an XML file when the inevitable changes happen. Of course this route leads to thoughts about the IMS content specifications, which I have not investigated as yet. I have been looking with much interest at TickiText http://www.mplode.com/tima/archives/000215.html , and am about to do a small trial using it. I had a brash idea about porting TikiText to PHP and incorporating it in Moodle, but I'm not sure if there is any point (as one can just preformat using TikiText and then load the resulting HTML). A bit of a ramble this... but does anybody out there have any thoughts or experiences in this area? It would be appreciated!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Easy formatting of material
ResponsesInList.Text: I would simply teach teachers how to save their office documents as HTML, then upload it themselves. For some it's much easier to just use the Richtext editor to edit their resources directly online (in the database ).

It will give you in Word a new choice: under files >> export to >> compact html. (see menu.gif) For the future : Moodle should create webforms with under the hood XML-structure..

ResponsesInList.Title: Low-end media...
ResponsesInList.Text: Interesting article about why "low-end media works better". It is probably applicable to virtual learning environments as well. http://www.useit.com/alertbox/20030421.html

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Low-end media...
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Gunther, It is an interesting article and Jakob Nielsen does have strong views and some knowledge of usability issues. Some agree with him always, some agree with him only sometimes. I think with the increased availability of broadband presentation options like the flash tutorial of Moodle become useful to a number of users. If this presentation is an option to those who have the ability to view it this must be viewed as a positive step forward. I think it would be a mistake if this was the only way that this introduction was available. Fortunately there are currently several tutorials being developed for Moodle most of which will be acceptable to traditional "dial-up" users. This presentation adds a little "Flash" for those who choose to view it. I see the flash presentation being used by the same group who would take the time to download large file sizes of all types anyway. I think this flash presentation would be great as part of a collection of introductory materials that would, for example, be on a CD-ROM that is mailed or delivered to someone interested in distance learning but who would never take the time to hang around the Moodle community long enough to understand the potential in this application. Suddenly this "high-end media" is valuable to anyone with a computer. I think sometimes Mr. Nielsen forgets that ARPA is now the WWW and technology is not always comprised of a 486 & 14.4 modem with a floppy drive to save the good stuff on. I have a fairly quick broadband connection but sometimes don't want, or need, the jazz that's used for no reason except to show off the skills of the web designer/builder. "Low-end media" is good and "high-end media" options are good, even for Jakob Nielsen. I personally NEVER use FLASH or high resolution graphics on entry points to my own sites as I do not want to discourage users from using them or returning to them. However making "high-end media" available and warning viewers that the file sizes are large gives them an option that they may, or may not, want. Catch 22 I think. No "high-end media" no need for broadband. No demand for broadband no point in building broadband networks. No widespread use of broadband we don't get to find out what the WWW could have become. I hope this doesn't sound like a rant and I'm sorry if it does. John

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Low-end media...
ResponsesInList.Text: I agree totally with the low-end media point of view. I teach design and HTML at the high school level. It is essentially a design issue. People don't realize that the web is just another method of publishing. The issues are just about the same as print when it comes to customer satisfaction. People appreciate clear concise communication. Most of us wouldn't consider publishing a monthly magazine. Just considering creating that amount of meaningful content makes me shiver. The result of having nothing to say is generally the urge to over-decorate the piece. *major euphemism*

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Low-end media...
ResponsesInList.Text: This is quite an interesting thread and article. I wonder about the validity of aiming at the low-end media side of online course delivery. I agree that there are some very valid reasons for doing so (as the article states, but after being involved with online course delivery for the last 7 / 8 years I have notice that a lot of what we present online is an electronic copy of the paper based type of course. I have read several articles and points of view that question why we should go the expense of presenting information / courses electronically if paper can do it as well and is already established. Granted that this is the comfort level for most learners but I think that we should be taking advantage of the capabilities of an electronic environment to deliver our course / information in a new way. That is one of the concepts of Moodle that excites me that most is that it allows us to take advantage of interaction over a distance and present a dynamic course. I think that Flash, Shockwave, synchronous and asynchronous interaction and a dynamic source of information (the Internet) are things we should take advantage of in our course design and delivery. Yes, there will be those that can't access that level of technology, but in the long run I think copying the traditional methods of delivering information won't allow us to establish online education as something to be sought after. And  technology will catch up, especially if there is a real demand for something better. I think that we are in a time of transition currently and while the article makes some very valid points that hold true for the present, I think we should look down that proverbial road and aim to make something better. In order to accomplish that, we need to allow ourselves the opportunity to learn how and to accept the mistakes that will be make along the way. Sorry about the ramble and I hope that I am on topic here, but ... my point of view.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Low-end media...
ResponsesInList.Text: Isn't the problem how we think about the medium rather than the medium itself and what can be accomplished with it? And if one wants to take advantage of the possibilities of e.g. Moodle, shouldn't it be with the focus on what content should be delivered rather than finding new ways of delivery? The content might of course lead us to deliver it in new ways if the medium permits it. Maybe the above is selfevident for teachers but here in Sweden there has been a lot of discussion about organisation, teacher work teams, IT in schools but almost nothing about what pupils and students are supposed to learn and why.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Low-end media...
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Gunther. I appreciate the points you make very much and I do agree that we should not use the medium just to use the medium. We should use the medium because it better serves student learning. The point I was making through was that if we are going to make use of this medium we should not use it as we would a paper medium. ICT is a different world we should not force the square peg of our old way of doing things into the round hole of a new approach, In a more philosophical vein, I think we should look at using technology and the ICT infrastructure in a completely new approach. Ursula Franklin from the University of Toronto - in her book - The Real World of Technology - talks about using technology redemptively. Currently technology use falls into two veins she says - Holistic - where we use technology to allow one of us to complete the whole task - and Prescriptively - where we are one part of an assembly line process and where technology dictates our one repetitive task. Redemptive technology takes the approach that we should use technology to focus on the needs of the individual or the society. In education, this translates into using technology to deliver an education catered to the learning needs of each individual student. Considering the power our technology has, it could allow us to conceivable manage the complexity of providing and Individual Education Plan for each of our students, based on their current point of learning and catered to the way they learn. I think that this would go a long way to make learning more relevant for everyone all the time. But, in order to realize this type of a learning environment we would have to retool most or all of our educational resources. Instead of writing courses, we would have to create a library of learning objects that cover all the learning outcomes at different levels of ability / reading, focusing on different learning styles, ... It is a huge change in our approach to learning and the infrastructure needed to support it. But  why cant we dream Sorry - that was a bit of a ramble. And I am getting of the topic of this thread. I agree whole-heartedly with you Gunther. Our efforts should focus on learners needs, not using technology just because we can.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Low-end media...
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Norbert, Interesting but I would like to problematise the concept of individualisation not because I disagree with you but rather to find out what you and others think about it (if the writing below is worth commenting). What is individualisation? Does individualisation make individuals socially capable individuals? Are the needs of the individual more important than the needs of a (small) group? What are the needs of the society, the private sector and the social environment where the student live. Does it sufficiently prepare the student for an "adult life"? In Japan teachers have an interesting idea about what circumstances are needed to be able to individualise (on-campus teaching). There shouldn't be fewer than 40 pupils in a class in order to be able to individualise! I always wondered how do they think and reason until I was told that only then it is possible for the teacher to create large enough groups so that no pupil would end up alone. Then they use "rich problems" (I'm referring to math) which pupils can work with for a week or more and starting at their own level of knowledge. The group as well as the teacher are there to support the individual (I don't know any more about the details unfortunately.). From a teachers' point of view individualisation presents some interesting challenges which also are applicable to the use of VLE's. 1. I must know my students enough as persons to be able to individualise. 2. I must know the knowledge level of each student. 3. I must know how well students are able to work together or at least if I'll be able to make the groups work with my support. 4. Choose problems which challenge less knowledgeable as well as more knowledgeable students. 5. What else? The idea of individualisation could be a terrible work trap for teachers if we don't define what we mean by it and also explain the consequences of implementing it. I'm afraid that it otherwise will degrade teaching to hand out (or deliver digitally) ready made fill out forms albeit "individualised". Quality of teaching will then be degraded to quantity of teaching and the pedagogics of choice will be "parrot pedagogics" ("repeat, please").
